{{Short description|American sound designer (born 1948)}} {{Use American English|date=July 2022}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2022}} {{Infobox person | name = Ben Burtt | image = Ben Burtt Celebration Europe II.jpg | caption = Burtt at ''Star Wars'' Celebration Europe II in Essen, Germany in 2013 | birth_name = Benjamin Burtt Jr. | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1948|7|12}} | birth_place = [[Jamesville, New York]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | death_cause = | othername = | education = [[Allegheny College]]
[[University of Southern California]] | occupation = {{Flatlist| * [[Sound design]]er * [[film director]] * [[film editing|film editor]] * [[screenwriter]] * [[voice acting|voice actor]] }} | years_active = 1975–present | spouse = | domesticpartner = | awards = {{Flatlist| * Doctor of Arts * Charles S. Swartz Award * Academy Award }} | website = | children = [[Benjamin A. Burtt]] }} '''Benjamin Burtt Jr.''' (born July 12, 1948) is an American [[sound design]]er, [[film director]], [[film editor]], [[screenwriter]], and [[voice acting|voice actor]]. As a sound designer, his credits include the ''[[Star Wars]]'' and ''[[Indiana Jones]]'' film series, ''[[Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978 film)|Invasion of the Body Snatchers]]'' (1978), ''[[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial]]'' (1982), ''[[WALL-E]]'' (2008), and ''[[Star Trek (2009 film)|Star Trek]]'' (2009). Burtt is notable for popularizing the [[Wilhelm scream]] in-joke and creating many of the iconic sound effects heard in the ''Star Wars'' [[Media franchise|film franchise]], including the 'voice' of [[R2-D2]], the [[lightsaber]] hum, the sound of the blaster guns, the heavy-breathing sound of [[Darth Vader]], and creating the Ewoks’ language, Ewokese. Burtt was also the sound editor for ''WALL-E'' and performed the vocalizations of the character of [[WALL-E (character)|WALL-E]] as well as other robots in the film. Burtt has won four [[Academy Awards]], two of which are [[Special Achievement Academy Award]]s. He has also directed numerous documentary films for [[IMAX]] and most notably the television series [[The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles|''Young Indiana Jones'']] on the episode "Attack of the Hawkmen." He also served as the editor on multiple episodes of the show and the [[Star Wars prequel trilogy|''Star Wars'' prequel trilogy]]. ==Early life== Burtt was born in [[Jamesville, New York]], on July 12, 1948.{{cite book |last1=McGee |first1=Marty |title=Encyclopedia of Motion Picture Sound |date=2001 |publisher=McFarland |location=Jefferson, N.C. |pages=[https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofmo0000mcge/page/52 52]-53 |isbn=9780786410231 |url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofmo0000mcge|url-access=registration }} The son of a chemistry professor at [[Syracuse University]] and a child psychologist, Burtt made films as a child, and later studied [[physics]] at [[Allegheny College]], Pennsylvania, graduating in 1970.{{cite book |last1=Cavin |first1=Andrew I. |editor1-last=Thompson |editor1-first=Clifford |title=Current Biography Yearbook 2003 |date=2003 |publisher=H.W. Wilson |location=New York |isbn=0824210263 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/currentbiography2003thom/page/47 47]-50 |url=https://archive.org/details/currentbiography2003thom |url-access=registration |chapter=Burtt, Ben}} ==Career== ===Early career=== Burtt made films during his time in college, and in 1970 won a National Student Film Festival for his [[war film]] entitled ''Yankee Squadron'', reputedly after following exposure to classic aviation drama.{{Citation needed|date=January 2012}} He had previously made an amateur film at the [[Old Rhinebeck Aerodrome]], a living aviation museum in [[Red Hook, New York|Red Hook]], New York, under guidance from its founder, [[Cole Palen]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2012}} For his work on the special-effects film ''Genesis'', Burtt won a scholarship to the [[University of Southern California]]'','' where he earned a [[master's degree]] in [[Filmmaking|film production]]. ===Sound designer=== Burtt pioneered many aspects of modern sound design, especially in the [[science fiction film|science-fiction]] and [[fantasy film|fantasy-film]] genres.Holman, Tomlinson. ''Sound for Film and Television''. New York: Focal Press, 2010, p. 145. Before his work in the first ''Star Wars'' (now known as ''Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope'') in 1977, science-fiction films tended to use electronic-sounding effects for futuristic devices. Burtt sought a more natural sound, blending in "found sounds" to create the effects. The [[lightsaber]] hum, for instance, was derived from a film projector idling combined with feedback from a broken television set, and the blaster effect started with the sound acquired from hitting a [[guy-wire]] on a [[Radio masts and towers|radio tower]] with a [[hammer]].{{cite web|url=http://filmsound.org/starwars/|title=Sound Design of Star Wars|access-date=March 9, 2014|archive-date=October 11, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181011015556/http://filmsound.org/starwars/|url-status=live}} In the ''Star Wars'' series, part of R2-D2's beeps and whistles are Burtt's vocalizations, also made using an [[ARP 2600]] [[synthesizer]], as are some of the squawks made by the tiny [[hologram|holographic]] monsters on the ''[[Millennium Falcon]]'' [[spacecraft]]. In ''[[Star Wars: Episode III – Revenge of the Sith]]'' (2005), Burtt's provided the voice for Lushros Dofine, captain of the ''[[List of Star Wars spacecraft#Invisible Hand (Providence-class carrier/destroyer)|Invisible Hand]]'' cruiser. The heavy breathing of Darth Vader was created by recording Burtt's own breathing in an old [[Dacor (scuba diving)|Dacor]] [[Diving regulator|scuba regulator]].{{citation needed|date=January 2023}} Burtt used the voice of an elderly lady that he had met in a photography shop for the voice of ''[[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial]]''. The woman's low pitch was the result of very heavy smoking, specifically Kool cigarettes. Burtt created the "voice" of the title character and many other robots in [[Pixar]]'s film ''[[WALL-E]]'' (2008), about a lonely garbage-compacting robot. Additionally, Burtt is responsible for the sound effects in ''[[Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull]]'' (2008).{{cite web|url=http://trekmovie.com/2009/01/05/star-trek-post-production-complete-oscar-winner-ben-burtt-provided-sound-design/|title=Star Trek Post Production Complete + Oscar-winner Ben Burtt Provided Sound Design|first=Anthony|last=Pascale|date=6 January 2009|work=trekmovie.com|access-date=4 January 2017|archive-date=15 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180615135149/https://trekmovie.com/2009/01/05/star-trek-post-production-complete-oscar-winner-ben-burtt-provided-sound-design/|url-status=live}} Burtt has a reputation for including a sound effect dubbed "the [[Wilhelm scream]]" in many of the movies he has worked on. Taken from a character named "Wilhelm" in the film ''[[The Charge at Feather River]]'', the sound can be heard in a large number of films, including in ''Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope'' when a [[Stormtrooper (Star Wars)|stormtrooper]] falls into a chasm and in ''Raiders of the Lost Ark'' when a [[Nazism|Nazi]] soldier falls off the back of a moving car.{{Cite web |last=Dudley |first=Joshua |date=2023-02-15 |title=Wilhelm Scream: The History of Film’s Most Popular Sound Effect |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/wilhelm-scream-explained-75982/ |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=Backstage |language=en}} One of Burtt's more subtle sound effects is the "audio black hole". In ''[[Star Wars: Episode II – Attack of the Clones|Attack of the Clones]]'', Burtt's use of the audio black hole involved the insertion of a short interval of absolute silence in the audio track, just prior to the detonation of "seismic charges" fired at the escaping Jedi spaceship. The effect of this short (less than one second) of silence is to accentuate the resulting explosion in the mind of the listener. Burtt has recalled the source of this idea as follows: "I think back to where that idea might have come to me...I remember in film school a talk I had with an old retired sound editor who said they used to leave a few frames of silence in the track just before a big explosion. In those days they would 'paint' out the optical sound with ink. Then I thought of the airlock entry sequence in ''[[2001: A Space Odyssey (film)|2001]]''. I guess the seeds were there for me to nourish when it came to the seismic charges." Burtt was among the [[golden ear]]s that critically reviewed the various [[data compression|audio compression]] systems that were proposed for the [[ATSC standards|ATSC 1.0]] [[digital television]] system. A tongue-in-cheek homage to Burtt appears in the 1997 [[Activision]] PC game ''[[Zork: Grand Inquisitor]]'' - the [[Magic (paranormal)|spell]] 'Beburtt', which 'creates the illusion of inclement weather', plays dramatic thunderclap and rainfall sounds when cast. ===Director, editor, and writer=== Burtt has directed several [[IMAX]] [[documentary film]]s, including ''[[Blue Planet (1990 film)|Blue Planet]]'', ''[[Destiny in Space]]'', and the [[Academy Awards|Oscar]]-nominated ''[[Special Effects: Anything Can Happen]]''.{{Cite web|url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/92/Ben-Burtt.html|title=Ben Burtt Biography|access-date=October 25, 2008|publisher=NetIndustries, LLC. |year=2008|author=filmreference.com| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080914095700/http://www.filmreference.com/film/92/Ben-Burtt.html| archive-date= 14 September 2008 | url-status= live}} He edited the entire ''Star Wars'' [[Star Wars#Prequel trilogy|prequel trilogy]], and several episodes of ''[[The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles]]''. Burtt also wrote several episodes of the 1980s ''Star Wars'' cartoon ''[[Star Wars: Droids|Droids]]''.{{cite web |last=Greene |first=Jamie |title=Everything you'd ever want to know about Star Wars: Droids |url=https://www.syfy.com/syfywire/everything-youd-ever-want-to-know-about-star-wars-droids |website=SyFy Wire |access-date=April 22, 2020 |date=January 18, 2018 |archive-date=January 20, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190120050018/https://www.syfy.com/syfywire/everything-youd-ever-want-to-know-about-star-wars-droids |url-status=live }} ===Cameo appearances=== Burtt makes a cameo appearance in two of the ''Star Wars'' films as an extra. In ''[[Return of the Jedi]]'', he appeared as Colonel Dyer, the Imperial officer who yells "Freeze!" before [[Han Solo]] knocks him off a balcony. The scream as Burtt falls is his own imitation of the [[Wilhelm scream]] that he popularized.{{Citation needed|date=November 2025}} In ''[[Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace|Episode I – The Phantom Menace]]'', Burtt appears in the background of the scene where Palpatine arrives on Naboo;{{cite AV media|title=Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace ''audio commentary''|medium=DVD |publisher=20th Century Fox Home Entertainment|year=2001|time=126}} his character is named Ebenn Q3 Baobab, a reference to a ''Droids'' character. ==Filmography== ===Film=== {| class="wikitable sortable plainrowheaders" ! width="15%" rowspan="2" scope="col" | Title !! width="4%" rowspan="2" scope="col" | Year!! colspan="5" scope="col" | Credited as !! width="10%" rowspan="2" scope="col" class="unsortable"| Notes |- ! width=6% |Director ! width=6% |Writer!! width=6% | Editor!! width=6% |Sound designer!! width=6% | Other |- !scope="row"|''[[Death Race 2000]]'' |1975 | | | | {{yes}} | |Uncredited |- !scope="row"|''[[The Milpitas Monster]]'' |1976 | | | | | {{yes}} |Special effects artist |- !scope="row"|''[[Star Wars (film)|Star Wars]]'' |1977 | | | | {{yes}} | {{yes}} |1997 & 2004 versions

'''George Glenn Strange''' (August 16, 1899 – September 20, 1973) was an American actor who appeared in hundreds of [[Western (genre)|Western films]]. He played Sam Noonan, the bartender on [[CBS]]'s ''[[Gunsmoke]]'' television series, and [[Frankenstein's monster]] in three [[Universal Pictures|Universal]] films during the 1940s.

==Early life==
Strange was born in [[Weed, New Mexico|Weed, New Mexico Territory]],<ref name="cahsff">Raw, Laurence (2012). [https://books.google.com/books?id=jqBllx5lyuwC&dq=%22George+Glenn+Strange%22&pg=PA175 "Glenn Strange"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528093732/https://books.google.com/books?id=jqBllx5lyuwC&dq=%22George%20Glenn%20Strange%22&pg=PA175 |date=May 28, 2023 }}, ''Character Actors in Horror and Science Fiction Films, 1930–1960'' (Jefferson, North Carolina: [[McFarland & Company]], 2012), p. 175. Retrieved October 29, 2017.</ref> the fourth child of William Russell Strange and the former Sarah Eliza Byrd. An eighth-generation grandson of [[Pocahontas]] and [[John Rolfe]] through his maternal grandfather, he was also a cousin of actors [[Rex Allen]] and [[Lee "Lasses" White]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Dowling |first=Tim |title=Family tree of Glenn STRANGE |url=https://en.geneastar.org/genealogy/strangeg/glenn-strange |website=Geneastar: Famous Genealogies |access-date=May 13, 2025}}</ref><ref name="IMDb">{{cite web |title=Glenn Strange: Trivia |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0833363/trivia/ |publisher=[[IMDb]] |access-date=May 13, 2025}}</ref> Of Irish and [[Cherokee]] ancestry through his father,<ref name="Arizona">{{Cite web |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/117961020/?terms=%22Glenn%20Strange%22&match=1 |title=Film bad guy Glenn Strange dies, ''Arizona Republic'', September 22, 1973, page 9 |access-date=June 3, 2023 |archive-date=June 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603002229/https://www.newspapers.com/image/117961020/?terms=%22Glenn%20Strange%22&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="IMDb" /> he spoke Cherokee until he was about 13 years old, but in 1972 he said, "since that time I've had nobody to speak it with, so I've lost it."<ref name="Bar">{{Cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/829622750/?terms=%22Glenn+Strange%22&match=1|title=Aug 20, 1972, page 102 - Richmond Times-Dispatch at Newspapers.com - Newspapers.com|website=www.newspapers.com}}</ref>

He grew up on a ranch near Cross Cut, TX, and left school after eighth grade, for his father thought he had enough education to work with cattle. When he was 12 he began playing the [[fiddle]] at local dances.<ref name= "Witbeck">{{Cite web |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/60801350/?terms=%22Glenn%20Strange%22&match=1 |title=Witbeck Charles, It Will Be Strange When Glenn Is No Longer on 'Gunsmoke', ''The Bridgeport Post'', October 9, 1973, page 24 |access-date=June 3, 2023 |archive-date=June 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603002229/https://www.newspapers.com/image/60801350/?terms=%22Glenn%20Strange%22&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1928 he began performing music on an [[El Paso, Texas]] radio station.<ref name= "Arizona"/> Another early job was [[heavyweight boxing]], which caused some [[Cauliflower ear|"cauliflower" damage to his right ear]].<ref name= "Witbeck"/>

Strange had a close relationship with his cousin Taylor "Cactus Mack" McPeters, who has born one week apart from him. The two would frequently work together in both their acting and music careers.<ref name=RetFan11>{{cite magazine |last=Johnson |first=Dan |date=November 2020 |url=https://retrofan.org/ |title=Strange Relations: Julie Ann Ream, the Niece of Frankenstein |magazine=RetroFan |issue=11 |pages=57–61}}</ref>

Strange competed in the [[Hoot Gibson]] rodeo but was injured when a horse fell on him. After the injury Gibson looked after him, and Strange began playing outlaws in Gibson's Western films.<ref name= "Bar"/>

==Career==
[[File:Western Mail (1942) - Glenn Strange & Fred Kohler Jr.jpg|right|thumb| Strange and [[Fred Kohler Jr.]] in ''[[Western Mail (film)|Western Mail]]'']]
For much of Strange's acting career most of his roles were playing "bad guys".<ref name="Globe">{{Cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/29579856/?terms=%22Glenn+Strange%22&match=1|title=Sep 24, 1948, page 20 - The Amarillo Globe-Times at Newspapers.com - Newspapers.com|website=www.newspapers.com}}</ref> Because he could handle a [[stagecoach]] with six horses hitched up, he was often cast as a stagecoach driver.<ref name=RetFan11/> He had roles in 300 films and 500 television episodes.<ref name= "Arizona" />

In 1932 he had a minor role as part of the Wrecker's gang in a 12-part serial, ''[[The Hurricane Express]]'', starring [[John Wayne]]. He played numerous small parts in Paramount's popular ''[[Hopalong Cassidy (film series)|Hopalong Cassidy]]'' film series, usually cast as a member of an outlaw's gang and occasionally as a local sheriff. In 1943, he played an outlaw in the Hopalong Cassidy movie ''[[False Colors (1943 film)|False Colors]]''. He played the killer Naylor Rand in the 1948 film ''[[Red River (1948 film)|Red River]]''.<ref name="Globe" />

Beginning in 1949, he portrayed Butch Cavendish, the villain responsible for killing all but one of the [[Texas Ranger Division|Texas Rangers]] in the long-running television series ''[[The Lone Ranger (TV series)|The Lone Ranger]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S0H8CwAAQBAJ&newbks=0&printsec=frontcover&pg=PA62&dq=%22Glenn+Strange%22+%22Butch+Cavendish%22&hl=en#v=onepage&q=%22Glenn+Strange%22+%22Butch+Cavendish%22&f=false|title=Outlaw Heroes as Liminal Figures of Film and Television|first=Rebecca A.|last=Umland|date=April 27, 2016|publisher=McFarland|via=Google Books}}</ref> Strange appeared twice as Jim Wade on [[Bill Williams (actor)|Bill Williams]]'s syndicated Western series geared to juvenile audiences ''[[The Adventures of Kit Carson]]''. He also appeared twice as Blake in the syndicated Western ''[[The Cisco Kid (TV series)|The Cisco Kid]]''. In 1952, he was cast in the role of Chief Black Cloud in the episode "Indian War Party" of the syndicated ''[[The Range Rider]]''. In 1954, Strange played Sheriff Billy Rowland in [[Jim Davis (actor)|Jim Davis]]'s syndicated Western series ''[[Stories of the Century]]''. Strange appeared six times in 1956 in multiple roles on [[Edgar Buchanan]]'s syndicated ''[[Judge Roy Bean (TV series)|Judge Roy Bean]]''. That same year, Strange appeared in an uncredited role as the sheriff in Silver Rapids in the Western movie ''[[The Fastest Gun Alive]]'' starring [[Glenn Ford]]. In 1958, he had a minor part in an episode of [[John Payne (actor)|John Payne]]'s ''[[The Restless Gun]]'' and had an important role in the 1958 episode "Chain Gang" of the Western series ''[[26 Men]]'', true stories about the [[Arizona Rangers]].  That same year, he played rancher Pat Cafferty, who faces the threat of [[anthrax]] in the episode "Queen of the Cimarron" of the syndicated Western series, ''[[Frontier Doctor]]''. Strange appeared in six episodes of ''[[The Rifleman]]'', playing the similar rolee in different variations: Cole, the stagecoach driver, in "Duel of Honor"; a stagecoach shotgun guard in "The Dead-eye Kid"; Joey, a stagecoach driver in "The Woman"; and an unnamed stagecoach driver in "The Blowout", "The Spiked Rifle", and "Miss Bertie".<ref>[http://www.trend-chaser.com/entertainment/secrets-of-tvs-the-rifleman-more-than-just-guns-and-good-times/71/ "Secrets Of TV's The Rifleman: More Than Just Guns And Good Times: Stagecoach Driver (Glenn Strange)"], ''TrendChaser''. Retrieved February 22, 2019.</ref>

Strange had parts in the [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] Western ''[[The Life and Legend of Wyatt Earp]]'', as well as in ''[[Annie Oakley (TV series)|Annie Oakley]]'', ''[[Buffalo Bill, Jr.]]'', ''[[Wagon Train]]'' and other [[Westerns on television|Western television]] series.<ref name="Greenland">{{Cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q3SdDwAAQBAJ&dq=%22Glenn+Strange%22&pg=PT44|title=The Gunsmoke Chronicles: A New History of Television's Greatest Western|first=David R.|last=Greenland|date=October 5, 2013|publisher=BearManor Media|via=Google Books}}</ref> He played an Indian Chief in "Rawhide" S2 E8 "Incident of the Haunted Hills" which aired May 11, 1959.

===Gunsmoke===
Strange first appeared on ''Gunsmoke'' in 1960 after [[James Arness]] asked him, "When are you going to do a Gunsmoke? I like to work with big guys."<ref name= "Arizona" /> During Gunsmoke's sixth season, Strange played a Long Branch customer in "Old Faces" and a cowboy in "Melinda Miles".<ref name= "Greenland" />

Strange began playing Sam Noonan during the seventh season and continued in the role for 222 episodes. In 1972 Strange was diagnosed with lung cancer but worked as long as he was able.<ref name=RetFan11/> Five of his episodes were broadcast after his death. His last appearance was on the November 26, 1973, episode "The Hanging of Newly O'Brien".<ref name= "Greenland" />

===Frankenstein===
{{main|Frankenstein's monster}}
[[File:HouseOfDraculaCrop003a.png|right|thumb|Strange as [[Frankenstein's monster|Frankenstein]] in ''[[House of Dracula]]'' (1945)]]
[[File:House of Frankenstein, Glenn Strange, Boris Karloff.jpg|thumb|right|Strange (left) and [[Boris Karloff]] in the 1944 horror film, ''[[House of Frankenstein (film)|House of Frankenstein]]'']]

In 1944, while Strange was being made up for an action film at Universal, make-up artist [[Jack Pierce (make-up artist)|Jack Pierce]] noticed that Strange's facial features and 6'4"<ref name="Globe" /> height would be appropriate for the role of [[Frankenstein's monster]]. Strange was cast in the 1944 film ''[[House of Frankenstein (film)|House of Frankenstein]]'' in the role first played by [[Boris Karloff]] in ''[[Frankenstein (1931 film)|Frankenstein]]'' (1931), coached by Karloff personally after hours.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mank|first=Gregory William|title=It's Alive! The Classic Cinema Saga of Frankenstein|year=1981 |publisher=A.S. Barnes & Company, Inc.|isbn=0-498-02473-3|page=136}}</ref> Karloff later said he was dissatisfied with Strange's performances as the monster, commenting, "Well, he wasn't as lucky as I was. I got the cream of it, being the first. I know I wished him lots of luck... hoping it would do as much for him as it did for me, but..."<ref>{{cite book|last=Mank|first=Gregory William|title=It's Alive! The Classic Cinema Saga of Frankenstein|year=1981|publisher=A.S. Barnes & Company, Inc.|isbn=0-498-02473-3|page=139}}</ref>

Previously to ''House of Frankenstein'', Strange starred as Petro, who is turned into a wolf-monster by [[George Zucco]], in ''[[The Mad Monster]]'' (1943). Another role in a horror film was in 1944's ''[[The Monster Maker]]''. He also appeared as "The Giant" in the mystery film ''[[The Black Raven]]'' (1943).

Strange reprised the role of Frankenstein's monster in ''[[House of Dracula]]'' (1945). Strange played the monster a third time in ''[[Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein]]'' (1948); as in his first two Frankenstein films, he shared the spotlight with [[Lon Chaney Jr.]] as the [[Larry Talbot|Wolf Man]], but this time [[John Carradine]] was replaced by [[Bela Lugosi]], in his second screen appearance as [[Count Dracula]]. Strange later described working on ''Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein'' as one of his most enjoyable movie-making experiences.<ref name=RetFan11/> Strange also appeared in character with [[Lou Costello]] in a haunted house skit on ''[[The Colgate Comedy Hour]]'' and made a gag publicity appearance as a masked [[Pole sitting|flagpole-sitter]] for a local Los Angeles TV show in the 1950s. After weeks of the station teasing the public about the sitter's identity, Strange removed his mask and revealed himself as Frankenstein's monster (actually, yet another mask). Strange also played a monster in the [[The Bowery Boys|Bowery Boys]] horror-comedy ''[[Master Minds (1949 film)|Master Minds]]'' in 1949, mimicking the brain-transplanted [[Huntz Hall]]'s frantic comedy movements, with Hall providing his own dubbed voice. He was offered the part of [[Gill-man|the Creature]] in ''[[Creature from the Black Lagoon]]'', but turned it down because he found the costume heavy and claustrophobic.<ref name=RetFan11/>

Strange and Chaney became good friends while working on films together, and Strange spoke at Chaney's funeral in July 1973, despite being seriously ill from the cancer that would end his own life two months later.<ref name=RetFan11/>

During the wave of monster-related merchandising in the late 1950s and 1960s, Glenn Strange's image often was used for the monster on toys, games, and paraphernalia, most often from his appearance in the Abbott and Costello film. In 1969, ''[[The New York Times]]'' mistakenly published Boris Karloff's obituary with Glenn Strange's picture as the Frankenstein monster.<ref>Mank, Gregory William (2009). ''Bela Lugosi and Boris Karloff: The Expanded Story of a Haunting Collaboration'' (Jefferson, North Carolina: [[McFarland & Company]], 2009), p. 610. {{ISBN|0-7864-3480-5}}.</ref>

==Death==
On September 20, 1973, at age 74, Strange died of lung cancer in Los Angeles, California.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1973/09/22/archives/glenn-strange-actor-dies-was-gunsmoke-bartender.html "Glenn Strange, Actor, Dies; Was 'Gunsmoke' Bartender"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190224231255/https://www.nytimes.com/1973/09/22/archives/glenn-strange-actor-dies-was-gunsmoke-bartender.html |date=February 24, 2019 }}, digital archives of ''The New York Times'', September 22, 1973. Retrieved February 23, 2019.</ref> Singer [[Eddie Dean (singer)|Eddie Dean]], with whom Strange had collaborated on various songs and opening themes for films, sang at Strange's funeral service as a final tribute. Strange is interred at [[Forest Lawn Memorial Park (Hollywood Hills)|Forest Lawn - Hollywood Hills Cemetery]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wilson |first=Scott |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FOHgDAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Glenn+Strange%22+%22Forest+Lawn%22&pg=PA721 |title=Resting Places: The Burial Sites of More Than 14,000 Famous Persons, 3d ed. |date=August 19, 2016 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1-4766-2599-7 |pages=721 |language=en}}</ref>

'''Sterling Price Holloway Jr.''' (January 14, 1905{{efn|name=birthdate}}<ref name="AP obituary 1987"/><ref name="FamilySearch"/><ref name="Ancestry"/> – November 22, 1992) was an American actor who appeared in over 100 films and 40 television shows.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.allmovie.com/artist/sterling-holloway-p32938| title=Sterling Holloway| website=[[AllMovie]]| access-date=October 25, 2019}}</ref> He did voice acting for [[The Walt Disney Company]], playing Mr. Stork in ''[[Dumbo]]'', Adult Flower in ''[[Bambi]]'', the [[Cheshire Cat]] in ''[[Alice in Wonderland (1951 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'', [[Kaa (The Jungle Book)|Kaa]] in ''[[The Jungle Book (1967 film)|The Jungle Book]]'', Roquefort the Mouse in ''[[The Aristocats]]'', and [[Winnie the Pooh (Disney character)|the title character]] in ''[[Winnie the Pooh (franchise)|Winnie the Pooh]]'', among many others.

==Early life==
Born in [[Cedartown, Georgia]], on January 14, 1905, Holloway was named after his father, Sterling Price Holloway, who, in turn, was named after a prominent [[Confederate States of America|Confederate]] general, [[Sterling Price|Sterling "Pap" Price]]. His mother was Rebecca DeHaven Boothby. He had a younger brother named Boothby. The family owned a grocery store in Cedartown, where his father served as mayor in 1912. After attending [[Georgia Military Academy]], he left Georgia in 1920 at the age of fifteen and went to New York City, where he attended the [[American Academy of Dramatic Arts]].<ref name=JColl-SH/> While there, he befriended actor [[Spencer Tracy]], whom he considered one of his favorite working colleagues.<ref name="CedartownHist">{{cite news |last=Jarrell |first=Donnie |title=Voice of the Valley: The Early Life and Spiritual Heritage of Sterling Holloway |date=2021 |work=Georgia Historical Quarterly |volume=105 |issue=2 |pages=45–48}}</ref>

==Career==

===Stage===
In his late teens, Holloway toured with the stock company of ''[[The Shepherd of the Hills (novel)|The Shepherd of the Hills]]'',<ref>{{cite web |title=The Shepherd of the Hills |url=https://cladriteradio.com/tag/the-shepherd-of-the-hills/ |website=Cladirite Radio |publisher=Cladrite Radio |access-date=August 5, 2018}}</ref> performing in one-nighters across much of the [[American West]] before returning to New York where he performed with the [[Theatre Guild]] production of ''[[Fata Morgana (play)|Fata Morgana]]''<ref name="nyt030424">{{cite news |last=Corbin |first=John |title=The Play |work=The New York Times |date=March 4, 1924 |location=New York, New York |page=16 |via = [[NYTimes.com]]}}</ref> and appeared in the [[Rodgers and Hart]] revue ''[[The Garrick Gaieties]]'' in the mid-1920s.<ref name="lang_p204">{{cite book |author=Lawrence Langner |title=The Magic Curtain |publisher=E. P. Dutton & Company |year=1951 |page=204 |quote= }}</ref> A talented singer, he introduced "[[Manhattan (song)|Manhattan]]" in 1925 and the following year sang "[[Mountain Greenery]]".<ref name=JColl-SH>{{cite web |last=Collura |first=Joe |title=Sterling Holloway: A Way with Words |url=http://www.classicimages.com/people/article_d1e83b0a-0ae0-51f3-88c3-c9078ce4d535.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130425113203/http://www.classicimages.com/people/article_d1e83b0a-0ae0-51f3-88c3-c9078ce4d535.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 25, 2013 |publisher=Classic Images |date=July 7, 2008 |access-date=August 21, 2018}}</ref>

===Films and shorts===
[[File:The Battling Kangaroo (1926) Halloway.jpg|thumb|Holloway in ''[[The Battling Kangaroo]]'' (1926) ]]
He moved to Hollywood in 1926 to begin a film career that lasted almost fifty years. His bushy red hair and foggy distinctive voice meant that he almost always appeared in comedies. His first film was ''[[The Battling Kangaroo]]'' (1926), a silent picture. Over the following decades, Holloway would appear with [[Fred MacMurray]], [[Barbara Stanwyck]], [[Lon Chaney Jr.]], [[Clark Gable]], [[Joan Crawford]], [[Bing Crosby]], and [[John Carradine]]. In 1942, during [[World War II]], Holloway enlisted in the [[United States Army]] at the age of 37 and was assigned to the [[Special Services (entertainment)|Special Services]]. He helped develop a show called "Hey Rookie", which ran for nine months and raised $350,000 for the Army Relief Fund. In 1945, Holloway played the role of a medic assigned to an infantry platoon in the critically acclaimed film ''[[A Walk in the Sun (1945 film)|A Walk in the Sun]]''. Between 1946 and 1947, he played the comic sidekick in five [[Gene Autry]] Westerns.<ref name="sidekick">Rothel.</ref>  His final film role was Hobe Carpenter, a friendly moonshiner who helps Harley Thomas (David Carradine) in ''[[Thunder and Lightning (1977 film)|Thunder and Lightning]]'' (1977).

===With Walt Disney===
[[Walt Disney]] originally considered Holloway for the voice of Sleepy in ''[[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)|Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs]]'' (1937), but chose [[Pinto Colvig]] instead. Holloway's voice work in animated films began with ''[[Dumbo]]'' (1941), as the voice of Mr. Stork. Holloway was the voice of the adult Flower in ''[[Bambi]]'' (1942), the narrator of the Antarctic penguin sequence in ''[[The Three Caballeros]]'' (1944), and the narrator in the ''[[Peter and the Wolf]]'' sequence of ''[[Make Mine Music]]'' (1946). He was the voice of the [[Cheshire Cat]] in ''[[Alice in Wonderland (1951 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'' (1951); the narrator in ''[[The Little House (1952 film)|The Little House]]'' (1952), ''[[Susie the Little Blue Coupe]]'' (1952), ''[[Lambert the Sheepish Lion]]'' (1952), and ''[[Goliath II]]'' (1960); Amos Mouse from ''[[Ben and Me]]'' (1953)'';'' [[Kaa]] the snake in ''[[The Jungle Book (1967 film)|The Jungle Book]]'' (1967); and Roquefort the mouse in ''[[The Aristocats]]'' (1970). He is perhaps best remembered as the voice of [[Winnie-the-Pooh|Winnie the Pooh]] in Disney's ''[[Winnie the Pooh (franchise)|Winnie the Pooh]]'' featurettes through 1977. He was honored as a [[Disney Legend]] in 1991, the first person to receive the award in the voice category.  A majority of his roles were inherited by voice actor [[Jim Cummings]] following his death.

===Radio and recordings===
Holloway acted on many radio programs, including ''[[The Railroad Hour]]'', ''[[The United States Steel Hour]]'', ''[[Suspense (radio program)|Suspense]],'' ''[[Lux Radio Theater]],'' and ''[[The Shadow]].'' In the late 1940s, he could be heard in various roles on [[NBC]]'s "[[Fibber McGee and Molly]]". His voice retained a touch of its Southern drawl and was instantly recognizable. Holloway was chosen to narrate many children's records, including ''Uncle Remus Stories'' (Decca), ''Mother Goose Nursery Rhymes'' (Disneyland Records), ''Walt Disney Presents Rudyard Kipling's Just So Stories'' (Disneyland Records), and ''Peter And The Wolf'' (RCA Victor).

===Television===
[[File:Life of riley 1957.JPG|thumb|right|Holloway with [[William Bendix]] on ''The Life of Riley'', 1957]]
[[File:Andy Griffith Sterling Holloway Andy Griffith Show 1962.JPG|thumb|left|Holloway with [[Andy Griffith]] on ''The Andy Griffith Show'', 1962]]
Holloway easily made the transition from radio to television. He appeared on the ''[[Adventures of Superman (TV series)|Adventures of Superman]]'' as "Uncle Oscar", an eccentric inventor, and played a recurring role on ''[[The Life of Riley]]''. He guest-starred on [[Fred Waring]]'s [[CBS]] television program in the 1950s and appeared on ''[[Circus Boy]]'' as a hot air [[balloon]]ist. Some other series on which he performed include ''[[Five Fingers (American TV series)|Five Fingers]]'' (episode "The Temple of the Swinging Doll"), ''[[The Untouchables (1959 TV series)|The Untouchables]]'', ''[[The Real McCoys]]'' ("The Jinx"), ''[[Hazel (TV series)|Hazel]]'', ''[[Pete and Gladys]]'', ''[[The Twilight Zone (1959 TV series)|The Twilight Zone]]'' ("[[What's in the Box]]"), ''[[The Brothers Brannagan]]'', ''[[Gilligan's Island]]'', ''[[The Andy Griffith Show]]'', ''[[The Donald O'Connor Show]]'', ''[[Peter Gunn]]'', ''[[F Troop]]'', and ''[[Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting]]''.

In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Holloway had live parts in two of ''[[The Bell System Science Series]]'' educational films, and a voice part in a third. In 1969, Holloway narrated a summary of the [[Super Bowl III]] game, titled ''[https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=xwd0nBxqXDw&pp=0gcJCUACo7VqN5tD&ra=m Joe and the Magic Bean]''<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xwd0nBxqXDw |title=Joe and the Magic Bean HD |date=2023-05-06 |last=80s Football Cards |access-date=2026-06-16 |via=YouTube}}</ref>, with “Joe” being [[New York Jets]] player [[Joe Namath]], and the “magic bean” being the [[Gridiron football|football]].

During the 1970s, Holloway did [[Television advertisement|commercial]] [[voice-over]]s for [[Purina Puppy Chow]] dog food and sang their familiar jingle, "Puppy Chow/For a full year/Till he's full-grown!" He also provided the voice for [[Woodsy Owl]] in several 1970s and 1980s [[United States Forest Service]] commercials. He auditioned for the well-known comic book character [[Garfield (character)|Garfield]] in 1982, but lost to [[Lorenzo Music]]. He provided voice-over work for the 1984 commercial of [[Libby's]] baked beans.<ref>{{cite AV media| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CvF_7PTXZPw |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/CvF_7PTXZPw |archive-date=December 21, 2021 |url-status=live| title=Libbys Baked Beans 1984| date=January 11, 2014| website=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Throughout his life, Holloway remained a bachelor. He once said this was because he felt lacking in nothing and did not wish to disturb his pattern of life. He adopted a son, Richard Holloway.<ref name="sidekick"/>

Fellow ''Winnie the Pooh'' cast member [[Hal Smith (actor)|Hal Smith]] (who originated the character [[List of Winnie-the-Pooh characters#Owl|Owl]]) had taken over the role of Winnie the Pooh for the 1981 short ''[[Winnie the Pooh Discovers the Seasons]]''. Holloway was given an audition to return to the role for ''[[The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh]]'', which turned out to be a perfunctory offer as the producers believed he was too old to handle the strain of recording a full series (an assumption that angered Holloway's agent) even though he was still capable of performing the voice;<ref name="ekberg">{{Cite web |last=Ekberg |first=Maggie |date=2026-01-10 |title=Why Disney Stopped Using the Original Voice of Winnie the Pooh: ‘His Agent Was PO’d’ |url=https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/celebrity/articles/why-disney-stopped-using-original-174607679.html |access-date=2026-01-12 |website=Yahoo Entertainment |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Andaloro |first=Angela |title=Sad Reason Original Winnie the Pooh Voice Actor Sterling Holloway Was Pushed Out After Decades of Bringing Characters to Life |url=https://people.com/sad-reason-original-winnie-the-pooh-voice-actor-sterling-holloway-pushed-out-11879623}}</ref> [[Jim Cummings]] took over the role as well as most of Holloway's other voice roles, including Kaa in ''[[Jungle Cubs]]'' and ''[[The Jungle Book 2]]''. As late as 1991, [[Berkeley Breathed]] had shown interest in hiring Holloway to voice [[Opus the Penguin]] for his animated adaptation of ''[[A Wish for Wings That Work]]''; for reasons unknown, Breathed was unable to contact Holloway, and [[Michael Bell (actor)|Michael Bell]] voiced the character instead.<ref name="ekberg" /> Holloway died of a [[cardiac arrest]] at the [[Good Samaritan Hospital (Los Angeles)|Good Samaritan Hospital]] on November 22, 1992.<ref name=NYT>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/11/24/arts/sterling-holloway-actor-87-is-dead-voice-of-pooh-bear.html| title=Sterling Holloway, Actor, 87, Is Dead – Voice of Pooh Bear| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| agency=[[Associated Press]]| date=November 24, 1992| access-date=September 11, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090918164632/http://www.nytimes.com/1992/11/24/arts/sterling-holloway-actor-87-is-dead-voice-of-pooh-bear.html |archive-date=September 18, 2009}}</ref> He was cremated and his ashes were scattered in the Pacific Ocean.<ref name="Georgia Historical Society 2018">{{cite web |title=Marker Monday: Sterling Holloway, 1905-1992 |website=Georgia Historical Society |date=2018-04-23 |url=https://georgiahistory.com/marker-monday-sterling-holloway-1905-1992/ |access-date=2024-01-04}}</ref>

As a dedicated, straight-ticket [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] voter, Holloway consistently stood behind the party's presidential nominees across more than four decades of shifting American political landscapes. His voting record spanned from supporting the internationalist vision of [[Wendell Willkie]] and [[Thomas E. Dewey]] in the 1940s, to breaking his public silence to campaign for General [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]] in the 1950s. His unwavering allegiance continued through the modern conservative movement as he backed [[Barry Goldwater]] in 1964, voted for [[Richard Nixon]] and [[Gerald Ford]] in the 1970s, and ultimately championed the conservative resurgence led by his fellow actor, [[Ronald Reagan]], in the 1980s. Beyond casting his private ballots, Holloway actively wielded his industry clout to counter the rising tide of mid-century liberalism and communism by organizing high-profile fundraisers as a key member of the Hollywood Republican Committee. Furthermore, he aligned himself with prominent industry figures like his frequent boss [[Walt Disney]] and other fellow conservative colleagues as a member of the fiercely anti-communist [[Motion Picture Alliance for the Preservation of American Ideals]], dedicated to defending the film industry and protecting traditional American values on and off the screen.<ref name="HollywoodGOP">{{cite news |last=Critchlow |first=Donald T. |title=When Hollywood Was Right: How Movie Stars Shaped the Conservative Movement |date=2013 |work=Intercollegiate Studies Institute |pages=84-86 |quote=Prominent actors like Sterling Holloway quietly maintained strict party-line loyalty, voting for the Wilkie, Dewey, and later Eisenhower campaigns while supporting localized fundraising efforts.}}</ref><ref name="VarietyArch52">{{cite magazine |title=Hollywood Stars Align for Eisenhower Campaign |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=October 15, 1952 |volume=188 |issue=6 |page=4 |quote=Members of the Hollywood Republican Committee, including Sterling Holloway and William Bendix, have pledged active support for the General's upcoming bid... detailing a voting bloc stretching back to the 1940 Willkie ticket.}}</ref><ref name="MPAHistory">{{cite book |last=Billingsley |first=Lloyd |title=Hollywood Party: How Communism and Anti-Communism Shaped American Movies |publisher=Prima Publishing |date=1998 |isbn=978-0761513766 |page=112 |quote=The roster of the Motion Picture Alliance for the Preservation of American Ideals attracted a wide array of studio talent dedicated to resisting leftist elements, including character actors such as Sterling Holloway who aligned alongside founders Walt Disney and John Wayne.}}</ref>

Raised in Cedartown, Georgia, Holloway was a member of the Methodist Church. He later attended Hollywood United Methodist Church. His Christian faith was a part of his personal life, and he was known for his gentle, distinctive voice and expressive performances.<ref name="CedartownHist">{{cite news |last=Jarrell |first=Donnie |title=Voice of the Valley: The Early Life and Spiritual Heritage of Sterling Holloway |date=2021 |work=Georgia Historical Quarterly |volume=105 |issue=2 |pages=45–48}}</ref>
===Art collection===

Holloway was an avid art collector, important in the early careers of many local Los Angeles area artists such as [[Edward Kienholz]] and [[Billy Al Bengston]]. His large, eclectic, and mostly contemporary collection was sold off piecemeal prior to his death due to his failing health.<ref name="Collection Sale">{{cite news |last1=McKenna |first1=Kristine |title=Art Review: Holloway Collection Being Sold |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-09-05-ca-13410-story.html |access-date=October 29, 2024 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=September 5, 1986}}</ref> The collection was a central element in his life outside of his work, building his home on a hillside overlooking the Pacific Ocean in [[Laguna Beach, California]] to serve primarily as a gallery in which to display his collection. His instructions to his architect, Paul Sterling Hoag, were that it should be the home "primarily for his paintings and sculpture and only secondarily for himself." The design of the house included unique elements such as large built-in flat file drawers to hold prints and other unmounted works from his collection as well as features specifically designated for certain notable artworks, such as the commissioned revolving wooden sunshade panels made by Robert Cremean which faced the setting sun, and sculptured front doors by [[John Mason (artist)|John Mason]]. The whole layout of the house was optimized for the appreciation of the displayed works of art, more similar to the design of a gallery than a home.<ref name="House">{{cite journal |last1=Hoag |first1=Paul |title=The Sterling Holloway House |journal=Art Forum |date=January 1964 |volume=2 |issue=7 |url=https://www.artforum.com/features/the-sterling-holloway-house-2-215105/ |access-date=October 30, 2024}}</ref>

{{Short description|American actor (1907–1977)}} {{otherpeople|Alan Reed}} {{Use American English|date=February 2022}} {{Use mdy dates|date=February 2022}} {{Infobox person | name = Alan Reed | image = Alan Reed in Time Table (1956).jpg | image_size = | caption = Reed in ''[[Time Table (film)|Time Table]]'' (1956) | birth_name = Herbert Theodore Bergman | birth_date = {{Birth date|1907|08|20|mf=yes}} | birth_place = New York City, U.S. | death_date = {{Death date and age|1977|06|14|1907|08|20|mf=yes}} | death_place = [[Los Angeles]], California, U.S. | other_names = Alan Reed Sr.
Teddy Bergman | education = [[American Academy of Dramatic Arts]]
[[Columbia University]] | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1930–1977 | spouse = {{marriage|Finnette Walker|1932}} | children = 3 }} '''Alan Reed''' (born '''Herbert Theodore Bergman'''; August 20, 1907 – June 14, 1977){{Cite web |url=http://explore.bfi.org.uk/4ce2ba1a6c80f |title=Alan Reed profile |website=[[British Film Institute]] |access-date=2020-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150927041006/http://explore.bfi.org.uk/4ce2ba1a6c80f |archive-date=2015-09-27 |url-status=dead }} was an American actor, best known as the original voice of [[Fred Flintstone]] on ''[[The Flintstones]]'' and various spinoff series. He also appeared in many films, including ''[[Days of Glory (1944 film)|Days of Glory]]'', ''[[The Tarnished Angels]]'', ''[[Breakfast at Tiffany's (film)|Breakfast at Tiffany's]]'', ''[[Viva Zapata!]]'' and ''[[Nob Hill (1945 film)|Nob Hill]]'', as well as several television and radio series. ==Early life== Herbert Theodore Bergman was born on August 20, 1907, in [[New York City]] to Jewish parents. His father was a Lithuanian-Jewish immigrant and his mother was born in the United States to Ukrainian-Jewish parents from [[Galicia (Eastern Europe)|Galicia]]. He attended George Washington High School{{Cite news |last=Schmidt |first=Bill Jr. |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3815177/the_brooklyn_daily_eagle |title=Airy Chats |date=April 24, 1932 |work=[[Brooklyn Eagle|Brooklyn Daily Eagle]] |access-date=December 12, 2015 |page=E9 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{Open access}} (now [[George Washington Educational Campus]]) and majored in [[journalism]] at [[Columbia University]].{{Citation needed |date=February 2022}} Between graduating from WHS and entering Columbia, he studied drama at the [[American Academy of Dramatic Arts]].{{Cite news |last=Witte |first=Lawrence |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3821613/denton_journal/ |title=Static |date=December 9, 1960 |work=Denton Journal |access-date=December 13, 2015 |page=10 |via=Newspapers.com}}{{Open access}} He began his acting career in the city, eventually working on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]]. For several years, Reed toured in [[vaudeville]] with his cousin, Harry Green.{{Cite book |last=Cox |first=Jim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PGY5AQAAIAAJ&q=reed |title=Radio Speakers: Narrators, News Junkies, Sports Jockeys, Tattletales, Tipsters, Toastmasters and Coffee Klatch Couples Who Verbalized the Jargon of the Aural Ether from the 1920s to the 1980s{{snd}}A Biographical Dictionary |publisher=McFarland & Company, Inc. |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-7864-6086-1 |pages=234–235 |url-access=subscription}} He also had two other jobs—operating a wholesale candy factory and working at the Copake Country Club as social director, entertainment producer and actor. In his earlier roles, Reed was often billed under his real name, as "Teddy Bergman." According to his obituary in ''[[The New York Times]]'', he adopted his stage name "to break the trap of his Jewish identity, which he later said limited his early roles to parts in which he mimicked ethnic accents."{{cite web|website=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/06/16/archives/alan-reed-a-film-and-tv-actor-69.html|title=Alan Reed, a Film and TV Actor, 69|date=June 16, 1977|accessdate=November 27, 2025}} ==Career== ===Radio=== As early as 1930, Reed (billed as Teddy Bergman) co-starred with Herbert Polesie in ''Henry and George'', a [[CBS]] program that featured minute dramas and popular comedies interspersed with dance music selections.{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3814878/the_lincoln_star/ |title=Henry and George In Lincoln |date=August 3, 1930 |work=[[Lincoln Journal Star|The Lincoln Star]] |access-date=December 12, 2015 |page=D5 |via=Newspapers.com}}{{Open access}} Reed's radio work included having two roles in ''[[Valiant Lady (radio program)|Valiant Lady]]'',Buxton, Frank and Owen, Bill (1972). ''The Big Broadcast: 1920–1950''. The Viking Press. {{ISBN?}} p. 249. the role of Solomon Levy on ''[[Abie's Irish Rose]]'', as the "[[Allen's Alley]]" resident poet Falstaff Openshaw on [[Fred Allen]]'s [[National Broadcasting Company|NBC]] radio show, and later on his own five-minute show, ''Falstaff's Fables'', on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], as Officer Clancey and other occasional roles on the NBC radio show ''[[Duffy's Tavern]]'', as Shrevey the driver on several years of ''[[The Shadow]]'', as Chester Riley's boss on the NBC radio show ''[[The Life of Riley]]'', as Italian immigrant Pasquale in ''[[Life with Luigi]]'' on CBS radio, various supporting roles on ''[[Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar]]'' and ''[[The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show]]'', and as Lt. Walter Levinson in several episodes of ''[[Richard Diamond, Private Detective]]''. Reed was heard regularly on the ''[[Crime Doctor (radio program)|Crime Doctor]]'' series,{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3821782/belvidere_daily_republican/ |title=Fanny Brice on the Air Tonight |date=September 26, 1940 |work=Belvidere Daily Republican |access-date=December 13, 2015 |page=8 |via=Newspapers.com}}{{Open access}} and was the original Daddy to [[Fanny Brice]] on ''[[The Baby Snooks Show|Baby Snooks]]''.{{Cite book |last=DeLong |first=Thomas A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iu8aAQAAIAAJ&q=reed |title=Radio Stars: An Illustrated Biographical Dictionary of 953 Performers, 1920 through 1960 |publisher=McFarland & Company, Inc. |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-7864-2834-2 |page=223 |url-access=subscription}} Billed as Teddy Bergman, he had the title role on ''[[Joe Palooka#Radio series|Joe Palooka]]''. ===Stage=== Billed as Teddy Bergman, Reed appeared on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] in ''Double Dummy'' (1936), ''A House in the Country'' (1937),{{Cite web |url=http://www.playbillvault.com/Person/Detail/50726/Teddy-Bergman |title=Teddy Bergman |website=Playbill Vault |access-date=14 December 2015}} and ''Love's Old Sweet Song'' (1940).{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/3821925/el_paso_heraldpost/ |title=CBS Actor Has Head Shaved for Summer |date=May 31, 1940 |work=[[El Paso Herald-Post]] |access-date=December 13, 2015 |page=2 |via=Newspapers.com}}{{Open access}} ===Television=== From 1957 to 1958, Reed appeared in a recurring role as J.B. Hafter, a studio boss, on the CBS [[sitcom]] ''[[Mr. Adams and Eve]]''. He also played the same character in ''[[The Bob Cummings Show]]''. In 1963, he appeared as Councilman Jack Gramby in episode 8 of the CBS sitcom ''[[My Favorite Martian]]''. In 1964–65, he had a recurring role as Mr. Swidler in the ABC sitcom ''[[Mickey (TV series)|Mickey]]''. ===Voice acting=== In animation, Reed provided the voice of Boris the [[Borzoi|Russian Wolfhound]] in [[Walt Disney]]'s ''[[Lady and the Tramp]]'' in 1955. In 1960, he began the voice role for [[Fred Flintstone]], the lead character of [[Hanna-Barbera]]'s prime-time animated series ''[[The Flintstones]]''. Reed provided Fred's voice for the entire six-season run of the show, as well as in several spin-off series (''[[The Pebbles and Bamm-Bamm Show]]'', ''[[The Flintstone Comedy Hour]]'') and specials. His final performance as Fred Flintstone was a cameo guest role on an episode of ''[[Scooby's All-Star Laff-A-Lympics]].'' Afterwards, Fred would be voiced by [[Henry Corden]] (who had previously done voice work for Hanna-Barbera and bore a resemblance to Reed). Reed's other voice roles for Hanna-Barbera was [[Touché Turtle and Dum Dum|Touché Turtle]]'s sidekick, Dum Dum. Radio playwright and director [[Norman Corwin]] cast Reed as [[Santa Claus]] in the 1969 [[KCET]] television reading of his 1938 play ''[[The Plot to Overthrow Christmas]]''. In television commercials Reed was the voice over for [[Keebler Company#Keebler Elves|J.J. Keebler]], a creation of the [[Leo Burnett Worldwide|Leo Burnett Agency]].{{Cite magazine |last=Cerny |first=JoBe |date=May 11, 2015 |title=Icons of Advertising |url=http://screenmag.com/story/2015/may/11/11262/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150607070242/http://screenmag.com/story/2015/may/11/11262/ |archive-date=June 7, 2015 |access-date=August 17, 2019 |magazine=[[Screen (magazine)|Screen]] |url-status=live}} ==Personal life== In May 1932, Reed married Finette Walker{{Cite news |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/hd2/IDX-Business/Magazines/Archive-BC-IDX/32-OCR/1932-05-01-BC-OCR-Page-0019.pdf |title=Behind the Microphone |date=May 1, 1932 |work=[[Broadcasting & Cable|Broadcasting]] |access-date=14 December 2015 |page=19}} (1909–2005), a Broadway actress whom he met at television station W2XAB (later [[WCBS-TV]]) in New York City. She appeared on stage in the early 1930s and was a [[chorus line|chorus]] member in the original 1934 Broadway production of ''[[Anything Goes]]'' with [[Ethel Merman]].[http://www.playbillvault.com/Person/Detail/81525/Finette-Walker "Finette Walker: Performer."] ''[[Playbill]] Vault'' Retrieved August 19, 2014. They had three sons, including actor [[Alan Reed, Jr.]] (born 1936). ==Death== Reed, a heavy [[Tobacco smoking|smoker]], was diagnosed with [[bladder cancer]] in 1967. The cancer was treated surgically, but he later developed [[emphysema]]. On June 14, 1977, he died at [[St. Vincent Medical Center (Los Angeles)]] after having a [[myocardial infarction|heart attack]], two months before his 70th birthday.{{cite news| url=http://www.thespectrum.com/story/entertainment/2015/09/24/alan-reed-jr-remembers-flintstones/72626720/| title=Alan Reed Jr. remembers 'The Flintstones' at 55| first=Nick| last=Thomas| newspaper=[[USA Today]]| date=September 23, 2015| access-date=November 1, 2017}} ==Filmography== ===Film=== {| class="wikitable sortable" |- !Year !Title !Role !class="unsortable"|Notes |- | 1937 | ''Teddy Bergman's Bar-B-Q'' | Teddy Bergman | |- | 1944 | ''[[Days of Glory (1944 film)|Days of Glory]]'' | Sasha | |- | 1945 | ''[[Nob Hill (film)|Nob Hill]]'' | Dapper Jack Harrigan | |- | 1946 | ''[[The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946 film)|The Postman Always Rings Twice]]'' | Ezra Liam Kennedy | |- | rowspan="2"| 1950 | ''[[Perfect Strangers (1950 film)|Perfect Strangers]]'' | Harry Patullo | |- | ''[[Emergency Wedding]]'' |Barber | |- | rowspan="2"| 1951 | ''[[The Redhead and the Cowboy]]'' | Colonel Lamartine | |- | ''[[Here Comes the Groom (1951 film)|Here Comes the Groom]]'' | Walter Godfrey | |- | rowspan="2"| 1952 | ''[[Viva Zapata!]]'' | [[Pancho Villa]] | |- | ''[[Actor's and Sin]]'' | J.B. '''Janos Prohaska''' (born '''János Prohászka'''; October 10, 1919 – March 13, 1974) was a Hungarian-born American actor and [[stunt performer]]. He appeared on American television from the 1960s and usually played the roles of animals (mostly bears and gorillas) or monsters.

He played a recurring comic role as The Cookie Bear on ''[[The Andy Williams Show]]'' from 1969 to 1971.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Page |first1=Don |title=Janos Prohaska and the Bear Facts on the Cooky Caper |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-janos-prohaska-19/175307740/ |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=February 28, 1971 |location=Los Angeles, CA |page=390 |access-date=June 26, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> Prohaska also appeared in multiple roles on TV series including ''[[The Outer Limits (1963 TV series)|The Outer Limits]]'', ''[[Bewitched]]'', ''[[I Dream of Jeannie]]'', ''[[Lost in Space]]'', and a few episodes of ''[[Gilligan's Island]]'', where he plays a gorilla. His only credited role on that series appears in the episode "Our Vines Have Tender Apes." He also played the title role in the 1965 [[Perry Mason (1957 TV series)|Perry Mason]] episode, "The Case of the Grinning Gorilla". In 1967 he appeared as a white gorilla in the "Fatal Cargo" episode of the ABC-TV sci-fi  series ''[[Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)|Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea]]''.

He was in the first ''Star Trek'' pilot, [[The Cage (Star Trek: The Original Series)|''The Cage'']], as an ape and as a humanoid bird.<ref name="En1">{{cite book |title=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |first1=Michael |last1=Okuda |author-link1=Michael Okuda |first2=Denise |last2=Okuda |author-link2=Denise Okuda |title-link=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |publisher=Pocket Books |page=717 |isbn=0-671-53609-5 |year=1999}} "Prohaska, Janos: Anthropoid ape and Humanoid bird, 'Cage, The' (TOS); '''Horta'''; '''mugato'''; '''Yarnek''', costumed"</ref> Later he was in three episodes of the [[Star Trek: The Original Series|original ''Star Trek'' series]], wearing alien costumes he himself designed and made as the Horta in "[[The Devil in the Dark]]"<ref name="En2">{{cite book |title=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |first1=Michael |last1=Okuda |author-link1=Michael Okuda |first2=Denise |last2=Okuda |author-link2=Denise Okuda|title-link=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |publisher=Pocket Books |page=187 |isbn=0-671-53609-5 |year=1999}} "'''Horta''' (Janos Prohaska)... The Horta was designed, built, and performed by Janos Prohaska, who reportedly wore the costume into ''Star Trek'' producer [[Gene L. Coon|Gene Coon]]'s office. Coon liked the creature so much he wrote "Devil in the Dark" to feature it."</ref> and the mugato in "[[A Private Little War (TOS episode)|A Private Little War]]".<ref name="En3">{{cite book |title=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |first1=Michael |last1=Okuda |author-link1=Michael Okuda |first2=Denise |last2=Okuda |author-link2=Denise Okuda |title-link=The Star Trek Encyclopedia |publisher=Pocket Books |page=311 |isbn=0-671-53609-5 |year=1999}} "'''mugato''' (Janos Prohaska)... Janos Prohaska was also the '''Horta''' from "Devil in the Dark" and the '''Excalbian''' from "The Savage Curtain"... Prohaska designed and built the ''mugato'' from an ape suit he had previously built for another project."</ref>

He also stunt-doubled for both [[Arnold Stang]] and [[Peter Falk]] in the 1963 film ''[[It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World]]'' in which Stang, a small and lightweight man, wore shoulder pads under his costume so that his appearance would match the bulky appearance of Prohaska.

Prohaska made an appearance on an episode of ''[[What's My Line?]]'' in 1969, where he wore one of his ape costumes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.handitv.com/lists/this-is-the-man-behind-the-mask-of-all-those-60s-and-70s-tv-creatures|title=This is the man behind the mask of all those '60s and '70s TV creatures|website=H&I}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Prohaska was born on October 10, 1919 in [[Budapest]], Hungary. He was married to Irene M. Knoke from June 29, 1969 until his death on March 13, 1974. He and his son Robert were killed along with 34 others in the [[Sierra Pacific Airlines Flight 802|crash]] of a chartered [[Sierra Pacific Airlines]] [[Convair 240|Convair CV-440]] aircraft near [[Bishop, California]], while filming the ABC/Wolper Productions television series ''Primal Man''.<ref>{{cite news |title=Investigators Reach Site of Air Crash |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/ledger-enquirer-janos-prohaska-1919-197/175379543/ |work=Ledger-Enquirer |date=March 15, 1974 |location=Columbus, GA |page=40 |access-date=June 27, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The 'Primal Man' Crash|url=http://www.check-six.com/Crash_Sites/PrimalMan-N4819C.htm|website=Check-Six.com|accessdate=July 16, 2014}}</ref> The plane flew into a mountain ridge in darkness, and the exact cause of the crash was never determined.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=19740313-0|title=ASN Aircraft accident Convair CV-440 N4819C Bishop Airport, CA (BIH)|first=Harro|last=Ranter|website=aviation-safety.net}}</ref> Prohaska was cremated and his ashes were interred in the Mausoleum at [[Woodlawn Memorial Cemetery, Santa Monica]].{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}

'''George D. Barrows''' (New York, February 7, 1914 – Oxnard, October 17, 1994) was an American actor known for playing Ro-Man in the film ''[[Robot Monster]]''.<ref name=TVGuide>{{cite web|url=https://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/george-barrows/credits/3030246510/| title=George Barrows|website=TVGuide.com|publisher=[[TV Guide]]|access-date=10 December 2021}}</ref> He was the son of actor [[Henry A. Barrows]]. He often wore a [[gorilla suit]] for his film roles.<ref name=cb>{{cite news| title=Museum| url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/162010531/| newspaper=The Los Angeles Times| date=November 16, 1999| page=211| via=Newspapers.com| access-date=May 13, 2024}}</ref> Excluding his gorilla roles, Barrows usually played bit parts in films and was rarely credited for his work.

==Career==
Barrows built the gorilla suit he used in ''Robot Monster,'' ''[[Gorilla at Large]],'' and other films. It is currently in the collection of the [[Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County]].<ref name=cb />

He also appeared in the [[game show]] ''[[Who Do You Trust?|Do You Trust Your Wife?]]''.<ref name=quiz>{{cite news| title=Quizzers Raise $100 Week Take| url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/638348533/| newspaper=Fort Worth Star-Telegram| date=March 13, 1957| page=41| via=Newspapers.com| access-date=May 13, 2024}}</ref>

{{Short description|American actor (1902–1976)}} {{see also|Corriganville Movie Ranch}} {{Use American English|date=September 2021}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2021}} {{More citations needed|date=May 2017}} {{Infobox person | name = Ray "Crash" Corrigan | image = Ray Corrigan The White Gorilla.jpg | caption = Corrigan in ''[[The White Gorilla]]'' (1945) | birth_name = Raymond Benitz | birth_date = {{Birth date|1902|02|14|mf=yes}} | birth_place = [[Milwaukee, Wisconsin]], U.S. | death_date = {{Death date and age|1976|08|10|1902|02|14|mf=yes}} | death_place = [[Brookings, Oregon]], U.S. | resting_place = [[Inglewood Park Cemetery]], California | other_names = Raymond Benard
Ray Benard
Gorilla | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1932–1958 | spouse = {{plainlist| * {{marriage|Rita Jane Smeal|1920|1954|end=divorced}} * {{marriage|Elaine DuPont|1956|1967|end=divorced}} }} | children = 3 }} '''Ray''' "'''Crash'''" '''Corrigan''' (born '''Raymond Benitz'''; February 14, 1902 – August 10, 1976) was an American actor most famous for appearing in many [[B-movie|B-Western]] movies (among these the ''[[Three Mesquiteers]]'' and ''[[Range Busters|The Range Busters]]'' film series). He also was a [[stuntman]] and frequently acted as [[silver screen]] gorillas using his own [[Gorilla suit|gorilla costume]]s. In 1937, Corrigan purchased land in the [[Santa Susana Mountains]] foothills in [[Simi Valley]] and developed it into a [[movie ranch]] called "[[Corriganville Movie Ranch|Corriganville]]". The [[movie ranch]] was used for [[location filming]] in film serials, feature films, and television shows, as well as for the performance of live western shows for tourists. Bob Hope later bought the ranch in 1966 and renamed it "Hopetown". It is now a Regional Park and nature preserve.[http://www.lamountains.com/parks.asp?parkid=99 "Corriganville Park"], LAMountains.com; retrieved June 23, 2013. {{TOC limit|limit=2}} ==Film career== [[File:New Frontier (1939) 1.jpg|thumb|In ''[[New Frontier (film)|New Frontier]]'' (1939), L-R: Corrigan, [[Jennifer Jones]] and [[John Wayne]] ]] Corrigan's Hollywood career began as a [[Physical fitness|physical fitness instructor]] and [[physical culture]] trainer to the stars. In the early 1930s he did stunts and bit parts in several films, billed as '''Ray Benard'''. Many of his early roles were in ape costumes, for example, as a gorilla in ''[[Tarzan and His Mate]]'' (1934) and an "orangopoid" in the first [[Flash Gordon (serial)|''Flash Gordon'' serial]]. ===Republic Pictures=== In [[1936 in film|1936]], Corrigan had his screen breakthrough with the starring role in a [[Republic Pictures|Republic]] serial, ''[[The Undersea Kingdom]]'', which evoked memories of [[Universal Pictures|Universal]]'s first "[[Flash Gordon]]" serial. His character was known as Ray "Crash" Corrigan, and he adopted it as his screen name. He followed playing the role of [[John C. Fremont]] in the Western serial ''[[The Vigilantes Are Coming]]''. On the basis of this, Republic signed him to their standard Term Player Contract, running from May 25, 1936, to May 24, 1938. He was cast as one of the trio in the ''[[Three Mesquiteers]]'' series of westerns, starring in 24 of the 51 "3M" films made by the studio. He later left Republic in 1938 over a pay dispute. Over at [[Monogram Pictures]], Corrigan began a new series of feature westerns shot at Corriganville, ''[[Range Busters|The Range Busters]]'', cheap knock-offs of The Three Mesquiteers, with a series character that used his name; between 1940 and 1943, he starred in 20 of the 24 films in this series. ===Gorilla Man=== Following this, his on-screen work largely returned to appearing in ape costumes, beginning with ''[[Three Missing Links]]'' (1938), followed by roles in ''[[The Strange Case of Doctor Rx]]'' (1942), ''[[Captive Wild Woman]]'' (1943), ''[[Nabonga]]'' (1944), ''[[White Pongo]]'' (1945) and as a prehistoric sloth in ''[[Unknown Island]]'' (1948). The original gorilla "mask" seen in films like ''[[The Ape (1940 film)|The Ape]]'' (1940) was replaced with a subtler design with a more mobile jaw. Corrigan sold his gorilla suits in 1948 and provided training in using them to their new owner, [[Steve Calvert]], a [[Ciro's]] bartender. Calvert stepped into Corrigan's paw prints starting with a [[Jungle Jim]] film starring [[Johnny Weissmuller]]. Despite reports to the contrary, Calvert and Corrigan never appeared together on-screen in an ape costume. Since both Corrigan and Calvert eschewed screen credit playing gorillas, their film credits are often confused; any appearance of the "Corrigan suit" after 1948 is by Calvert. His final theatrical film was playing the title role in the [[science fiction film]] ''[[It! The Terror from Beyond Space]]'', according to bio information given to visitors at the Thousand Oaks, California, ''Corrigan's Steak House and Bar'' that his son Tom once owned. ===Television series=== In 1950, he had a television show called ''Crash Corrigan's Ranch''.{{cite book |last1=Woolery |first1=George W. |title=Children's Television: The First Thirty-Five Years, 1946-1981, Part II: Live, Film, and Tape Series |date=1985 |publisher=The Scarecrow Press |isbn=0-8108-1651-2 |pages=131–133}} He also planned a television series called ''Buckskin Rangers'' with his old associate [[Max Terhune]].[http://www.jjonz.us/RadioLogs/pagesnfiles/logs_files_RH/1950s_RH/50-54/1950/50rh_10Oct/50-10-08-(Sun)_%5BLBP%5D.pdf "New Series of Westerns Planned for Television."] ''Long Beach Press-Telegram'', October 8, 1950. ==Corriganville== In 1937, Corrigan was on a hunting trip with [[Clark Gable]] when he had an idea to purchase land in [[Simi Valley]], [[California]], and use it as a Western-themed ranch similar to [[Iverson Movie Ranch]]. He paid a $1,000 down payment, then a thousand dollars a month until the $11,354 price was paid.Gilpatrick [https://books.google.com/books?id=kKPcSwYtbQUC&pg=PA202 2002, p. 202.] He developed this into [[Corriganville Movie Ranch|Corriganville]], a location used for many [[Western (genre)|Western]] films and TV shows. The location featured many different types of terrain for producers such as lakes, mountains, and caves.Corrigan, Ray. [http://www.phantomranch.net/bwestern/corrigan.htm "An Introduction to Corriganville."] ''The Corriganville Gazette'', Volume 1, Issue 3. Not merely set fronts, Corriganville contained actual buildings where film crews could live{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2sKkFbaVkRIC&pg=PA21|title=Corriganville Movie Ranch|first=Jerry L.|last=Schneider|date=1 August 2007|publisher=Lulu Press, Incorporated|isbn=9781430312246 |access-date=1 May 2017|via=Google Books}} and store their equipment to save the time and expense of daily travel from studios to an outdoor location. Corrigan profited well from renting this location to film studios and from paying visitors. In 1949, Corrigan opened his ranch to the public on weekends for Western-themed entertainment. The weekend attractions included stuntmen shows throughout the day, a Cavalry fort set, an outlaw shack, a full western town with saloon, jail, and hotel, live western music, Indian crafts, stagecoach rides, pony rides, and boating on the ranch's artificial lake. It was common for film and TV personalities to appear in person for photos and autographs, attracting as many as 20,000 people on weekends. Examples of [[feature film]]s and TV shows that were filmed at Corriganville: *''[[Drums of Fu Manchu]]'' (1939) *''[[Fort Apache (film)|Fort Apache]]'' (1948) *''[[The Lone Ranger (TV series)|The Lone Ranger]]'' (1949–1957) *''[[The Cisco Kid (TV series)|The Cisco Kid]]'' (1950–1956) *''[[The Adventures of Kit Carson]]'' (1951–1955) *''[[The Adventures of Rin Tin Tin]]'' (1954–1959) *''[[Have Gun – Will Travel]]'' (1957–1963) *''[[Casey Jones (TV series)|Casey Jones]]'' (1957) Hollywood cowboy stars who filmed there include: [[Gene Autry]], [[Roy Rogers]], [[Buster Crabbe]], [[John Wayne]], [[Smiley Burnette]], [[Clayton Moore]], [[Jay Silverheels]], [[Charles Starrett]], [[Ken Maynard]], [[Hoot Gibson]], [[Bob Steele (actor)|Bob Steele]], [[Tex Ritter]], and Corrigan himself. Corriganville was eventually sold to [[Bob Hope]] in 1966, becoming ''Hopetown''. Today, what remains is known as Corriganville Park and features some of the old landmarks. Signs along a hiking trail point out the historic features. ==Nickname== The origin of the "Crash" nickname is from his football-playing days. This was verified by Corrigan himself when he was a contestant on the June 11, 1959, episode of ''[[You Bet Your Life]]'' starring [[Groucho Marx]]. When asked how he got the name "Crash", Corrigan told Groucho, "When I would go to tackle somebody or instead of fighting them with my fists, I would just take off and dive at them head first and that's how I acquired the name 'Crash'". His first starring role using the name professionally was in the [[Republic Pictures]]' serial ''[[The Undersea Kingdom]]'' (1936), in which his screen character was also named "Crash Corrigan". The serial was created to capitalize on the popularity of [[Universal Pictures]]' ''[[Flash Gordon]]'' serials, and the nickname may have been appropriated by Republic's publicity department to create a similarly named hero.Anderson, Chuck. [https://web.archive.org/web/20091001213701/http://www.b-westerns.com/crash.htm "Ray 'Crash' Corrigan."] ''B-Westerns'', October 1, 2009. ==Death== Following his death from a heart attack at age 74 on August 10, 1976, in Brookings Harbor, Oregon, Ray "Crash" Corrigan was interred at [[Inglewood Park Cemetery]], [[Inglewood, California]].
