'''Hans Georg Conried Jr.''' (April 15, 1917 – January 5, 1982) was an American actor and comedian. Among his numerous roles, he voiced [[Captain Hook]] and [[George Darling (Peter Pan character)|George Darling]] in [[Walt Disney]]'s ''[[Peter Pan (1953 film)|Peter Pan]]'' (1953), [[Snidely Whiplash]] in [[Jay Ward]]'s ''[[Dudley Do-Right]]'' cartoons, and Professor Waldo P. Wigglesworth in Ward's ''[[Hoppity Hooper]]'' cartoons. Conried was host of Ward's live-action ''[[Fractured Flickers]]'' show, and had a recurring role as Professor Kropotkin in the radio and film versions of ''[[My Friend Irma]]''. He also appeared as Uncle Tonoose on the [[Danny Thomas]] sitcom ''[[The Danny Thomas Show|Make Room for Daddy]]'', twice on ''[[I Love Lucy]]'', and as the [[Mad Hatter]] in ''[[The Bell System Science Series#The Alphabet Conspiracy (1959)|The Alphabet Conspiracy]]'' (1959).

==Early life==
Conried was born on April 15, 1917, in [[Baltimore]], [[Maryland]], to parents Edith Beryl (née Gildersleeve, 1892–1970)<ref>{{cite news |title=Edith B. Conried |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-edith-beryl-gilder/189929187/ |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=May 3, 1970 |location=Los Angeles, CA  |page=312 |access-date=January 27, 2026 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> and Hans Georg Conried (1883–1957).<ref>{{cite news |title=Hans G. Conried Sr. |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-hans-georg-conried/189929119/ |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=March 2, 1957 |location=Los Angeles, CA  |page=80 |access-date=January 27, 2026 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> His Connecticut-born mother was a descendant of [[Pilgrims (Plymouth Colony)|Pilgrims]], and his father was a Jewish immigrant from Vienna, Austria.<ref name="book1">{{cite book| last=Gargiulo| first=Suzanne| author2=Leonard Maltin| title=Hans Conried: a biography| publisher=McFarland| year=2002| pages=9–10| isbn=0-7864-1338-7}}</ref> He was raised in Baltimore and in New York City.{{Citation needed |date=October 2023}}

==Career==
Conried studied acting at [[Columbia University]] and went on to play major classical roles onstage. This led him into radio in 1937, when he appeared in a supporting role in a broadcast of ''[[The Taming of the Shrew]]'' on [[KABC (AM)|KECA]] in Los Angeles, California.<ref>{{cite news| title=Toscanini Will Conduct Vienna Orchestra on Air| url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2339301/the_san_bernardino_county_sun/| newspaper=The San Bernardino County Sun| date=July 26, 1937| page=11| via=[[Newspapers.com]]| access-date=May 2, 2015}} {{Open access}}</ref> Four years later, a newspaper reported about his role on ''Hedda Hopper's Hollywood'': "But at the mic, he's equally convincing as old men, drunks, dialeticians, or Shakesperean tragedians. [[Hedda Hopper|Miss Hopper]] favors him for her dramatizations when the script will allow him, as she puts it, 'to have his head.'"<ref>{{cite news| title=Shirley Temple on Air Tonight| url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2343010/belvidere_daily_republican/| work=Belvidere Daily Republican| date=January 27, 1941| page=5| via=Newspapers.com| access-date=May 3, 2015}} {{Open access}}</ref> 
Impressed with Conried's versatility,  a scout for [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] signed him as a character player in 1938.{{Citation needed |date=October 2023}} He was in eight radio performances of ''[[Cavalcade of America]]''.{{sfn|Gargiulo|2002|pages=185–186}}

Conried's early screen roles were incidental bits, usually comic but sometimes shady or cowardly, depending on the context. He stayed with MGM until 1941, then began freelancing. His first major featured role was at [[Columbia Pictures]] as a worldly, architectural visionary who disrupted the household in ''[[Blondie (comic strip)#Film|Blondie's Blessed Event]]'' (1942). That established him as a comic figure in feature films. His Germanic surname got him cast as enemy agents in many wartime films, and he became a dialect specialist.{{Citation needed |date=October 2023}}

During [[World War II]], Conried enlisted in the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] in September 1944.<ref>National Archives and Records Administration. ''U.S. World War II Army Enlistment Records, 1938-1946'' [database on-line]. Provo, UT, US: The Generations Network, Inc., 2005.</ref> He trained at [[Fort Knox]] as a tank crewman until the army decided he was too tall. He became a [[M2 4.2-inch mortar|heavy mortar]] crewman then was sent to the Philippines as an engineer laborer until fellow actor [[Jack Kruschen]] obtained his release for service with the [[Armed Forces Radio Network]].<ref>Gargiulo, Suzanne. ''Hans Conried: A Biography; With a Filmography and a Listing of Radio, Television, Stage and Voice Work'', page 46. McFarland, August 22, 2002.</ref>

Conried remained active in radio during the 1940s and 1950s. He was in the regular cast of [[Orson Welles]]' ''[[Ceiling Unlimited]]'', for which he wrote the December 14, 1942, episode, "War Workers".<ref>[[Orson Welles|Welles, Orson]], and [[Peter Bogdanovich]], edited by [[Jonathan Rosenbaum]], ''This Is Orson Welles''. New York: HarperCollins Publishers 1992 {{ISBN|0-06-016616-9}} page 375</ref> On ''[[The George Burns and Gracie Allen Show]]'', he played a psychiatrist whom George regularly consults for help in dealing with the ditzy Gracie.  Conried also provided various characters on ''[[The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show]]'', including portraying one of [[Phil Harris]]' writers.

Conried was also a regular on the [[CBS Radio]] program ''[[Life with Luigi]]'', portraying Schultz, a German classmate. He also played occasional dialect roles on CBS's detective series ''[[Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar]]''.

Even as a younger man, Conried appeared much older than his actual age and he was frequently cast as middle-aged or even elderly pompous, scholarly types. His impeccable diction and inimitable growl were well suited to the roles he played, whether portraying the dim Professor Kropotkin on the radio show ''[[My Friend Irma (radio-TV)|My Friend Irma]]'' or as comic villains and mock-sinister or cranky types. In 1949, while filming the movie version of ''My Friend Irma'',  character actor [[Felix Bressart]], cast as Professor Kropotkin, died suddenly during production. Conried,  who played Kropotkin on radio, stepped in to finish the picture. Most of the finished film features Bressart with Conried's voice overdubbed; Conried appears in a few scenes in identical costume and makeup, with his voice used throughout.{{Citation needed |date=October 2023}}

Hans Conried's first leading film role was the independent science fiction comedy ''[[The Twonky]]'' in 1953.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Twonky (1953)|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307090045/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/17361/The-Twonky/articles.html|archive-date=7 March 2016|url-status=dead |quote=Conried was interviewed in 1970 and said that he told [[Arch Oboler|Oboler]] during production of The Twonky that he was worried that the film was not working and that it would bomb at the box office. According to Conried, the producer replied, "That's all right. I need a tax write-off this year anyway." - no doubt to offset the enormous profits reaped from [[Bwana Devil]].|url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/17361/the-twonky#articles-reviews}}</ref> Two years later, Conried appeared as a riverboat gambler in ''[[Davy Crockett, King of the Wild Frontier]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Maltin |first1=Leonard |title=The Disney Films |publisher=Bonanza Books |page=122}}</ref>

==Dr. Seuss==
Theodor Geisel, better known as children's author [[Dr. Seuss]], was preparing a documentary feature largely made up of captured Japanese newsreel footage, ''[[Design for Death]]'' (1948). Geisel hired actor [[Kent Smith]] as the "American" narrator, and Hans Conried as the "Japanese" narrator. The film won an [[Academy Award]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sheaffer |first1=Lew |title='Death' a Brilliant Documentary; George Raft and 'Millie' at the Fox |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/brooklyn-eagle-design-for-death-1947/190000509/ |work=Brooklyn Eagle |date=June 11, 1948 |location=Brooklyn, NY |page=8 |access-date=January 28, 2026 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Frey |first1=Virginia |title=Victoria Shows Prize Jap Film |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-design-for-death-1947/190000662/ |work=Daily News |date=June 11, 1948 |location=New York, NY |page=814 |access-date=January 28, 2026 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref>

Geisel remembered Conried when he was preparing an expensive [[Technicolor]] fantasy, ''[[The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T.]]'' (1953), which included the dominant role of a demanding, dictatorial piano teacher. Conried was cast as the foreboding "Dr. Terwilliker" and turned in a bravura performance that might have changed his career. Unfortunately, the film was a costly failure. In 1970, Conried reflected on the film's poor box-office take in an interview with [[Leonard Maltin]]: "The picture never made its print money back. It was comparable only to ''[[Wilson (1944 film)|Wilson]]'' as one of the great money-losers of all time; it would stop conversation for some years at any Hollywood social gathering."<ref>Hans Conried to Leonard Maltin, reprinted in ''The Real Stars'', New York: Curtis Books, 1973, p. 84.</ref>

The film's financial failure didn't affect Conried's working relationship with Geisel, who went on to cast him in three Dr. Seuss television specials, including the 1977 [[Halloween]] TV special ''[[Halloween is Grinch Night]]'', produced by [[DePatie-Freleng Enterprises]]. Conried voiced both the Narrator and the [[Grinch]], a role originated in 1966 by [[Boris Karloff]] in ''[[How the Grinch Stole Christmas! (TV special)|How the Grinch Stole Christmas]]''. In 1981, Conried was set to reprise his role as the Grinch for ''[[The Grinch Grinches the Cat in the Hat]]'', but he was in poor health and died early in 1982. Voice actor [[Bob Holt (actor)|Bob Holt]] took over the role.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Seuss at DePatie-Freleng {{!}} |url=https://cartoonresearch.com/index.php/dr-seuss-at-depatie-freleng/ |access-date=2026-07-02 |website=cartoonresearch.com}}</ref>

==Cartoons==
Conried's colorful voice gained him much work in animated cartoons, such as [[The Walt Disney Company|Disney]] and [[Jay Ward]]. His prominent work for Disney was in [[Walt Disney]]'s ''[[Peter Pan (1953 film)|Peter Pan]]'' where he voiced and provided live-action reference for both [[Captain Hook]] and Mr. Darling (following the tradition of having both characters portrayed by the same actor). He then went on to pose live-action movesets and audition for [[Aurora (Sleeping Beauty)|Aurora]]'s father, [[List of Disney's Sleeping Beauty characters#King Stefan|King Stefan]], in another Disney animated film, ''[[Sleeping Beauty (1959 film)|Sleeping Beauty]]'', but the voice role of Stefan was officially taken by [[Taylor Holmes]] for the film's final cut. Nevertheless, Conried hosted several episodes of ''[[Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color]]'' as the [[Magic Mirror (Snow White)|Magic Mirror]] from ''[[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)|Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs]]''.

He supplied the storybook narration for [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM]]'s ''[[Johann Mouse]]'', the 1952 [[Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film|Academy Award for Best Short Subject: Cartoons]], the seventh and last Oscar given to a ''Tom and Jerry'' short.

Conried also became a charter member of the [[Jay Ward]]-[[Bill Scott (voice actor)|Bill Scott]]  stock company. He  voiced the character of [[Snidely Whiplash]] in the [[Dudley Do-Right]] segments of ''[[The Rocky and Bullwinkle Show]]'', and Professor Waldo P.  Wigglesworth on ''Hoppity Hooper''. 

Ward and Scott also cast him as the live-action host of ''[[Fractured Flickers]]'', a wildly satirical, tongue-in-cheek redub of silent movies. During that show he had a tightly scripted segment where he absurdly interviewed guest stars and celebrities, while usually mistaking their identities, misunderstanding answers, taking umbrage or getting into mock disagreements. 

He also voiced [[Wally Walrus]] on ''[[The Woody Woodpecker Show]]'' and Dr. Dred on ''[[Drak Pack]]''. According to the DVD commentary of ''[[Futurama]]'', he was the inspiration for the voice created for Robot Devil.

==Television==
[[File:Hans Conried Uncle Tonoose Danny Thomas Show 1959.JPG|thumb|Conried as the grumpy Uncle Tonoose, a recurring role he played on ''[[The Danny Thomas Show|Make Room for Daddy]]'']]
From 1955 to 1964, Conried made 19 guest appearances as "Uncle Tonoose" in ''[[The Danny Thomas Show|Make Room for Daddy]]'' on ABC and then CBS, and four appearances as other characters.

He was featured in the 1958 episode, "What Makes Opera Grand?", on the anthology series ''[[Omnibus (U.S. TV series)|Omnibus]]''. The episode, an analysis by [[Leonard Bernstein]], showing the powerful effect of music in opera, featured Conried as Marcello in a spoken dramatization of Act III of Puccini's ''[[La Bohème]]''. The program demonstrated the effect of the music in ''La Bohème'' by having actors speak portions of the libretto in English, followed by opera singers singing the same lines in the original Italian.<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0664962/ What Makes Opera Grand? Omnibus (1952–1961)Season 6, Episode 27]. Accessed online December 14, 2019.</ref>

Conried was a regular guest on [[Jack Paar]]'s ''[[The Tonight Show|Tonight Show]]'' from 1959 to 1962. He was a regular panelist on the pantomime program ''[[Stump the Stars]]'' and a semi-regular guest on the [[Ernie Kovacs]]-hosted game show ''[[Take a Good Look (TV series)|Take a Good Look]]''.

In 1977, Conried joined the cast for the second and final season of ''[[The Tony Randall Show]]'' in the recurring role of Judge Franklin's irascible father, Wyatt.

His many guest appearances included ''[[I Love Lucy]]'', ''[[Davy Crockett (miniseries)|Davy Crockett]]'', ''[[The Californians (TV series)|The Californians]]'', ''[[Hey, Jeannie!]]'', ''[[Meet Mr. McNutley|The Ray Milland Show]]'', ''[[The DuPont Show with June Allyson]]'', ''[[The Real McCoys]]'', ''[[Mister Ed]]'', ''[[The Islanders (TV series)|The Islanders]]'', ''[[Ben Casey]]'', ''[[Dr. Kildare (TV series)|Dr. Kildare]]'', ''[[Lost in Space]]'', ''[[Daniel Boone (1964 TV series)|Daniel Boone]]'', ''[[The Beverly Hillbillies]]'', ''[[The Lucy Show]]'', ''[[The Monkees (TV series)|The Monkees]]'', ''[[Have Gun – Will Travel]]'', ''[[Love, American Style]]'', ''[[Here's Lucy]]'', ''[[Kolchak: The Night Stalker|Kolchak]]'', ''[[Alice (American TV series)|Alice]]'', ''[[Laverne & Shirley]]'', ''[[The Love Boat]]'', ''[[Hogan's Heroes]]'', ''[[Match Game]]'', ''[[Maverick (TV series)|Maverick]]'', ''[[The Donna Reed Show]]'', ''[[Fantasy Island]]''  and ''[[Quark (TV series)|Quark]]''. On ''[[Gilligan's Island]]'', he appeared in two episodes as the confused pilot Wrong Way Feldman, one of the show's few recurring characters.
===Stage appearances===
Conried made his Broadway debut in the Cole Porter musical ''[[Can-Can (musical)|Can-Can]],''<ref>{{cite news |date=1953-03-07 |title=Delmar to return to radio |newspaper=Billboard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OgsEAAAAMBAJ&q=my%20friend%20irma%20kenny%20delmar&pg=PA14 |access-date=2015-03-26}}</ref> where he played a struggling artist and sang two musical numbers.<ref>Liner notes for the cast album of ''Can-Can'', Broadway Angel Records</ref> In 1971, he appeared in ''[[70, Girls, 70]]'' and two years later was a replacement performer in the revival of ''[[Irene (musical)#Later productions|Irene]]'' starring [[Debbie Reynolds]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Hans G. Conried, Jr. – Broadway Cast & Staff {{!}} IBDB |url=https://www.ibdb.com/broadway-cast-staff/hans-g-conried-jr-79120 |website=www.ibdb.com}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Conried married Margaret Grant on January 29, 1942; they had four children.<ref name=nyt>{{cite news |title=Hans Conried, 66 |url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F30811F7385C0C758CDDA80894DA484D81 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 6, 1982 |access-date=2009-01-21}}</ref>

Conried had a long history of heart problems and had a stroke in 1974 and a mild heart attack in 1979.<ref>{{cite news| title=Hans Conried, the versatile comedian who delighted radio, TV,...| url=http://www.upi.com/Archives/1982/01/06/Hans-Conried-the-versatile-comedian-who-delighted-radio-TV/4437379141200/| date=January 6, 1982| website=[[United Press International]]| access-date=January 9, 2019}}</ref> He remained active until his death on January 5, 1982, one day after suffering a major heart attack.<ref name=nyt/> His body was donated to medical science.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d&d=DS19820106.2.40&e=-------en--20--1--txt-txIN--------1 |title=Hans Conried Actor dies of heart ailment |newspaper=Desert Sun |location=Palm Springs, CA |number=132 |page=5 |date=January 6, 1982 |via=University of California Riverside Center for Bibliographical Studies and Research |access-date=May 15, 2020}}</ref>

'''Atlantis''' (born September 28, 1962) is a Mexican [[professional wrestling|professional wrestler]] signed to [[Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre]] (CMLL). One of the longest-tenured wrestlers in CMLL history, his [[ring name]] is derived from [[Atlantis|the fabled city]]. His real name is not a matter of public record, as is often the case with [[Wrestling mask|masked]] wrestlers in Mexico, where their private lives are kept a secret from the wrestling fans.<ref name="Mondo">{{cite book|author=Madigan, Dan|title=Mondo Lucha A Go-Go: the bizarre and honorable world of wild Mexican wrestling|publisher=HarperCollins Publishers|year=2007|chapter=Okay... what is Lucha Libre?|pages=29–40|isbn=978-0-06-085583-3}}</ref>

Trained by [[Diablo Velasco]], Atlantis made his in-ring debut in 1983 and has since held a large number of professional wrestling championships, including the [[CMLL World Light Heavyweight Championship]], [[CMLL World Tag Team Championship]], [[CMLL World Trios Championship]], [[Mexican National Light Heavyweight Championship]], [[Mexican National Middleweight Championship]], [[Mexican National Tag Team Championship]], [[Mexican National Trios Championship]], [[NWA World Light Heavyweight Championship]] and [[NWA World Middleweight Championship]]. He has also won the masks of several prominent wrestlers including [[Arturo Beristain|Talismán]], [[Kung Fu (wrestler)|Kung Fu]], [[Villano III]], [[Último Guerrero]] and [[Andrade El Idolo|La Sombra]]. Outside of CMLL, Atlantis has wrestled in Japan for [[New Japan Pro-Wrestling]] (NJPW) and [[Michinoku Pro Wrestling]], where he won the [[Tohoku Junior Heavyweight Championship]], and in the United States for [[World Championship Wrestling]] (WCW), [[Chikara (professional wrestling)|Chikara]], [[Ring of Honor]] (ROH) and [[Major League Wrestling]] (MLW).

Atlantis earned the nickname ''El idolo de los Niños'' (the "Children's Idol") as he was always a favorite with the younger fans. He even retained the nickname when he worked as a ''rudo'' ([[Heel (professional wrestling)|heel]] or "bad guy" character) for several years as part of ''[[Los Guerreros Laguneros|Los Guerreros de la Atlantida]]''. He starred in several [[Luchador films|lucha films]] in the 1990s, including one in which he co-starred with [[Octagón]]: ''Octagón y Atlantis, la revancha'' ("Octagón and Atlantis, the rematch"). 

==Professional wrestling career==
=== Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (1983–present) ===
==== El idolo de los Niños (1983–2005) ====
He made his professional wrestling debut on June 12, 1983, after training for under a year with world-renowned Mexican wrestling trainer [[Diablo Velasco]].<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" /> He adopted the [[Wrestling mask|masked]] ''tecnico'' ([[Face (professional wrestling)|face]]) [[ring name|ring persona]] of "Atlantis", a supposed warrior from the lost city of [[Atlantis]], donning a mask with an image of two fish, becoming a regular for [[Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre|Empresa Mexicana de Lucha Libre]] (EMLL).<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" /> On November 30, 1984, he defeated [[Jerry Estrada]] to win the [[Mexican National Middleweight Championship]], the first title of his career, holding it for 457 days until losing to [[Arturo Beristain|Talismán]] on March 2, 1986.<ref name="MexMiddle" /><ref name="Lucha2000">{{cite news|title=Los Reyes de Mexico: La Historia de Los Campeonatos Nacionales|work=Lucha 2000|id=Especial 21|date=December 20, 2004|language=es}}</ref> By 1988, Atlantis had formed a regular [[tag team]] with [[Ángel Azteca]], defeating ''[[Los Infernales]]'' ([[Masakre]] and [[MS-1 (wrestler)|MS-1]]) to win the [[Mexican National Tag Team Championship]] on March 6.<ref name="MexTag" /> Three months later, he became a double champion, defeating [[Kung Fu (wrestler)|Kung Fu]] for the [[NWA World Middleweight Championship]], the highest championship in the [[Lucha Libre#Weight classes|middleweight division]]; he lost it to [[Emilio Charles Jr.]] 37 days later.<ref name="NWAMiddle" /> He regained the title on July 20, losing it back to Charles two weeks later.<ref name="NWAMiddle" /> On May 25, 1990, after 811 days, Atlantis and Azteca lost their championship to [[Bestia Salvaje]] and [[Pierroth Jr.]],<ref name="MexTag" /> leading to a [[Narrative thread|storyline]] where Azteca attacked Atlantis, [[Glossary of professional wrestling terms#turn|turning]] ''rudo'' ([[Heel (professional wrestling)|heel]]). The feud between the two continued off and on over the years until Azteca's death in 2007; they remained close friends backstage.<ref name="MundoHispano">{{cite web|url=http://www.munhispano.com/?nid=247&sid=1008433|title=Reportan súbita muerte del luchador Angel Azteca en Campeche|date=March 19, 2007|access-date= August 11, 2009|publisher= Mundo Hispano de KSL|language=es}}</ref>

Atlantis was one of the key figures in the "rebranding" of EMLL to Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (CMLL) in 1990. In 1991, Atlantis starred in the movie ''La Fuerza Bruta'' ("The Brute Power") and subsequently featured in another with [[Octagón]], ''Octagón y Atlantis, la revancha'' ("Octagón and Atlantis, the revenge"), which premiered in 1992. On April 4, 1991, Atlantis, Octagón, and [[Máscara Sagrada]], nicknamed "Los Movie Stars", defeated ''Los Thundercats'' (Leono, Panthro and Tigro) to win the [[Mexican National Trios Championship]], but lost it to ''[[Los Capos|Los Hermanos Dinamita]]'' ([[Cien Caras]], [[Máscara Año 2000]] and [[Universo 2000]]) on August 11.<ref name="MexTrio" /> Not long after, Octagón and Sagrada left CMLL to join the recently formed [[Lucha Libre AAA Worldwide|Asistencia Asesoría y Administración]] (AAA) before the "Atlantis y Octagón" movie premiered in theaters. Atlantis was also offered an AAA contract, but chose to stay with CMLL.<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" /> On March 3, 1993, Atlantis lost the NWA World Middleweight Championship to [[Mano Negra (wrestler)|Mano Negra]], later unmasking Negra by defeating him in a ''[[Lucha libre#Luchas de Apuestas|Lucha de Apuestas]]'' ("bet match") in the main event of the [[CMLL 60th Anniversary Show]] on October 1.<ref name="Ovaciones20999" /> On March 2, 1994, Atlantis moved to the [[Lucha Libre#Weight classes|light heavyweight division]], defeating [[Dr. Wagner Jr.]] to win the [[CMLL World Light Heavyweight Championship]], which he held for 655 days.<ref name="CMLLLHeavy" /> 

On November 3, 1995, Atlantis and [[Rayo de Jalisco Jr.]] won the [[CMLL World Tag Team Championship]] from [[Headhunters (professional wrestling)|The Headhunters]].<ref name="CMLLTag1and2" /> Despite losing the title in August 1996, Atlantis and [[Lizmark]] won it from ''La Ola Blanca'' ([[Arturo Beristain|El Hijo del Gladiador]] and [[Gran Markus Jr.]]), which was vacated twelve days later after an inconclusive match with the Headhunters.<ref name="CMLLTag1and2" /> In 1997, they and [[Mr. Niebla]] formed ''La Ola Azul'' ("The Blue Wave"), defeating Charles, [[El Satánico]] and [[Rey Bucanero]] for the [[CMLL World Trios Championship]] on April 29, holding it until an injury to Mr. Niebla forced them to give up the title in October 1998.<ref name="CMLLTrios1" /> On May 10, 1999, Atlantis defeated Wagner for his second CMLL World Light Heavyweight Championship, losing it to [[Villano III]], whom he had a long-running feud with, on November 22.<ref name="CMLLLHeavy" /> The feud culminated in a ''Lucha de Apuestas'' at ''[[Juicio Final (2000)|Juicio Final]]'' ("Final Judgment") on March 17, 2000, where Atlantis unmasked Villano III in a match that was voted the ''[[Wrestling Observer Newsletter]]''<nowiki/>'s 2000 [[Wrestling Observer Newsletter awards#Match of the Year|Match of the Year]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Luchas 2000|work=Atlantis y sus Victimas|publisher=Publicaciones citem, S.A. de C.V.|location=[[Ciudad Juárez|Juárez]], [[Mexico]]|id=Especial 30|pages=32–36|language=es}}</ref> On June 16, 2002, Atlantis, Mr. Niebla and [[Black Warrior (wrestler)|Black Warrior]] defeated [[Blue Panther]], [[Fuerza Guerrera]] and Wagner to win the trios championship, holding it for 278 days.<ref name="CMLLTrios2" /> On June 25, 2004, Atlantis and Blue Panther defeated ''[[Los Guerreros del Infierno]]'' ([[Último Guerrero]] and Bucanero) to win the CMLL World Tag Team Championship. By this time, Atlantis was stagnating as a ''tecnico'', prompting him to turn on Panther during a title match, ending their reign at 280 days and turning ''rudo'' for the first time in his career.<ref name="FigurasAtlantis" />

==== ''Los Guerreros de la Atlantida'' (2005–2011) ====
{{main|Los Guerreros del Infierno}}
The ''rudo'' Atlantis subsequently joined ''Los Guerreros del Infierno'', which was renamed ''Los Guerreros de la Atlantida'' ("The Warriors of the Atlantis") out of respect for their new co-leader.<ref name=FigurasAtlantis/> 2005 turned out to be Atlantis' strongest and most successful year, as he won the [[CMLL International Gran Prix#International Gran Prix 2005|International Gran Prix]] ,<ref name=PWHGP2005/> the [[NWA World Light Heavyweight Championship]],<ref name="CMLLTrios3" /> and that year's ''[[Leyenda de Plata#Leyenda de Plata 2005|Leyenda de Plata]]'' ("The Silver Legend") tournament.<ref name="Plata2005" /> On September 29, 2009, ''Los Guerrero de la Atlantida'' won the vacant CMLL World Trios Championship by defeating Aguayo Jr., [[Héctor Garza]] and [[Shocker (wrestler)|Shocker]] in a tournament final.<ref name="CMLLTrios3" /> On November 2, Atlantis won his fourth CMLL World Tag Team Championship, this time teaming with Último Guerrero to defeat [[Místico]] and [[Negro Casas]].<ref name=CMLLTag3/>

[[File:LuchadorAtlantis.jpg|thumb|Atlantis often wore a red mask as a ''rudo''|195x195px]]

On June 15, 2018, Atlantis made his [[Ring of Honor]] (ROH) debut at State of the Art, teaming with Guerrero Maya Jr. and Stuka Jr. as "Team CMLL" to defeat [[SoCal Uncensored]] ([[Christopher Daniels]], [[Frankie Kazarian]] and [[Scorpio Sky]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last=R. Pageot |first=Harley |date=June 15, 2018 |title=6/15 ROH State of the Art report: Live coverage featuring Bullet Club vs. Killer Elite Squad & The Kingdom, SCU vs. CMLL, Shane “Hurricane” Helms debuts |url=https://www.pwtorch.com/site/2018/06/15/6-15-roh-state-of-the-art-report-live-coverage-featuring-bullet-club-vs-killer-elite-squad-the-kingdom-scu-vs-cmll-hurricane-helms-debuts/ |access-date=March 30, 2026 |website=Pro Wrestling Torch |publisher=TDH Communications Inc.}}</ref> The next night, they unsuccessfully challenged [[The Kingdom (professional wrestling)|The Kingdom]] ([[Matt Taven]], [[T. K. O'Ryan|TK O'Ryan]] and [[Vinny Marseglia]]) for the [[ROH World Six-Man Tag Team Championship]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=R. '''William Campbell''' (October 30, 1923<ref name=":0">{{cite news |first=Keith |last=Thursby |date=May 1, 2011 |title=Veteran actor had numerous film, TV roles |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2011-may-01-la-me-william-campbell-20110501-story.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230225064729/https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-william-campbell-20110501-story.html |archive-date=February 25, 2023 }}</ref> – April 28, 2011<ref>{{cite news |first=Mike |last=Barnes |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/star-trek-favorite-william-campbell-183795 |title='Star Trek' Favorite William Campbell Dies at 84 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=April 29, 2011}}</ref>) was an American actor. He played [[supporting actor|supporting]] roles in major [[film]] productions during the 1950s and '60s, and starred in several low-budget [[B-movie]]s and [[horror fiction|horror]] films. He also had several roles in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise.<ref name=":1" />

== Early life ==
Campbell was born in [[Newark, New Jersey]] in 1923. He served in the [[U.S. Navy]] during [[World War II]], on a minesweeper in the Pacific theater.<ref name="Thursby">{{cite news |first=Keith |last=Thursby |date=May 1, 2011 |title=William Campbell dies at 87; actor had numerous film, TV roles |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-william-campbell-20110501-story.html}}</ref> He studied acting at the [[HB Studio]], under [[Herbert Berghof]] and [[Uta Hagen]].

==Career==
Campbell's film career began in 1950, with a small part in the [[John Garfield]] film ''[[The Breaking Point (1950 film)|The Breaking Point]].'' After several years of similar supporting performances in a number of films, including as a co-pilot in [[William Wellman]]'s ''[[The High and the Mighty (film)|The High and the Mighty]]'' (1954), he won his first starring role in ''[[Cell 2455 Death Row (film)|Cell 2455 Death Row]]'' (1955), a low-budget prison film for [[Columbia Pictures]]. He played a [[death row]] inmate, based loosely on the true story of [[Caryl Chessman]], who staunchly proclaimed his innocence and obtained numerous reprieves over many years until finally being executed. Campbell's surprisingly powerful performance received generally good notices from critics, but it did very little for his career;{{Citation needed |date=September 2024}} his next several roles were again providing support to lead actors, including ''[[Man Without a Star]]'' (1955), ''[[Love Me Tender (1956 film)|Love Me Tender]]'' (1956)  in which he became the first person to lip sync portions of a song onscreen (actually recorded on August 24, 1956, by the Ken Darby Trio){{Citation needed |date=September 2024}} with [[Elvis Presley]], and [[The Naked and the Dead (film)|the 1958 film version]] of [[Norman Mailer]]'s ''[[The Naked and the Dead]].  ''

In 1958, Campbell co-starred with [[Paul Birch (actor)|Paul Birch]] in ''[[Cannonball (series)|Cannonball]]'',<ref>{{cite news |title=TV Notes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/santa-barbara-news-press-william-campbel/172603105/ |work=[[Santa Barbara News-Press]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=July 19, 1958 |page=14 |access-date=May 18, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> a short-lived [[television series]] about truck drivers. After that, he worked for more years in small parts in increasingly lower grade movies.

Campbell made two guest appearances on ''[[Perry Mason (1957 TV series)|Perry Mason]]'' in 1959 and 1960. In his first appearance he played the title character and murder victim Allen Sheridan in "The Case of the Artful Dodger," then he played murderer and title character Jim Ferris in "The Case of the Ill-Fated Faker."

In 1963, Campbell began a brief association with [[Roger Corman]], starring in the director's ''[[The Young Racers]]'' that year. The auto-racing-themed movie, written for the screen by Campbell's brother [[Robert Wright Campbell]], was shot in Ireland. After production was completed, the film's sound man, [[Francis Ford Coppola]], talked Corman into allowing Coppola to remain in Ireland with a small crew and direct a low-budget horror film, to be produced by Corman. Coppola promised it would be the cheapest film Corman was ever involved in. Shot for approximately $40,000, the resultant film, ''[[Dementia 13]]'' (1963), was an atmospheric and violent horror thriller clearly made in imitation of ''[[Psycho (1960 film)|Psycho]]''.{{Citation needed |date=September 2024}} Campbell starred as a moody loner who at one point becomes the chief suspect in a series of gruesome axe killings; [[Patrick Magee (actor)|Patrick Magee]] and [[Luana Anders]] led the supporting cast. Many years later, Campbell would provide an [[audio commentary]] for the film's [[DVD]] release.

Campbell also starred in another Corman-produced horror yarn. Filmed in 1963 in [[Yugoslavia]] under the title ''Operacija Ticijan'', again with Magee in the cast, the film was never released in its original form. It was re-edited, re-dubbed, and briefly shown on television as ''Portrait in Terror''. Years later, additional footage was shot in California, first by [[Jack Hill]], then by [[Stephanie Rothman]], transforming what was once a spy thriller into the story of a [[vampire]] stalking the streets of [[Venice, California]]. Retitled ''[[Blood Bath]],'' although it also became known as ''Track of the Vampire'', the film received a limited theatrical release in 1966. Campbell also filmed ''[[The Secret Invasion]]'' in Yugoslavia, directed by Roger Corman and written by his brother Robert Wright Campbell.  Campbell was the only one of the team of commandos not given screen credit above the title.

One year previously in 1965 he landed a supporting role as a reporter in the classic suspense horror; ''[[Hush...Hush, Sweet Charlotte]]''. In ''Blood Bath'' Campbell's character was an artist who killed women and hid their bodies inside his sculptures; he is also a vampire who can freely walk during the daylight in search of victims. However, the fanged vampire was confusingly played by another actor who did not resemble Campbell. Like ''Dementia 13'', the film has managed to develop a following despite its deficiencies. In the early 1990s, ''[[Video Watchdog]]'' magazine devoted lengthy articles in three separate issues painstakingly detailing the convoluted production history of this strange but fascinating movie.

Campbell had guest-starring roles in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise, appearing first as the mischievous super-being [[List of Star Trek characters (T–Z)#T|Trelane]] in an episode of [[Star Trek: The Original Series|the original series]] called "[[The Squire of Gothos]]".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Spelling |first1=Ian |title=Characters Cling On to 'Blood Oath' |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/ventura-county-star-william-campbell-19/172602615/ |work=[[Ventura County Star]] |agency=[[New York Times Syndicate]] |date=March 18, 1994 |page=92 |access-date=May 18, 2025 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> Campbell also appeared twice as the [[Klingon]] Captain [[Koloth]]. Campbell first played Koloth on the original ''Star Trek'' series in the episode "[[The Trouble with Tribbles]]". He reprised the role on the series ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' episode entitled "[[Blood Oath (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Blood Oath]]", some thirty years later.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |date=March 11, 2021 |first=Laurie |last=Ulster |title=13 Original Series Actors Who Couldn't Get Enough Trek |url=https://www.startrek.com/news/13-tos-actors-who-appeared-on-other-tv-treks-decades-later |website=StarTrek.com}}</ref> Campbell appeared at several Trek conventions in the 1980s and 1990s. His last appearance was at the convention organized by [[Creation Entertainment]] at the [[Las Vegas Hilton]] in August 2006.

After retiring from acting, Campbell worked for the [[Motion Picture & Television Fund]] as its chief fundraiser.<ref name=":0" />

==Personal life==
Campbell was married twice. His first marriage was to [[Judith Exner]] in 1952. They divorced in 1958.<ref name="Thursby" /> He married Tereza in 1963. They were married until his death.<ref name="Thursby" />

Campbell is a relative of [[Jeff Janiak]], vocalist of the band [[Discharge (band)|Discharge]].<ref>{{cite web |first=Luxi |last=Lahtinen |title=Soundtracks of My Youth – Part Three |url=https://www.metalcrypt.com/pages/features.php?featureid=58 |website=The Metal Crypt |access-date=March 26, 2021}}</ref>

=== Death ===
Campbell died on April 28, 2011, at the [[Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital]] in [[Woodland Hills, California]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://startrek.com/article/remembering-william-campbell |title=Remembering William Campbell |website=StarTrek.com |date=April 29, 2011}}</ref>

'''John Alexander''' (November 29, 1897 – July 13, 1982) was an American stage, film, and television actor.

==Early life==
He was born on November 29, 1897, in [[Newport, Kentucky]]. His father owned steamboats and his mother was a [[telegraph operator]].{{cn|date=August 2022}}

==Career==
He had a career spanning more than 55 years on Broadway with his first role as the title character in ''Elmer Brown, the Only Boy in Town'' in 1908/1909.<ref name=NewYorkT>{{cite news| newspaper=[[The New York Times]]| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/15/obituaries/john-alexander-85-film-and-stage-actor.html| title=John Alexander, 85; Film and Stage Actor| date=July 15, 1982| url-access=subscription}}</ref>

He is best remembered for his performance as Teddy Brewster, a lunatic who thinks he is [[Theodore Roosevelt]], in the 1944 classic film ''[[Arsenic and Old Lace (film)|Arsenic and Old Lace]]'' opposite [[Cary Grant]]. He had previously portrayed that role in the 1941 [[Broadway theater|Broadway]] [[Arsenic and Old Lace (play)|play of the same name]] on which the film was based. He went on to play the "real" Roosevelt in the 1950 [[Bob Hope]] comedy ''[[Fancy Pants (film)|Fancy Pants]]'' and reprised his role as Teddy "Roosevelt" Brewster in the 1955 TV adaptation of ''Arsenic and Old Lace'' in the anthology series ''[[The Best of Broadway]]''.

Among his other notable film roles, Alexander played Steve Edwards in ''[[A Tree Grows in Brooklyn (1945 film)|A Tree Grows in Brooklyn]]'' in 1945, Mr. McComber in ''[[Summer Holiday (1948 film)|Summer Holiday]]'' in 1948, Jack Riker in ''[[Winchester '73]]'' in 1950 and Howard Shipley in ''[[The Marrying Kind]]'' in 1952.

During the 1950s and early 1960, he guest starred on television series, such as ''[[The Phil Silvers Show]]'', ''[[Adventures of the Sea Hawk]]'' and ''[[Car 54, Where Are You?]]'' Alexander's last performance was as Mayor Crane in the Broadway comedy ''[[Never Too Late (play)|Never Too Late]]'', a role he had played since 1962.

Alexander died on July 13, 1982, in New York City.<ref name="NewYorkT"/> He is buried in the Actors Fund of America plot in [[Kensico Cemetery]] in [[Valhalla, New York]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wilson |first1=Scott |title=Resting Places: The Burial Sites of More Than 14,000 Famous Persons, 3d ed. |date=19 August 2016 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1-4766-2599-7 |page=14 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FOHgDAAAQBAJ&q=Mary+Alden |access-date=January 22, 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

'''Judith Therese Evans''' (born July 20, 1975), known professionally as '''Judy Greer''', is an American actress. She is primarily known as a [[character actress]] who has appeared in [[Judy Greer filmography|a wide variety of films]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Bramesco |first=Charles |work=[[Nylon (magazine)|Nylon]] |url=https://nylon.com/articles/judy-greer-joy-frustration-character-actress |title=Fact: Judy Greer Is the Best Person in Hollywood |date=March 28, 2017 |access-date=September 19, 2018}}</ref> She rose to prominence for her supporting roles in the films ''[[Jawbreaker (film)|Jawbreaker]]'' (1999), ''[[What Women Want]]'' (2000), ''[[13 Going on 30]]'' (2004), ''[[Elizabethtown (film)|Elizabethtown]]'' (2005), ''[[27 Dresses]]'' (2008), and ''[[Love & Other Drugs]]'' (2010).

Greer expanded into multiple genres with roles in films such as ''[[The Wedding Planner]]'' (2001), ''[[Adaptation (film)|Adaptation]]'' (2002), ''[[The Village (2004 film)|The Village]]'' (2004), ''[[The Descendants]]'' (2011), ''[[Jeff, Who Lives at Home]]'' (2011), ''[[Carrie (2013 film)|Carrie]]'' (2013), ''[[Men, Women & Children (film)|Men, Women & Children]]'' (2014), ''[[Grandma (2015 film)|Grandma]]'' (2015), ''[[Lemon (2017 film)|Lemon]]'' (2017), ''[[Where'd You Go, Bernadette (film)|Where'd You Go, Bernadette]]'' (2019), ''[[Uncle Frank (film)|Uncle Frank]]'' (2020), and ''[[Hollywood Stargirl]]'' (2022). She appeared in numerous [[blockbuster (entertainment)|blockbusters]], such as ''[[Dawn of the Planet of the Apes]]'' (2014) its sequel ''[[War for the Planet of the Apes]]'' (2017), ''[[Jurassic World]]'' (2015), ''[[Halloween (2018 film)|Halloween]]'' (2018) its sequel ''[[Halloween Kills]]'' (2021), and the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films ''[[Ant-Man (film)|Ant-Man]]'' (2015), ''[[Ant-Man and the Wasp]]'' (2018), and ''[[Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3]]'' (2023).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kit |first=Borys |date=April 3, 2014 |title=Judy Greer Joins 'Jurassic World' |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/judy-greer-joins-jurassic-world-693459/ |access-date=April 11, 2022 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Davids |first=Brian |date=October 16, 2021 |title='Halloween Kills' Stars Judy Greer and Andi Matichak on the Ending: "It's a Bummer" |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/halloween-kills-ending-explained-stars-1235032341/ |access-date=April 11, 2022 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> She made her directorial debut with the comedy-drama film ''[[A Happening of Monumental Proportions]]'' (2017).

On television, Greer is best known for her starring voice role as [[Cheryl Tunt]] in the [[FXX]] animated comedy series ''[[Archer (2009 TV series)|Archer]]'' (2009–2023) and as Lina Bowman in the [[FX (TV channel)|FX]] sitcom ''[[Married (TV series)|Married]]'' (2014–2015). She also appeared in the comedy series ''[[The Big Bang Theory]]'' (2010), ''[[Arrested Development]]'' (2003–2006, 2013–2019), ''[[Two and a Half Men]]'' (2003–2015), ''[[It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia]]'' (2007–2011), ''[[Kidding]]'' (2018–2020), ''[[Let's Go Luna!]]'' (2018–2022), and ''[[Reboot (2022 TV series)|Reboot]]'' (2022).

==Early life==
Greer was born in [[Detroit]], Michigan, on July 20, 1975.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/entertainment/article/judy-greer-laments-rom-com-decline-while-promoting-new-book/ |title=Judy Greer laments rom-com decline while promoting new book |website=CTV News |date=April 9, 2014 |access-date=April 21, 2014 |first=Victoria |last=Ahearn}}</ref><ref name=allmovie>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/235491/Judy-Greer/biography |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141214044034/http://www.nytimes.com/movies/person/235491/Judy-Greer/biography |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 14, 2014 |title=Judy Greer; Alternate Name: Judy Evans Greer, Judith Laura Evans, Judy Evans, Judith Laura Evans |first=Andrea |last=LeVasseur |department=Movies & TV Dept. |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=2014 |access-date=September 26, 2014}}</ref> Her mother, Mollie Ann (''née'' Greer), is a hospital administrator, and her father, Rich Evans, is a mechanical engineer.{{sfn|Greer|2014|p=25}}<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2012/dec/27/judy-greer-arrested-development-get-flashed |title=Judy Greer: 'I get flashed all the time. It's mostly men' |newspaper=The Guardian |date=December 27, 2012 |first=Hermione |last=Hoby}}</ref> Her mother was once a nun, who was "kicked out" of the convent after eight years for wild behavior, including owning a red bathing suit.<ref name="colbert2017">{{cite news |title=Judy Greer Starred Alongside Stephen In A Rejected 2002 Pilot |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NZ05TIoEYUM |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211030/NZ05TIoEYUM |archive-date=October 30, 2021 |access-date=June 16, 2017 |work=[[The Late Show with Stephen Colbert]] |date=June 16, 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Greer was raised [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]]<ref name=wsj>{{cite web |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/behind-the-scenes-with-judy-greer-1400285798 |title=Behind the Scenes with Judy Greer |last=Wolfe |first=Alexandra |date=May 16, 2014 |access-date=September 19, 2018}} {{closed access}}</ref> and grew up in [[Redford, Michigan|Redford Township]] and [[Livonia, Michigan|Livonia]].<ref name=krug/> She attended [[Winston Churchill High School (Wayne County, Michigan)|Churchill High School]],<ref name=krug>{{cite web |work=[[Metro Times|The Metro Times]] |location=Detroit |url=https://www.metrotimes.com/news-hits/archives/2014/10/23/livonia-native-judy-greer-on-films-tv-and-her-new-book |title=Livonia native Judy Greer on films, TV, and her new book |last=Krug |first=Kurt Anthony |date=October 23, 2014 |access-date=April 23, 2026}}</ref> where she was a part of the Creative and Performing Arts Program and graduated from [[The Theatre School at DePaul University]] in 1997 with a [[Bachelor of Fine Arts]] degree.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://theatreschool.depaul.edu/special_programs_awards.php |title=Awards For Excellence In The Arts |date=May 4, 2006 |website=The Theater School at DePaul University |access-date=July 30, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 13, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060813042958/http://theatreschool.depaul.edu/special_programs_awards.php}}</ref> She later adopted her mother's maiden name for her stage name, as several other actresses are named Judy or Judi Evans.

==Career==
===1997–2003===
Greer made her film debut in the horror film ''Stricken'' (1998), as a college student involved in a fatal prank.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/stricken/ |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |title=Stricken (1998) |access-date=September 17, 2018}}</ref> This was followed by a small role in the Chicago-filmed drama ''[[Kissing a Fool]]'' (1998). She was cast in her first major role as Fern Mayo, a nerdy teenager who uncovers her classmates' murder of their friend, in [[Darren Stein]]'s black comedy ''[[Jawbreaker (film)|Jawbreaker]]'' (1999).<ref name=jb>{{cite web |work=[[Vice Media|Broadly]] |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/perverting-the-youth-of-america-the-oral-history-of-teen-classic-jawbreaker/ |title='Perverting the Youth of America': The Oral History of Teen Classic 'Jawbreaker' |date=August 14, 2016 |access-date=September 19, 2018 |last=Sunderland |first=Mitchell}}</ref> Greer followed this with small parts in the romantic comedy films, ''[[What Women Want]]'' (2000)<ref>{{cite web |work=[[BBC One]] |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b0074dkr |title=What Women Want |access-date=April 23, 2026}}</ref> and ''[[The Wedding Planner]]'' (2001).<ref name=talks>{{cite magazine |url=https://ew.com/article/2015/10/01/judy-greer-married-memorable-roles/ |date=October 1, 2015 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |title=Judy Greer talks 'Arrested Development,' '13 Going on 30,' 'The Descendants,' 'The Wedding Planner,' and more... |last=Li |first=Shirley |access-date=September 19, 2018}}</ref> She was cast in a 2002 pilot for NBC alongside [[Stephen Colbert]], ''Untitled Ken Finkleman Project'' ([[Imagine Entertainment]]), based on the Canadian show ''[[The Newsroom (Canadian TV series)|The Newsroom]]'' from [[Ken Finkleman]]. Colbert portrayed Finkleman and Greer played his sister.<ref name="colbert2017"/>

Greer had a recurring role on the [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]] comedy series ''[[Arrested Development]]'' (2003–2005, 2013, 2018), playing [[List of Arrested Development characters|Kitty Sanchez]] in ten episodes total and appearing in each of the series' three original seasons. In a 2009 interview, she said that she is most recognized for this role.<ref name="goldman">{{cite web |url=http://tv.ign.com/articles/101/1014154p1.html |title=Judy Greer Gets Animated with Glenn Martin, DDS and Archer |access-date=July 30, 2010 |last=Goldman |first=Eric |date=August 14, 2009 |website=IGN}}</ref> She also had a supporting role in ''[[Adaptation (film)|Adaptation]]'' (2002).

===2004–2010===
In 2004, Greer co-starred in the romantic comedy ''[[13 Going on 30]]'', starring [[Jennifer Garner]] as a girl who wakes up one morning as a 30-year-old woman. Greer played Lucy, an untrustworthy fellow editor of Garner's at a fashion magazine where both work.<ref>{{cite news |title="13 Going on 30" Gets Underway |url=http://movies.about.com/cs/upcomingreleases/a/13goingnews.htm |access-date=October 28, 2014 |website=[[About.com]] |date=May 13, 2003 |archive-date=September 22, 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050922165433/http://movies.about.com/cs/upcomingreleases/a/13goingnews.htm |url-status=dead}}</ref> The film was a commercial success, grossing $96.5 million worldwide, and received positive reviews from critics.<ref>{{cite web |title=13 Going on 30 (2004) |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=13goingon30.htm |website=[[Box Office Mojo]] |access-date=September 9, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/13_going_on_30 |title=13 Going on 30 (2004) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=January 1, 2021}}</ref> Greer had a supporting role in [[M. Night Shyamalan]]'s thriller film ''[[The Village (2004 film)|The Village]]'', about a village whose population lives in fear of creatures inhabiting the woods beyond it. Despite mixed reviews, the film was a success at the box office, grossing $256.7 million worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/village |title=The Village (2004) |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=October 20, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=village.htm |title=The Village (2004) |website=[[Box Office Mojo]]}}</ref> Greer then played another supporting role in [[Jenna Fischer]]'s directorial debut, the comedy ''[[LolliLove]]'', which premiered at the [[St. Louis International Film Festival]] to positive reviews from critics, though it was ultimately released straight-to-DVD.<ref>{{cite news |title=St. Louis theaters become an import-export market |last=Williams |first=Joe |department=Talking Pictures |newspaper=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]] (MO) |date=March 18, 2005 |page=E1 |url=http://docs.newsbank.com/g/GooglePM/SL/lib00170,108F399CC06A405F.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130129204033/http://docs.newsbank.com/g/GooglePM/SL/lib00170,108F399CC06A405F.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 29, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Bill |last=Gibron |date=February 9, 2006 |title=DVD Talk Review: LolliLove |url=https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/read.php?ID=20095 |website=DVD Talk |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061009161528/https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/read.php?ID=20095 |archive-date=October 9, 2006}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=February 7, 2006 |first=Christopher |last=Curry |title=LolliLove (DVD) |website=[[Film Threat]] |url=https://www.filmthreat.com/reviews/8614/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110711003748/https://www.filmthreat.com/reviews/8614/ |archive-date=July 11, 2011}}</ref>

In 2005, Greer first played a female werewolf in [[Wes Craven]]'s horror film ''[[Cursed (2005 film)|Cursed]]'', starring [[Christina Ricci]] and [[Jesse Eisenberg]]. The film was a failure at the box office and was widely panned by critics, with Craven later expressing disappointment in the film.<ref>{{cite web |author=Capone |url=http://www.aintitcool.com/node/37854 |title=Wes Craven talks to Capone about 25/8, remakes, and the 'Cursed' experience of revisiting old franchises!! |website=Ain't It Cool News |date=March 1, 2009 |access-date=September 2, 2017}}</ref> Greer then starred in the comedy-drama ''[[The Great New Wonderful]]'', which depicts the lives of several New Yorkers one year after the [[September 11th attacks]]. In her character's vignette, Greer played a woman struggling to keep her marriage together. The film premiered at the [[Tribeca Film Festival]] to mostly positive reviews.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/great_new_wonderful/ |title=''The Great New Wonderful'' (2005) |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> Ty Burr of the ''Boston Globe'' called the film "an actor's playpen", and remarked that "Greer has been stuck so long in goofball supporting roles that she tears into this part – a smart, loving mother frightened of her own son – as if it were prime rib."<ref>{{cite web |last=Burr |first=Ty |url=https://archive.boston.com/ae/movies/articles/2006/06/23/wonderful_is_a_quietly_rich_post_911_study/ |title='Wonderful' is a quietly rich post-9/11 study |work=Boston Globe |date=June 23, 2006 |access-date=July 5, 2021}}</ref> Following an appearance in the drama ''[[In Memory of My Father]]'', Greer featured in [[Cameron Crowe]]'s tragic-romantic comedy ''[[Elizabethtown (film)|Elizabethtown]]'', starring [[Orlando Bloom]], [[Kirsten Dunst]], [[Alec Baldwin]] and [[Susan Sarandon]]. The film premiered at the [[Venice International Film Festival]] and garnered negative reviews from critics.<ref>{{cite web |title=Elizabethtown (2005) |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/elizabethtown |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media]] |location=San Francisco, California |language=en |access-date=February 12, 2021}}</ref>

[[File:Judy Greer LF.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Greer at the premiere of ''[[27 Dresses]]'' in 2008]]

scriptwriter ([[David Duchovny]]) of a television series.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/american_dreamz/ |title=American Dreamz (2007) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=June 14, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100213002421/http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/american_dreamz/ |archive-date=February 13, 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> The film premiered at the [[Tribeca Film Festival]] to generally positive reviews from critics.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0473709/releaseinfo |title=The TV Set release dates |work=[[IMDb]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The TV Set (2007) |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/tv_set |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=May 21, 2020}}</ref> Dana Stevens of ''Slate'' comedy-drama series ''[[Love Monkey]]'' (2006).<ref name="zap">{{cite web |url=http://tv.zap2it.com/tveditorial/tve_main/1,1002,271%7C99968%7C1%7C,00.html |title=CBS Breaks Up with 'Love Monkey' |date=February 10, 2006 |website=Zap2It |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061206094435/http://tv.zap2it.com/tveditorial/tve_main/1,1002,271%7C99968%7C1%7C,00.html |archive-date=December 6, 2006}}</ref> The following year, Greer made brief appearances in the independent road film ''[[The Go-Getter (2007 film)|The Go-Getter]]'' and the comedy ''[[The Grand (film)|The Grand]]'' (both 2007).<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_pwwi/is_200806/ai_n25497811 |title=Peace Arch Entertainment Sets U.S. Theatrical Release of "The for producer [[Chuck Lorre]], having appeared in his sitcoms ''[[Two and a Half Men]]'' (2007–2015), ''[[The Big Bang Theory]]'' (2010), and ''[[Mom (TV series)|Mom]]'' (2015).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.seattlepi.com/ae/tv/tvguide/article/Exclusive-Judy-Greer-to-Star-as-Ashton-Kutcher-s-2146393.php |title=Greer to star on Two and a Half Men |date=September 2, 2011 |website=[[Seattle Post-Intelligencer]] |access-date=August 29, 2011}}{{dead link |date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref>

In 2008, Greer starred opposite [[Zach Galifianakis]] in the independent satire ''[[Visioneers]]'', and played the best friend of a bridesmaid in the romantic comedy ''[[27 Dresses]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/visioneers/ |title=Visioneers (2008) |website=Rotten Tomatoes}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Film > 27 Dresses – Production Notes |url=http://www.kheigl.com/press/27-dresses-production-notes/ |website=Kheigl.com |access-date=August 16, 2013}}</ref> The latter film received mostly negative reviews from critics, but was a commercial success, grossing $162.6 million worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/27_dresses/ |title=27 Dresses – Movie Reviews, Trailers, Pictures – Rotten Tomatoes |access-date=April 6, 2019 |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080117093536/http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/27_dresses/#rate |archive-date=January 17, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=27dresses.htm |title=27 Dresses |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |publisher=[[Amazon.com]]}}</ref> Greer played a similar role in the romantic drama ''[[Love Happens (2009 film)|Love Happens]]'' (2009), starring [[Jennifer Aniston]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/love_happens |title=Love Happens (2009) |website=Rotten Tomatoes |access-date=May 21, 2020}}</ref> Greer also took on the leading role in the [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] sitcom ''[[Miss Guided]]'' (2008), in which she played a guidance counselor working at a high school. The series was canceled after one season.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://thefutoncritic.com/news.aspx?id=7645 |title=11 series didn't make the cut for ABC's 2008–09 season schedule |date=May 13, 2008 |website=TheFutonCritic}}</ref> That same year, Greer appeared as a [[yoga]] instructor in the "[[Get a Mac]]" advertisements, which also featured [[John Hodgman]] and [[Justin Long]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Foresman |first=Chris |url=https://arstechnica.com/apple/2008/04/new-get-a-mac-ads-feature-some-geek-chic-co-stars/ |title=New Get a Mac ads feature some geek chic co-stars |website=Ars Technica |date=April 2, 2008 |access-date=January 17, 2013}}</ref> Beginning in 2009, Greer has provided the voice of [[Cheryl Tunt]] in the FX animated adult sitcom ''[[Archer (2009 TV series)|Archer]]'', as well as Wendy Park in the [[Nick at Nite]] stop-motion animated sitcom ''[[Glenn Martin, DDS]]'' (2009–2011).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://collider.com/comic-con-archer-interviews-judy-greer-chris-parnell-adam-reed/ |title=SDCC 2010: Archer Interviews with Judy Greer, Chris Parnell, and Creator Adam Reed |access-date=July 30, 2010 |last=Lasker |first=Jake |date=July 23, 2010 |website=Collider.com |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100726140124/http://www.collider.com/2010/07/23/comic-con-archer-interviews-judy-greer-chris-parnell-adam-reed |archive-date=July 26, 2010}}</ref>

In 2010, Greer first starred in the comedy ''[[Barry Munday]]'', in which she played a woman who becomes pregnant by a lonely womanizer ([[Patrick Wilson]]). Hall]]) is revealed to have an addiction to pornography from his brother's thinly veiled novel about their family. ===2011–2014===
In 2011, Greer first starred in the crime thriller ''[[The Key Man (2011 film)|The Key Man]]'', as the wife of a salesman who becomes involved in an insurance scam. The film premiered at South by Southwest.<ref>{{cite web |title=Meet the 2011 SXSW Filmmakers: "The Key Man" Director Peter Himmelstein |date=March 10, 2011 |website=[[IndieWire]] |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2011/03/meet-the-2011-sxsw-filmmakers-the-key-man-director-peter-himmelstein-243365/ |access-date=March 24, 2018}}</ref> Though Seth Freilich of ''Pajiba'' considered Greer to be "lovely as always", he felt that she was "underused", and called for the film industry to offer her better roles.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pajiba.com/film_reviews/the-key-man-review-theres-a-sucker-born-every-minute.php |title=The Key Man Review: There's A Sucker Born Every Minute |last=Freilich |first=Seth |work=Pajiba |date=March 8, 2011 |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref> Greer starred in [[Alexander Payne]]'s film ''[[The Descendants]]'', alongside [[George Clooney]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Jason |last=Guerrasio |title=Alexander Payne's 'The Descendants' Begins Shooting |url=http://filmmakermagazine.com/news/2010/03/alexander-paynes-the-descendants-begins-shooting/ |work=[[Filmmaker (magazine)|Filmmaker]] |date=March 15, 2010 |access-date=October 29, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100323033843/http://filmmakermagazine.com/news/2010/03/alexander-paynes-the-descendants-begins-shooting/ |archive-date=March 23, 2010 |url-status=live}}</ref> Greer played a woman who discovers that her husband had an extramarital affair with the now-comatose wife of the attorney. The film premiered at the [[Telluride Film Festival]] to critical acclaim.<ref name="variety09072011">{{cite news |url=https://variety.com/2011/film/news/descendants-gets-earlier-bow-1118042405/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110915221329/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1118042405 |archive-date=September 15, 2011 |date=September 7, 2011 |access-date=September 15, 2011 |title='Descendants' gets earlier bow: Clooney starrer beats Thanksgiving glut with Nov. 18 rollout |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |first=Rachel |url-status=live |last=Abrams}}</ref> Greer herself received particularly strong reviews for her performance; David Thomson of ''The New Republic'' found Greer to be "touching", while Philip Kemp of ''Sight & Sound'' praised Greer for turning "her few brief scenes [...] into a moving portrayal of undeservedly broken trust."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Thomson |first=David |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/97757/the-descendents-george-clooney-alexander-payne |title=David Thomson on Films: A Mainstream Movie for People Tired of Noise and Violence |magazine=The New Republic |date=November 24, 2011 |access-date=July 4, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Kemp |first=Philip |url=http://old.bfi.org.uk/sightandsound/review/6771 |title=Film of the month: The Descendants |work=Sight & Sound |date=February 2012 |access-date=July 4, 2021 |archive-date=July 11, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711030357/http://old.bfi.org.uk/sightandsound/review/6771 |url-status=dead}}</ref> For her performance in the film, Greer received nominations for the [[Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast in a Motion Picture]] and the [[Satellite Award for Best Supporting Actress – Motion Picture]].<ref name="Pond">{{cite web |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-sagensemble-rules/sag-ensemble-rule-rewards-stars-shortchanges-key-actors-idUSTRE7BG02Q20111217 |work=Reuters |title=SAG ensemble rule rewards stars, shortchanges key actors |last=Pond |first=Steve |date=December 16, 2011 |access-date=September 17, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pressacademy.com/award_cat/2011/ |title=2011 Satellite Awards |website=International Press Academy |access-date=April 28, 2016}}</ref>

In an interview with ''Glamour'', Greer revealed that she had wanted to venture into directing and contacted AOL herself, which was impressed by her passion for the meditation.<ref name=glam>{{cite web |last=Radloff |first=Jessica |title=Judy Greer Has the Perfect Solution for Coping With Stress in Her New AOL Short |date=May 5, 2014 |url=http://www.glamour.com/entertainment/blogs/obsessed/2014/05/judy-greer-has-the-perfect-sol.html |access-date=May 14, 2014 |quote=Greer is adding director to her resume as she showcases why Transcendental Meditation has become such a huge part of her life.}}</ref> Greer also released her first autobiographical collection of essays, titled ''I Don't Know What You Know Me From: Confessions of a Co-Star'', which details her life experiences and career in the film industry.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Luberecki |first1=Beth |title=Judy Greer dishes on her new book 'I Don't Know What You Know Me From' |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/express/wp/2014/05/14/judy-greer-dishes-on-her-new-book-i-dont-know-what-you-know-me-from/ |access-date=July 14, 2014 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=May 14, 2014}}</ref> The book received positive reviews; ===2015–2018===
In 2015, Greer appeared in two major film franchises—''[[Jurassic World]]'', and the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] entry, ''[[Ant-Man (film)|Ant-Man]]''.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://hollywoodreporter.com/heat-vision/judy-greer-joins-jurassic-world-693459 |title=Judy Greer Joins 'Jurassic World' |magazine=The Hollywood Reporter |access-date=April 3, 2014}}</ref><ref name="Greer">{{cite web |url=http://www.heyuguys.com/interview-judy-greer-men-women-and-children/ |title=The HeyUGuys Interview: Judy Greer on Men, Women and Children, Twitter and Marvel's Ant-Man |website=HeyUGuys.com |date=December 3, 2014 |access-date=December 3, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141203214557/http://www.heyuguys.com/interview-judy-greer-men-women-and-children/ |archive-date=December 3, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref> In ''Jurassic World'', Greer played the mother of two of the film's protagonists, Gray and Zach. The film was a major success at the box-office, grossing $1.670 billion worldwide, and received positive reviews from critics.<ref>{{cite Box Office Mojo |title=Jurassic World |id=0369610 |access-date=January 24, 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210124224508/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0369610/ |archive-date=January 24, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite Rotten Tomatoes |id=jurassic_world |type=m |title=Jurassic World |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151128182157/http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/jurassic_world/ |archive-date=November 28, 2015 |url-status=live |access-date=January 16, 2021}}</ref> In ''Ant-Man'', Greer played the ex-wife of the film's titular hero ([[Paul Rudd]]). That same year, Greer made her feature-film directorial debut in the comedy-drama ''[[A Happening of Monumental Proportions]]'', which depicts one day in the lives of students and staff at a Los Angeles private school. In an interview with ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'', Greer discussed her motivations towards making the film: "I wanted to tell a story where adults act like kids and kids act like adults [...] As I age I'm noticing that more and more, as we see our kids pointing things out to us that we really should know ourselves, you start to realize that you and your adult friends are king of acting like idiots sometimes. We're regressing, clawing at the walls as if to say, I don't want to grow up."<ref>{{cite web |last=Saval |first=Malina |url=https://variety.com/2017/film/news/judy-greer-a-happening-of-monumental-proportions-1202410554/ |title=Judy Greer Talks Directing for the First Time and How to Find a Story to Tell |work=Variety |date=May 5, 2017 |access-date=June 29, 2021}}</ref> The film stars [[Allison Janney]], [[Katie Holmes]], [[Bradley Whitford]], [[Jennifer Garner]] (Greer's co-star from ''13 Going on 30'') and rapper [[Common (rapper)|Common]], received largely negative reviews from critics.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/a_happening_of_monumental_proportions |title=A Happening of Monumental Proportions (2018) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=July 13, 2020}}</ref>

In 2018, Greer first played a supporting role in [[Clint Eastwood]]'s biographical film ''[[The 15:17 to Paris]]'', as the mother of U.S. Air Force Staff Sergeant [[Spencer Stone]]. As part of an overall negative response, Tim Grierson of ''ScreenDaily'' lamented that Greer and co-star [[Jenna Fischer]] were "trapped playing supportive-parent clichés."<ref>{{cite web |last=Grierson |first=Tim |url=https://www.screendaily.com/reviews/the-1517-to-paris-review/5126349.article |title='The 15:17 To Paris': Review |work=ScreenDaily |date=February 7, 2018 |access-date=June 29, 2021}}</ref> Greer followed with [[Jim Loach]]'s comedy-drama ''[[Measure of a Man (film)|Measure of a Man]]''. [[Mick LaSalle]] of the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' felt she was "wasted" in the role of a mother whose teenage son is experiencing bullying.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/news/judy-greer-luke-wilson-find-measure-man/ |title=Judy Greer And Luke Wilson Find Measure Of A Man |first=Owen |last=Williams |work=[[Empire Online]] |date=October 6, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/movies/article/Sutherland-Greer-and-Wilson-wasted-in-Measure-12897844.php |title=Sutherland, Greer and Wilson wasted in 'Measure of a Man' |first=Mick |last=LaSalle |author-link=Mick LaSalle |date=May 10, 2018 |newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]}}</ref> Greer co-starred in the biographical film ''[[Driven (2018 film)|Driven]]'', in which she played the wife of a man ([[Jason Sudeikis]]), who gets busted by the [[FBI]] for trying to smuggle [[cocaine]] and subsequently becomes an informant to [[John DeLorean]] of [[DeLorean Motor Company]] (DMC). The film premiered at the [[75th Venice International Film Festival|Venice International Film Festival]].<ref name="deadlinetoronto">{{Cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2018/09/driven-movie-first-look-john-delorean-hurricane-maria-video-1202458925/ |title=John DeLorean Story 'Driven' Closing Venice, Hoping For Big Toronto Sale After Barely Surviving Puerto Rico Hurricane |last=Hammond |first=Pete |date=September 8, 2018 |website=Deadline Hollywood |access-date=July 29, 2019 |archive-date=June 19, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190619142619/https://deadline.com/2018/09/driven-movie-first-look-john-delorean-hurricane-maria-video-1202458925/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Guy Lodge of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' remarked that Greer was "reliably game in a princess-to-patsy part," while Boyd Van Hoeij of ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'' felt that Greer was "especially good" in a scene where she finds a wire on her husband.<ref name="varietyreview">{{cite web |date=September 8, 2018 |last=Lodge |first=Guy |title=Film Review: 'Driven' |url=https://variety.com/2018/film/reviews/driven-review-1202933205/ |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |access-date=September 9, 2020 |archive-date=November 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125033407/https://variety.com/2018/film/reviews/driven-review-1202933205/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Van Hoeij |first=Boyd |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-reviews/driven-review-1141286/ |title='Driven': Film Review {{!}} Venice 2018 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=September 8, 2018 |access-date=June 29, 2021}}</ref>

==Personal life==
[[File:Judy Greer July 14, 2014 (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|upright|100px|Greer in July 2014]]
In 2011, Greer married Dean E. Johnsen, an executive producer of ''[[Real Time with Bill Maher]]'', becoming the stepmother to his two children from an earlier marriage.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.usmagazine.com/celebrity-news/news/actress-judy-greer-marries-dean-johnson-20111912 |title=Actress Judy Greer Marries Dean Johnsen |first=Zach |last=Johnson |date=December 19, 2011 |website=US magazine |access-date=February 1, 2012}}</ref>

Greer grew up Catholic, although at the age of 10 in 1985, she convinced her parents to let her go to a Presbyterian church, claiming that she thought she would be closer to God there. The real reason was that she thought the boys were cuter at that church.<ref name="colbert2017"/> In 2014, Greer stated that she was no longer a Catholic.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://interviewly.com/i/judy-greer-apr-2014-reddit |title=Interviewly -Judy Greer April 2014 – reddit AMA |work=Interviewly |access-date=April 28, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160428092723/http://interviewly.com/i/judy-greer-apr-2014-reddit |archive-date=April 28, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2014, she told ''[[Glamour (magazine)|Glamour]]'', "I had been wanting to try to learn how to meditate, and I did research on the different types of meditation. [[Transcendental Meditation technique|TM]] seemed the easiest, and I liked that it wasn't religious in any way."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.glamour.com/story/judy-greer-has-the-perfect-sol |title=Judy Greer Has the Perfect Solution for Coping With Stress in Her New AOL Short |last=Radloff |first=Jessica |work=Glamour |date=May 5, 2014 |access-date=October 7, 2020}}</ref>

Greer is a member of the board of directors of [[Project Chimps]], a sanctuary for former research chimpanzees.<ref>[https://projectchimps.org/about/board-of-directors/ Board of Directors], Project Chimps, accessed November 15, 2022</ref>

She is a registered [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Judy Greer Does The Michigan Minute! |url=https://michigandems.com/hometown-pride-famous-michiganders-connect-with-voters-in-their-hometown/ |date=October 29, 2020 |website=Michigan Democratic Party |access-date=May 12, 2021}}</ref>

'''Anthony Asbury''' is an American actor and puppeteer. He has been working as a puppeteer for over three decades.

==Career==
Asbury, a native of [[Arlington, Texas]], began his career as a puppeteer on the [[ITV Network|ITV]] satire show ''[[Spitting Image]]'', where he performed a majority of characters between 1984 and 1992, these included voicing several of the characters including [[Pope John Paul II]], [[John McEnroe]], and [[Edwin Meese]], together with [[Steve Nallon]] he was the puppeteer for [[Margaret Thatcher]] from the second season. It was on Spitting Image that he met [[Louise Gold]], who introduced Asbury to [[Jim Henson]], who at the time was currently in the proceeds of production for ''[[Labyrinth (1986 film)|Labyrinth]]''. Henson invited Asbury to perform some of the creatures for the film, he was the puppeteer for Firey 5, One of the Four Guards, Right Door Knocker. He later remained associated with the Henson company, performing puppets for other film and television roles these included ''[[The Witches (1990 film)|The Witches]]'', ''[[The Flintstones (film)|The Flintstones]]'', and ''[[The Wubbulous World of Dr. Seuss]]''.

Asbury's other roles include ''[[Little Shop of Horrors (film)|Little Shop of Horrors]]'' and ''[[Absolutely Fabulous]]''.
