'''René Marie Murat Auberjonois''' ({{IPAc-en|r|ə|ˈ|n|eɪ|_|oʊ|ˌ|b|ɛər|ʒ|ən|ˈ|w|ɑː}} {{respell|rə|NAY|_|oh|BAIR|zhən|WAH}};<ref>{{YouTube|lGnDakkxZCQ|Video Greeting from Rene Auberjonois}}</ref> June 1, 1940 – December 8, 2019) was an American actor. He was a [[Tony Awards|Tony Award]] and [[Drama Desk Awards|Drama Desk Award]] winner, and a three-time [[Emmy Awards|Emmy Award]] (two [[Primetime Emmy Awards|Primetime]], one [[Daytime Emmy Awards|Daytime]]) nominee, among other accolades.

He first achieved fame as a stage actor, winning the [[Tony Award for Best Featured Actor in a Musical]] in 1970 for his portrayal of Sebastian Baye opposite [[Katharine Hepburn]] in the [[André Previn]]–[[Alan Jay Lerner]] musical ''[[Coco (musical)|Coco]]''. He went on to earn three more Tony nominations for performances in [[Neil Simon]]'s ''[[The Good Doctor (play)|The Good Doctor]]'' (1973), [[Roger Miller]]'s ''[[Big River (musical)|Big River]]'' (1985), and [[Cy Coleman]]'s ''[[City of Angels (musical)|City of Angels]]'' (1989); he won a [[Drama Desk Award]] for ''Big River''. In 2018, Auberjonois was inducted into the [[American Theater Hall of Fame]].<ref name=":0"/>

A screen actor with more than 200 credits, Auberjonois was most famous for portraying characters in the main casts of several long-running television series, including Clayton Endicott III on ''[[Benson (TV series)|Benson]]'' (1980–86), for which he was an Emmy nominee; [[Odo (Star Trek)|Odo]] on ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' (1993–99), and [[Paul Lewiston]] on ''[[Boston Legal]]'' (2004–08). In films, Auberjonois appeared in several [[Robert Altman]] productions, notably [[List of M*A*S*H characters#Father John Mulcahy|Father John Mulcahy]] in the film version of ''[[M*A*S*H (film)|M*A*S*H]]'' (1970); the expedition scientist Roy Bagley in ''[[King Kong (1976 film)|King Kong]]'' (1976); Chef Louis in ''[[The Little Mermaid (1989 film)|The Little Mermaid]]'' (1989), in which he sang "[[Les Poissons]]"; and Reverend Oliver in ''[[The Patriot (2000 film)|The Patriot]]'' (2000). Auberjonois also performed as a voice actor in several video games, most notable being his role as Mr. Robert Edwin House, the reclusive Las Vegas casino owner in ''[[Fallout: New Vegas]]'' (2010).

== Early life and education ==
René Marie Murat Auberjonois was born June 1, 1940, in [[Manhattan]], New York City.<ref name="NYTO">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/08/obituaries/rene-auberjonois-dead.html|title=René Auberjonois, a 'Deep Space Nine' Star, Dies at 79|newspaper=The New York Times|date=December 8, 2019|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191209001004/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/08/obituaries/rene-auberjonois-dead.html|archive-date=December 9, 2019|last=Genzlinger|first=Neil|author-link=Neil Genzlinger}}</ref> His father, Swiss-born [[Fernand Auberjonois]], was a [[Cold War]]–era foreign correspondent and [[Pulitzer Prize]]–nominated writer. Auberjonois' mother, Princess Laure Louise Napoléone Eugénie Caroline Murat, was a great-great-granddaughter of [[Joachim Murat]] (one of [[Napoleon]]'s [[Marshal of the Empire|marshals]] and [[Kingdom of Naples|King of Naples]] during the [[First French Empire]]), and his wife—Napoleon's youngest sister—[[Caroline Bonaparte]]. Auberjonois had a sister and a brother, and two half-sisters from his mother's first marriage.<ref>{{Cite news| url=http://www.postgazette.com/pg/04241/369197.stm| title=Obituary: Fernand Auberjonois/Much admired foreign correspondent who lived a chronicle of 20th century| newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]| date=August 28, 2004| first=Jack| last=Lessenberry| agency=Block News Alliance| access-date=November 2, 2019| archive-date=January 22, 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090122213236/http://www.postgazette.com/pg/04241/369197.stm| url-status=dead}}</ref> Auberjonois wrote that his French family name, an uncommon one in the United States, means "[[armorer]]."<ref>{{Cite web| url=https://renefiles.com/facts-biography/rene-answers-your-questions/trek/| title=Trek Questions |website= renefiles.com| access-date=November 2, 2019}}</ref>

Auberjonois' grandfather, also named [[René Auberjonois (painter)|René Auberjonois]], was a Swiss [[post-Impressionist]] painter. His maternal grandmother, Hélène Macdonald Stallo, was an American from [[Cincinnati]], Ohio; his maternal grandfather's mother was a Russian noblewoman, Eudoxia Michailovna Somova, and his maternal grandfather's paternal grandmother, Caroline Georgina Fraser, who was the wife of [[Prince Napoleon Lucien Charles Murat]], was a Scottish American from [[Charleston, South Carolina]].

Auberjonois' family moved to Paris after [[World War II]]. After a few years in France, the family moved back to the United States and joined the [[South Mountain Road]] artists' colony in [[Rockland County, New York]], whose residents included [[Burgess Meredith]], [[John Houseman]], and [[Lotte Lenya]].<ref>{{Cite court | litigants=New York Trap Rock Corp. v. The Town of Clarkstown et al.| reporter=NY 272 App. Div.| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x83ffjFYLB4C| opinion=1021| court=Appellate Division, Supreme Court of New York, Second Department| date=May 11, 1955| access-date=December 9, 2019}}</ref>

The Auberjonois family also lived for a time in London, where Auberjonois completed high school while studying theater.<ref name="Rawson">{{Cite news| title=Theater Hall of Fame inductee Rene Auberjonois has Pittsburgh ties| url=https://www.post-gazette.com/ae/theater-dance/2018/11/16/Theater-Hall-of-Fame-inductee-Rene-Auberjonois-has-Pittsburgh-ties/stories/201811160111| date=November 16, 2018| newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]| last=Rawson| first=Christopher| access-date= December 9, 2019}}</ref> To complete his education, he attended the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now [[Carnegie Mellon University]]), and graduated with a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the College of Fine Arts in 1962.<ref>{{Cite journal| url= https://www.cmu.edu/cmnews/051001/051001_rene.html| journal=Carnegie Mellon News| date=May 10, 2001| title="Esteemed Group" Garners Honorary Degrees at 104th Commencement| quote= Called an 'actor's actor' by his peers, Auberjonois, a 1962 graduate of the School of Drama, earned many accolades for his performances in television, in film and on Broadway during his 40-year career.| access-date=November 2, 2019}}</ref>

== Career ==
=== Theater ===
After college, Auberjonois worked with several different theater companies, beginning with three years at the prestigious [[Arena Stage]] in Washington, D.C. Auberjonois later stated that the school was his unofficial graduate school.<ref name="Rawson"/> He traveled between Los Angeles, California, and New York, working in numerous theater productions. He helped found Bill Ball's [[American Conservatory Theater]] in Pittsburgh, playing the title roles in both "[[Tartuffe]]" and "[[King Lear]]," before moving with the company to San Francisco. Then came the [[Mark Taper Forum]] in Los Angeles, and the [[Brooklyn Academy of Music]] Repertory Company in New York City. He was a member of the [[Peninsula Players]] summer theater program during the 1962 season.<ref>Peninsula Players 65th Anniversary Program, 1999</ref>

Auberjonois was a member of the original faculty of the [[Juilliard School]]'s Drama Division when it opened in 1968 under [[John Houseman]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Farah |date=September 14, 2007 |title=Juilliard Drama Division Opens (1968) |url=https://journal.juilliard.edu/journal/juilliard-drama-division-opens-1968 |work=Juilliard Journal|first=Jeni Dahmus}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Kathleen |date=December 9, 2019 |title=Remembering René Auberjonois |url=https://www.geekscape.net/remembering-rene-auberjonois |website=Geekscape|first=Deidra}}</ref>

In 1968, Auberjonois landed a role on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]], and appeared in three plays that season: as Fool to [[Lee J. Cobb]]'s ''[[King Lear]]'' (the longest running production of the play in Broadway history), as Ned in ''[[A Cry of Players]]'' (which played in repertory with ''King Lear'') opposite [[Frank Langella]], and as Marco in ''Fire!'' In 1969, he earned a [[Tony Award]] for his performance as Sebastian Baye alongside [[Katharine Hepburn]] in ''[[Coco (musical)|Coco]]''.<ref name="tony-db">{{Cite web| title=Tony Awards Database: René Auberjonois| url=http://www.tonyawards.com/p/tonys_search?start=0&year=&award=&lname=Ren%E9+Auberjonois&fname=&show=| publisher=American Theatre Wing| access-date=January 29, 2008| archive-date=January 23, 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090123174949/http://www.tonyawards.com/p/tonys_search?start=0&year=&award=&lname=Ren%E9+Auberjonois&fname=&show=| url-status=dead}}</ref>

He received Tony nominations for his roles in [[Neil Simon]]'s ''[[The Good Doctor (play)|The Good Doctor]]'' (1973) opposite [[Christopher Plummer]]; as the Duke in ''[[Big River (musical)|Big River]]'' (1984), winning a [[Drama Desk Award]]; and, memorably, as Buddy Fidler/Irwin S. Irving in ''[[City of Angels (musical)|City of Angels]]'' (1989), written by [[Larry Gelbart]] and [[Cy Coleman]].<ref name="tony-db"/>

Auberjonois' other [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] appearances included Malvolio in ''[[Twelfth Night]]'' (1972); Scapin in ''Tricks'' (1973); Mr. Samsa in ''[[The Metamorphosis|Metamorphosis]]'' (1989); Professor Abronsius in ''[[Dance of the Vampires (musical)|Dance of the Vampires]]'', the English-language version of [[Jim Steinman]]'s musical adaptation of ''Tanz der Vampire''; and Jethro Crouch in ''[[Sly Fox]]'' (2004), for which he was nominated for Outstanding Featured Actor in a Play, an [[Outer Critics Circle Award]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.playbill.com/article/outer-critics-circle-award-nominations-announced-wicked-soars-with-10-com-119162|title=Outer Critics Circle Award Nominations Announced; Wicked Soars with 10|last=Ernio |first=Hernandez |date=April 18, 2004|website=Playbill|access-date=December 24, 2019}}</ref>

Auberjonois appeared many times at the [[Mark Taper Forum]], notably as [[Malvolio]] in ''Twelfth Night'' and as [[Stanislavski]] in ''Chekhov in Yalta''. As a member of the Second Drama Quartet,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Woodard|first=Josef|title=Theater: The Second Drama Quartet Follows in Famous Footsteps : It reprises a 'Don Juan in Hell' acclaimed when done by Charles Laughton, Tyrone Power and Agnes Moorehead. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-04-28-vl-51435-story.html |website=Los Angeles Times |access-date=December 9, 2019 |date=April 28, 1994}}</ref> he toured with [[Ed Asner]], [[Dianne Wiest]], and [[Harris Yulin]]. He appeared in the [[Tom Stoppard]] and [[André Previn]] work, ''[[Every Good Boy Deserves Favour (play)|Every Good Boy Deserves Favor]]'', at the [[John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts]] in Washington, D.C., and the [[Metropolitan Opera]] in New York.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gussow |first=Mel |date=July 31, 1979 |title=Theater: Stoppard's 'Every Good Boy' |pages=C8 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/120793056 |url-access=subscription |access-date=September 14, 2023 |id={{ProQuest|120793056}} |author-link=Mel Gussow}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McLellan |first=Joseph |date=August 8, 1979 |title=Deja-Vu Brilliance: 'EGBDF,' the Second Time Around |pages=E1, E9 |newspaper=The Washington Post|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/147189876 |url-access=subscription |access-date=September 14, 2023 |id={{ProQuest|147189876}}}}</ref>

He directed many theatrical productions, and starred in the Washington, D.C. production of ''[[Twelve Angry Men (1964 play)|12 Angry Men]]'' (2004), where he portrayed "Juror #5" to [[Roy Scheider]]'s "#8" and [[Robert Prosky]]'s "#3". He made his debut at the [[Shakespeare Theatre Company]] in Washington, D.C., in 2008 as the titular character in [[Molière]]'s ''[[The Imaginary Invalid]]''.

He was on the advisory board of [[Sci-Fest LA]], the first annual Los Angeles Science Fiction One-Act Play Festival, held in May 2014.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Sci-Fest Team| url=http://www.sci-fest.com/#!team/c1a9y| access-date=January 26, 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181204013945/http://www.sci-fest.com/#!team/c1a9y| archive-date=December 4, 2018| url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2018, Auberjonois was inducted into the [[American Theater Hall of Fame]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/ae/theater-dance/2018/11/16/2018-Theater-Hall-of-Fame-inductees-Rene-Auberjonois-Christine-Baranski-Cicely-Tyson/stories/201811160109 |title=2018 Theater Hall of Fame inductees include Rene Auberjonois, Christine Baranski, Cicely Tyson and more |last=Rawson |first=Christopher |date=November 16, 2018 |work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |access-date=December 26, 2018}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=René Auberjonois – Broadway Cast & Staff {{!}} IBDB |url=https://www.ibdb.com/broadway-cast-staff/ren-auberjonois-66778#Awards |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=ibdb.com}}</ref>

=== Films ===
Auberjonois played Father Mulcahy in the original film version of ''[[M*A*S*H (film)|M*A*S*H]]''. His subsequent film roles included the gangster Tony in ''[[Police Academy 5: Assignment Miami Beach]]'' (1988), and Reverend Oliver in ''[[The Patriot (2000 film)|The Patriot]]'' (2000). He made [[cameo appearance]]s in a number of films, including a mental asylum doctor patterned after [[Tim Burton]], in ''[[Batman Forever]]'' (1995), and a bird expert who gradually transforms into a bird in [[Robert Altman]]'s 1970 film ''[[Brewster McCloud]]''. He appeared as Colonel West, a minor role in the 1991 ''[[Star Trek]]'' film ''[[Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country]]'', but his part was cut from the theatrical release. His other notable film appearances include: ''[[McCabe & Mrs. Miller]]'' (1971), ''[[Images (film)|Images]] ''(1972), ''[[Pete 'n' Tillie]]'' (1972), ''[[The Hindenburg (film)|The Hindenburg]]'' (1975), ''[[King Kong (1976 film)|King Kong]]'' (1976), ''[[The Big Bus]]'' (1976), ''[[Eyes of Laura Mars]]'' (1978), ''[[Where the Buffalo Roam]]'' (1980), ''[[Walker (film)|Walker]]'' (1987), ''[[My Best Friend Is a Vampire]]'' (1987), ''The Feud'' (1989), ''[[Inspector Gadget (film)|Inspector Gadget]]'' (1999), and ''[[Eulogy (film)|Eulogy]]'' (2004).

Auberjonois portrayed the character of Straight Hollander in the 1993 [[Miramax]] film ''[[The Ballad of Little Jo]]''. He voiced [[Professor Genius]] in ''[[Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland]]'', [[List of The Little Mermaid characters#Chef Louis|Louis the Chef]] in ''[[The Little Mermaid (franchise)|The Little Mermaid]]'' franchise, Flanagan in ''[[Cats Don't Dance]]'', the Butler in ''[[Joseph: King of Dreams]]'', and André in ''[[Planes: Fire & Rescue]]''.

In 2019, Auberjonois portrayed the title role in ''[[Raising Buchanan]]'' as U.S. president [[James Buchanan]].

=== Television ===
[[File:Shimerman, Visitor and Auberjonois by Beth Madison, 2.jpg|thumb|Auberjonois (right) with ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' co-stars [[Armin Shimerman]] (left) and [[Nana Visitor]] (center)]]
In addition to having been a regular actor on three television shows (''[[Benson (TV series)|Benson]]'', a situation comedy; ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' in science fiction; and ''[[Boston Legal]]'', a [[legal drama|legal]] [[comedy drama]]), Auberjonois guest starred on many television series, including; ''[[Nash Bridges]]'', ''[[Ellery Queen]]'', ''[[Family (1976 TV series)|Family]]'', ''[[Grey's Anatomy]]'', ''[[The Rockford Files]]'', ''[[Charlie's Angels]]'', ''[[Starsky & Hutch]]'', ''[[Wonder Woman (TV series)|Wonder Woman]]'', ''[[Harry O]]'', ''[[The Jeffersons]]'', ''[[The Outer Limits (1995 TV series)|The Outer Limits]]'', ''[[Night Gallery]]'', ''[[Hart to Hart]]'', ''[[Matlock (1986 TV series)|Matlock]]'', ''[[Murder, She Wrote]]'', ''[[The Bionic Woman]]'', ''[[Frasier]]'', ''[[Judging Amy]]'', ''[[Chicago Hope]]'', ''[[The Bob Newhart Show]]'', ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'', ''[[Stargate SG-1]]'', ''[[Warehouse 13]]'', ''[[Archer (2009 TV series)|Archer]]'', ''[[L.A. Law]]'', ''[[The Practice]]'' (for which he received an Emmy nomination, playing a different character than the one he played on ''The Practice'' spinoff ''Boston Legal''), ''[[Saving Grace (American TV series)|Saving Grace]]'', ''[[It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia]]'', ''[[Criminal Minds]]'', ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'', ''[[The Good Wife]]'', ''[[The Librarians (2014 TV series)|The Librarians]]'', and ''[[Madam Secretary (TV series)|Madam Secretary]]''.

His television film credits include ''[[The Rhinemann Exchange]]'', ''[[The Dark Secret of Harvest Home]]'', Disney's ''[[Geppetto (film)|Geppetto]]'', [[Gore Vidal]]'s ''Billy The Kid'', the remake of ''A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court'', and the ''Sally Hemings: An American Scandal'' (2000) miniseries. He portrayed the character [[The Cask of Amontillado|Fortunato]] in an episode of ''[[American Masters]]'' entitled "[[Edgar Allan Poe|Edgar Allan Poe: Terror of the Soul]]" (1995). He received a third Emmy Award nomination for his performance in ABC's ''The Legend of Sleepy Hollow''. He played NASA scientist Dr. Felix Blackwell in the ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'' episode "Phoenix".

[[File:Odo.jpg|thumb|Auberjonois as Odo in ''Star Trek: Deep Space Nine'']]Auberjonois directed television shows, including ''[[Marblehead Manor]]'', and various episodes of ''Deep Space Nine''.

=== Voice acting ===
[[File:Rene Auberjonois by Luigi Rosa, 11.jpg|thumb|upright|Pictured in 2010]]
Auberjonois was active in radio drama. He read "The Stunt" by Mordechai Strigler for the [[National Public Radio]] (NPR) series ''Jewish Stories From the Old World to the New'', and he recorded novels on tape. On [[Public Radio International|PRI]], he was featured numerous times on ''[[Selected Shorts]]'', reading works of dramatic fiction. His voice was heard in Disney's ''[[The Little Mermaid (1989 film)|The Little Mermaid]]'' (in the supporting role of Chef Louis, singing "Les Poissons").

He did voice work on the ''Challenge of the GoBots'' series in 1980s as Dr. Braxis and was the voice of Peter Parker on the 1972 [[Buddah Records]] [[Spider-Man]] LP "From Beyond the Grave" (BDS 5119), a radio-style narrative replete with sound effects and rock and roll song interludes.

He voice acted in ''[[The Last Unicorn (film)|The Last Unicorn]]'' as the Skull that guards the clock that serves as an entryway into the Red Bull's lair. [[Peter S. Beagle]], the author of the [[The Last Unicorn|original book]], praised Auberjonois' performance, saying "he could have played any role in that movie and I would have been happy ... He's that talented."

In 1984–1985, Auberjonois voiced [[DeSaad]] in the animated series ''[[Super Friends]]''. From 1986 to 1987, he voiced Alvinar in the series ''[[Wildfire (1986 TV series)|Wildfire]]''.

He provided the voice for Janos Audron, an ancient vampire in the ''[[Legacy of Kain]]'' video game series; he was in ''[[Soul Reaver 2]]'', ''[[Blood Omen 2]]'', and ''[[Legacy of Kain: Defiance]]''. He provided the voice of Angler in the ''[[Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End (video game)|Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End]]'' video game. He voiced [[General Zod]] in the [[Ruby-Spears]] animated ''[[Superman (TV series)|Superman]]'' series episode "The Hunter".

Auberjonois provided minor character voices for ''[[Justice League (TV series)|Justice League]]'', reprising his role as DeSaad and voicing [[Kanjar Ro]] and [[Galius Zed]].

Auberjonois lent his voice talents to the 2001 Public Broadcasting System (PBS) ''[[American Experience]]'' documentary "Woodrow Wilson" as the title character, along with the 2003 PBS historical documentary ''[[Kingdom of David: The Saga of the Israelites]]''.

In 2003, he provided the voice of Natori in the English dubbed version of semi-sequel to the [[Hayao Miyazaki]] film ''[[Whisper of the Heart]]'', ''[[The Cat Returns]]''. He reprised an animated version of his character [[Odo (Star Trek)|Odo]] from ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' in a cutaway joke in ''[[Family Guy]]''{{'}}s ''[[Stewie Griffin: The Untold Story]]''. The cutaway featured a more humanoid-faced Odo threatening [[Stewie Griffin|Stewie]]'s alleged cousin [[Quark (Star Trek)|Quark]]. Auberjonois also lent his voice to ''[[Skylanders: SuperChargers]]''.

In 2011, he voiced villain [[Blockbuster (DC Comics)|Mark Desmond]] in [[Cartoon Network]]'s ''[[Young Justice (TV series)|Young Justice]]''. He was also the voice of Leonard McLeish and Junkyard Jim in the ''[[Pound Puppies (2010 TV series)|Pound Puppies]]'' series, [[Pepé Le Pew]] in ''[[The Looney Tunes Show]]'', [[Azmuth]] in ''[[Ben 10: Omniverse]]'', and [[Ebony Maw]] in ''[[Avengers Assemble (TV series)|Avengers Assemble]]''.<ref name="btva">{{cite web |title=Rene Auberjonois (visual voices guide) |url=http://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/Rene-Auberjonois/ |access-date=September 23, 2023 |website=Behind the Voice Actors}} A green check mark indicates that a role has been confirmed using a screenshot (or collage of screenshots) of a title's list of voice actors and their respective characters found in its credits or other reliable sources of information.</ref>

==== Video games ====
{{More citations needed|date=December 2019}}
One of Auberjonois' earliest forays into video game voice acting was the role of Janos Audron in ''[[Soul Reaver 2]]''; he continued to voice the character in subsequent releases in the ''[[Legacy of Kain]]'' series. According to a behind-the-scenes featurette in ''Soul Reaver 2'', showing candid discussions among the voice actors during recording, he was surprised at the quality of the writing, asking, "This is for a video game?!" when the purpose of the recordings was brought to light.

Auberjonois provided the voice of [[List of Uncharted characters#Karl Schäfer|Karl Schäfer]], the honorable German explorer in the video game ''[[Uncharted 2: Among Thieves]]'', and Mr. House, the reclusive New Vegas casino owner in the 2010 video game ''[[Fallout: New Vegas]]''. He also voiced Dr. Ignatio Mobius in ''[[Command & Conquer: Renegade]]''. He reprised his role as Odo in the game ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine: The Fallen]]''. In June 2018 he reprised his role as Odo in the [[massively multiplayer online role-playing game]] ''[[Star Trek Online]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.arcgames.com/en/games/star-trek-online/news/detail/10838844-victory-is-life-our-fourth-expansion,-coming-june-2018! |title=Victory Is Life – Our Fourth Expansion, Coming June 2018! |website=March 21, 2018 |publisher=Perfect World Entertainment |access-date=November 26, 2018}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Auberjonois was married to Judith Helen Mihalyi from 1963 until his death in 2019. They had a daughter, Tessa,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Robin |first=Brian |date=February 21, 2023 |title=Leaping into Her Father's Advice |url=https://www.scr.org/scr-blog/posts/leaping-into-her-father-s-advice/ |access-date=October 2, 2025 |website=South Coast Repertory}}</ref> and a son, [[Remy Auberjonois|Rèmy-Luc]],<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/rene-auberjonois-died-beson-star-trek-deep-space-nine-actor-dead-age-79-cause-of-death-metastatic-lung-cancer/ |title=René Auberjonois, "Benson," "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" actor, has died at age 79 |date=December 9, 2019 |publisher=CBS News |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> both of whom also became actors.

=== Illness and death ===
In an interview with ''[[Compassion & Choices]] Magazine'', Judith Auberjonois revealed that René Auberjonois underwent chemotherapy for lung cancer in 2018. It was discovered in 2019 that the cancer had spread to his brain. Due to the potential for [[Radiation-induced cognitive decline|serious cognitive side effects]], Auberjonois chose not to pursue the [[whole-brain radiation]] treatment suggested by his doctors.<ref name="CompassionChoicesMagazine">{{cite magazine |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Five Questions for Judith Auberjonois |url=https://compassionandchoices.org/docs/default-source/magazine/2021-summer-magazine-online-final.pdf?sfvrsn=23f52545_1 |magazine=Compassion & Choices Magazine|pages=18–20 |date=Summer 2021 |access-date=February 6, 2022}}</ref>

As a resident of California, Auberjonois decided to seek [[Assisted suicide in the United States|medical aid in dying]] under the [[California End of Life Option Act]].<ref name="CompassionChoicesMagazine"/><ref name="CTPostAidInDying">{{cite news |last=Tucker |first=Michael |date=February 19, 2021 |title=Opinion: Actor explains how medical aid in dying bill can provide comfort |url=https://www.ctpost.com/opinion/article/Opinion-Actor-explains-how-medical-aid-in-dying-15961624.php |work=Connecticut Post |location=Bridgeport, CT |access-date=February 6, 2022 |archive-date=October 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221013031734/https://www.ctpost.com/opinion/article/Opinion-Actor-explains-how-medical-aid-in-dying-15961624.php |url-status=dead }}</ref> On December 6, 2019, he spent his final hours with his family at his home in Los Angeles reminiscing over photos and listening to music.<ref name="CTPostAidInDying"/> He then took the medication prescribed for assisted suicide and died two days later at the age of 79. The California End of Life Option Act stipulates that death certificates should list the underlying terminal illness as the cause of death, rather than the use of life-ending medications.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tinker |first1=Ben |title=111 people died under California's new right-to-die law |url=https://www.cnn.com/2017/06/28/health/california-end-of-life-2016-bn/index.html |publisher=CNN|access-date=February 6, 2022 |date=June 29, 2017}}</ref> His cause of death was given as [[metastatic]] lung cancer.<ref name=NYTO/><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/benson-star-trek-actor-rene-auberjonois-has-died-at-79/2019/12/08/db319e26-1a05-11ea-977a-15a6710ed6da_story.html |title='Benson,' 'Star Trek' actor René Auberjonois has died at 79 |first=Andrew |last=Dalton |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=December 8, 2019 |access-date=December 8, 2019}}</ref>

{{short description|American actor (born 1956)}} {{Use American English|date=July 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2026}} {{Infobox person | name = Tim Russ | image = Tim Russ by Gage Skidmore.jpg | caption = Russ at the 2022 [[Phoenix Fan Fusion]] | birth_name = Timothy Darrell Russ | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1956|6|22}} | birth_place = Washington, D.C., U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | education = [[St. Edward's University]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[Illinois State University]] (attended) | occupation = {{hlist|Actor|musician|screenwriter|producer|director}} | years_active = 1985–present | children = 1 }} '''Timothy Darrell Russ'''{{cite web| url= http://www.filmreference.com/film/92/Tim-Russ.html|title=Tim Russ Biography (1956-)|publisher= | website= filmreference.com}} (born June 22, 1956) is an American actor, musician, screenwriter, director and amateur astronomer. He is best known for his roles as [[Lieutenant Commander]] [[Tuvok]] on ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]''; [[Robert Johnson]] in ''[[Crossroads (1986 film)|Crossroads]]'' (1986); Casey in ''[[East of Hope Street]]'' (1998); Frank on ''[[Samantha Who?]]''; Principal Franklin on the [[Nickelodeon]] sitcom ''[[iCarly]]''; D. C. Montana on ''[[The Highwayman (TV series)|The Highwaymen]]'' (1987–1988), and for his brief role in ''[[Spaceballs]]'' (1987). He appeared in ''[[The Rookie: Feds]]'' (2022) and reprised his role as Captain Tuvok on Season 3 of ''[[Star Trek: Picard]]''. == Early life, family and education == Russ was born in Washington, D.C., on June 22, 1956, to a [[government employee]] mother and a [[U.S. Air Force]] officer father. He spent part of his childhood in [[Turkey]]. He attended his senior year of high school at [[Rome Free Academy]], from which he graduated in 1974.{{cite web|url= https://youtube.com/watch?v=W-vq-lJrXwM|title=Knight Time Interview w Tim Russ |date=January 21, 2021 | via= YouTube}} He graduated from [[St. Edward's University]] with a degree in theater arts. He additionally attended graduate school at [[Illinois State University]] where he was inducted into its Hall of Fame. With a girlfriend, Jedda Roskilly, he has a daughter.{{cite web |last1= Nausch|first1=Maria |title=Biographical notes |url=https://www.timrusstribute.com/Bio.htm |website=timrusstribute.com |access-date=April 20, 2026}} == Career == === Acting === In 1985, Russ appeared in ''[[The Twilight Zone (1985 TV series)|The Twilight Zone]]'' episodes "[[Kentucky Rye (The Twilight Zone)|Kentucky Rye]]" as Officer No. 2 and "[[Voices in the Earth (The Twilight Zone)|Voices in the Earth]]" as Archer. He made a brief appearance in the comedy film ''[[Spaceballs]]'' as a trooper who "combs" the desert with a giant comb.{{cite web |title=Clip of 'combing the desert', from the movie 'Spaceballs' | date= July 15, 2012| via= YouTube| url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g3iFJpGJiug}}{{cite web | url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0750913/?ref_=fn_al_nm_1 | title=Tim Russ | website=[[IMDb]] }} Russ had a prominent role in the Charles Bronson film ''[[Death Wish 4]].'' Russ has been involved in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise as a voice and film actor, writer, director, and producer. He played several minor roles before landing the role as the main character [[Tuvok]] in ''Star Trek: Voyager''. Russ screentested, in 1987, for the role of [[Geordi La Forge]] on ''Star Trek: The Next Generation'' before being cast as Tuvok. Russ went into ''Voyager'' as a dedicated [[Trekkie]] with an extensive knowledge of [[Vulcan (Star Trek)|Vulcan]] lore,{{cite web| url= http://www.ifmagazine.com/feature.asp?article=1726 | title= Set Report: iF Magazine Boldly Goes To Vulcan For Star Trek: Of Gods And Men| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090202091010/http://ifmagazine.com/feature.asp?article=1726 |archive-date= February 2, 2009| website= ifmagazine.com | publisher= }} and has played the following roles in the ''Star Trek'' universe: * Devor, a mercenary aboard the ''Enterprise-D'' disguised as a service engineer in ''The Next Generation'' episode "[[Starship Mine]]" (1993) * T'Kar, a [[Klingon]] in the ''Deep Space Nine'' episode "[[Invasive Procedures (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Invasive Procedures]]" (1993) * A human tactical Lieutenant on the USS ''Enterprise-B'' in the film ''[[Star Trek Generations]]'' (1994). * Tuvok's [[Mirror Universe]] counterpart in the ''Deep Space Nine'' episode "[[Through the Looking Glass (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Through the Looking Glass]]" (1995). * A changeling impersonating Tuvok in ''Star Trek: Picard'' season 3. In 1995, Russ co-wrote the story for the [[Malibu Comics]] ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' No. 29 and 30, with Mark Paniccia. Russ performed voice acting roles as Tuvok for the video games ''[[Star Trek: Voyager – Elite Force]]'' and ''[[Star Trek: Elite Force II]]''. Russ is the director and one of the stars of the fan series ''[[Star Trek: Of Gods and Men]]'', the first third of which was released in December 2007, with the remaining two-thirds released in 2008.{{Cite web |last=Administrator |title=Star Trek: Of Gods and Men |url=http://startrekofgodsandmen.com/main/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=58&Itemid=173 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081219182240/http://startrekofgodsandmen.com/main/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=58&Itemid=173 |archive-date=December 19, 2008 |access-date=September 30, 2025 |website=startrekofgodsandmen.com |language=en-gb}} Russ's character's name D. C. Montana in ''[[The Highwayman (TV series)|The Highwayman]]'' was a reference to ''Trek'' writer [[D. C. Fontana]].{{citation needed|date=June 2015}} In 1990, he appeared in an episode of ''[[Freddy's Nightmares]]''.{{Cite news|last1= Englund|first1=Robert|title=Dust to Dust|date= February 25, 1990|last2=Bergman|last3=Brestoff|last4=Dow|first2=Sandahl|first3=Richard|first4=Tony}}{{full citation needed|date=April 2019}} Russ directed and co-starred in ''[[Star Trek: Renegades]]'', and in both 2013 and 2014 reprised his role as the voice of Tuvok in the [[massively multiplayer online game]] ''[[Star Trek Online]]''.{{cite news |title=Star Trek producers and Voyager actor Tim Russ discuss Renegades| website= filmindustry.network |url= https://filmindustry.network/star-trek-producers-and-voyager-actor-tim-russ-discuss-renegades/18220 |publisher=Film Industry Network |date=November 17, 2012}} === Later work === [[File:Tim Russ (32382294283).jpg|thumb|Russ at the Paradise City Comic Con, December 2016]] Russ appeared as Frank, a sarcastic doorman in the sitcom ''[[Samantha Who?]]'' from 2007 to 2009, and appeared for six seasons as Principal Ted Franklin in [[Nickelodeon]]'s show ''[[iCarly]]''. He also portrayed a doctor on an episode of ''[[Hannah Montana]]'', "[[I Am Hannah, Hear Me Croak]]". Russ won an [[Emmy Award]] in 2014 for [[public service ad]]s he did for the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office on intellectual property theft and [[cyberbullying]].{{cite web|title=National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences Pacific Southwest Chapter 2014 Emmy Recipients List| url= http://nataspsw.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/2014-Recipient-List-for-Website.pdf| website= nataspsw.org| access-date= June 26, 2014}} He played Captain Kells in the 2015 [[Bethesda Game Studios]] video game ''[[Fallout 4]]''.{{cite web|url=https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/video-games/Fallout-4/Lancer-Captain-Kells/|title=LANCER CAPTAIN KELLS|publisher=Behind the Voice Actors|access-date=April 26, 2021|archive-date=November 15, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151115060900/https://www.behindthevoiceactors.com/video-games/Fallout-4/Lancer-Captain-Kells/}} In June 2025, following [[Mel Brooks]]' announcement of ''Spaceballs 2'', slated for release in 2027, Russ teased on social media that he may appear in the film, along with his more famous co-stars.{{Cite web|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/movies/news/tim-russ-who-has-the-best-line-in-the-original-hints-at-spaceballs-2-return/ar-AA1GRGNE|title=MSN|website=Msn.com|access-date=July 29, 2026}} === Music and astronomy === Russ has been a lifelong musician and a singer.{{cite web|title=Tim Russ – Star Trek: Voyager's Tuvok|url=http://www.successcircuit.com/interviews/tim-russ/|publisher=Success Circuit|access-date=April 4, 2015|archivedate=April 8, 2015|url-status=usurped|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150408194420/http://www.successcircuit.com/interviews/tim-russ/}} In addition, Russ has been an avid amateur astronomer most of his adult life, and is a member of the Los Angeles Astronomical Society. In 2021 he was among a small group of citizen astronomers who assisted in detection of the asteroid [[617 Patroclus]] in preparation for [[NASA]]'s [[Lucy (spacecraft)|Lucy probe]].{{Cite news |last=Kochi |first=Sudiksha |date=August 27, 2021 |title='Star Trek' star Tim Russ helps detect asteroid for NASA's upcoming mission |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/2021/08/27/star-trek-actor-tim-russ-helps-nasa-detect-asteroid/8204195002/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230319050620/https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/2021/08/27/star-trek-actor-tim-russ-helps-nasa-detect-asteroid/8204195002/ |archive-date=March 19, 2023 |access-date=January 27, 2024 |work=USA Today}} In February 2022, he stated that he owned a 10-inch Dobsonian telescope, an 8" Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope, and a Unistellar eVscope.{{Cite news |date=February 1, 2022 |title=Tim Russ: Actor, Director, and Amateur Astronomer |language=en-US |work=Sky & Telescope |url=https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-resources/famous-astronomers/tim-russ-actor-director-amateur-astronomer/#:~:text=Tim%20Russ%20is%20best%20known,Tuvok%20on%20Star%20Trek:%20Voyager. |access-date=February 20, 2023}} == Filmography == === Film === {| class="wikitable sortable" |+ {{Screen reader-only| Tim Russ film credits}} |- ! '''Roy Brocksmith''' (September 15, 1945 – December 16, 2001) was an American actor.

==Life and career==
Brocksmith was born in [[Quincy, Illinois]], the son of Vera Marguerite (''[[Maiden and married names|née]]'' Hartwig) and Otis E. Brocksmith, who was a [[mechanic]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Roy Brocksmith Biography (1945-) |url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/76/Roy-Brocksmith.html |website=Filmreference.com |access-date=April 15, 2025}}</ref> He graduated from [[Quincy University]] in 1970. He then moved to [[New York City]] where he began a career on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]]. His roles included Louis XIII in ''[[The Three Musketeers (musical)|The Three Musketeers]]'' and the balladeer in a revival of ''[[The Threepenny Opera]]'' with [[Raul Julia]].

Brocksmith's film and television roles included Dr. Edgemar in ''[[Total Recall (1990 film)|Total Recall]]'', a police sergeant possessed by Bill in ''[[Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey]]'', principal Michael Oslo in ''[[Picket Fences]]'' and mortician Irv Kendall in ''[[Arachnophobia (film)|Arachnophobia]]''.

He died in 2001, aged 56, from complications of [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetes]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://playbill.com/article/roy-brocksmith-actor-director-and-theatre-founder-is-dead-at-56-com-100360 |title=Roy Brocksmith, Actor, Director and Theatre Founder, Is Dead at 56 |last=Simonson |first=Robert |work=Playbill |date=December 17, 2001 |access-date=April 15, 2025}}</ref>

{{short description|American actress (born 1965)}} {{family name hatnote|Forbes|Guajardo|lang=Mexican}} {{BLP sources|date=March 2014}} {{Use mdy dates|date=April 2018}} {{Infobox person | name = Michelle Forbes | image = Michelle Forbes 2009a Comic-Con.jpg | caption = Forbes at Comic-Con 2009 | birth_name = {{nowrap|Michelle Renee Forbes Guajardo}} | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1965|1|8}} | birth_place = [[Austin, Texas]], U.S. | known_for = {{hlist|''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]''|''[[Homicide: Life on the Street]]''|''[[Guiding Light]]''|''[[True Blood]]''|''[[The Killing (American TV series)|The Killing]]''}} | other_names = | occupation = Actress | years_active = 1980–present | awards = [[38th Saturn Awards|Saturn Award]] | spouse = {{marriage|[[Ross Kettle]]|1990|1999|end=divorced}} }} '''Michelle Renee Forbes Guajardo''' (born January 8, 1965){{cite web|title=Michelle Forbes {{!}} Biography|url=https://movies.yahoo.com/person/michelle-forbes/|publisher=Yahoo|access-date=March 10, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130719060217/http://movies.yahoo.com/person/michelle-forbes/ |archive-date=July 19, 2013}} is an American actress who has appeared on television and in independent films. She is a [[Saturn Award]] winner with three nominations. Forbes first garnered attention for her dual role in the daytime soap opera ''[[Guiding Light]]'', for which she received a [[Daytime Emmy Award]] nomination. She is known for her recurring appearances on genre and drama shows, including Ensign [[Ro Laren]] in ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]] and [[Star Trek: Picard]],'' and her regular role as medical examiner [[Julianna Cox]] on ''[[Homicide: Life on the Street]]'' during the 1990s. She played recurring roles throughout the 2000s in ''[[Battlestar Galactica (2004 TV series)|Battlestar Galactica]]'', ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]'', ''[[In Treatment (U.S. TV series)|In Treatment]]'', ''[[Durham County (TV series)|Durham County]]'', ''[[Prison Break]]'' and her series regular role as Maryann Forrester on ''[[True Blood]]''. She has appeared in significant roles in films such as ''[[Escape from L.A.]]'', ''[[Kalifornia]]'', ''[[Swimming with Sharks]]'' and ''[[Columbus (2017 film)|Columbus]]''. She starred in the 2011–2012 [[AMC (TV channel)|AMC]] television series ''[[The Killing (U.S. TV series)|The Killing]]'', for which she received a [[Primetime Emmy Award]] nomination.{{cite news |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/awards/2011/07/emmys-michelle-forbes.html |title=Emmys: Michelle Forbes on her nomination and the 'Killing' backlash |first=Steven |last=Zeitchik |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=July 14, 2011 |access-date=July 14, 2011}} On June 18, 2019 it was announced that Forbes would join USA Network's [[Action fiction|action]] [[Drama (film and television)|drama]] series ''[[Treadstone]]'', a prequel/sequel to the [[Bourne (franchise)|''Bourne'' franchise]].{{Cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2019/06/treadstone-michelle-forbes-casting-1202634130/|title='Treadstone': Michelle Forbes Joins USA Network's CIA Drama Alongside Patrick Fugit, Michael Gaston, Tess Haubrich & Shruti Haasan|last=White|first=Peter|date=2019-06-18|website=Deadline|language=en|access-date=2019-07-07}} == Early life == Forbes was born in [[Austin, Texas]], of [[Mexican Americans|Mexican American]] heritage.{{cite news |url=http://www.slate.com/articles/news_and_politics/politics/2012/05/majority_minority_america_will_more_hispanics_and_asians_become_white_.html |title=The Myth of Majority-Minority America |first=Matthew |last=Yglesias |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |date=May 22, 2012 |access-date=October 21, 2018}} Forbes hoped to become a ballet dancer. She began receiving formal acting training at the [[High School for the Performing and Visual Arts]] in [[Houston, Texas|Houston]]. While on vacation in [[New York City]] at the age of 16, she found herself auditioning for a film;{{Cite book |last=Nemecek |first=Larry |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Next_Generation_Companion.html?id=VTifVpk6cekC&source=kp_book_description |title=The Next Generation Companion: Star Trek The Next Generation |date=2012-09-25 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-1-4711-0679-8 |pages=164 |language=en}} although she was not selected, she signed with the [[William Morris Agency]] and began her professional acting career. == Career == {{BLP sources section|date=July 2018}} In 1987, at age 22, Forbes landed the contract role of Sonni Carrera Lewis on the daytime soap opera ''[[Guiding Light]]''. The role was expanded to a dual role, with a second character, Solita Carrera, added. Forbes was a cast member for three years and in 1990 earned a [[Daytime Emmy Award]] nomination for her performance. She then continued in theater and began appearing in small guest roles on television to raise her profile. She went on to make guest appearances on a few other TV shows before landing the recurring role of Ensign [[Ro Laren]] in ''[[Star Trek: The Next Generation]]''. The producers of ''Star Trek: The Next Generation'' invited Forbes to reprise Ro in the spin-off series ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' but Forbes declined the offer{{cite book |title=The Making of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine |first=Judith & Garfield|last=Reeves-Stevens|publisher=Pocket Books|isbn=0-671-87430-6|year=1994|pages=70, 105}} and decided to focus on a career in films. She received praise, as well as a [[Saturn Award]] nomination from the [[Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror Films]], for her performance as photographer Carrie Laughlin in the 1993 thriller ''[[Kalifornia]]''. This was followed with the lead female role in the 1994 black comedy ''[[Swimming with Sharks]]'' as well as supporting roles in films such as ''[[Roadflower]]'', ''Just Looking'' (1995), and [[John Carpenter]]'s 1996 science fiction/action sequel ''[[Escape from L.A.]]'' She continued performing on television during this period, with guest spots on ''[[Seinfeld]]'', ''[[The Outer Limits (1995 TV series)|The Outer Limits]]'' and ''Star Trek: The Next Generation'', to which she returned to tie up the Ro Laren storyline in the series' [[Preemptive Strike (Star Trek: The Next Generation)|penultimate episode]]. In 1995, she played one of the leads in [[J. S. Cardone]]'s [[crime thriller]] ''[[Black Day Blue Night]]'', alongside [[Mia Sara]] and [[Gil Bellows]]. The reviews for ''Black Day Blue Night'' were positive. Without breaking new grounds, they highlighted its strengths as a well-executed, low-budget noir with engaging performances.{{cite web |title=Black Day Blue Night — EW.com |url=http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,293893,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081011035644/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,293893,00.html |archive-date=October 11, 2008 |work=Entertainment Weekly's EW.com}}{{Cite web |title=Black Day Blue Night |url=https://www.tvguide.com/movies/black-day-blue-night/2030009192/ |access-date=2024-10-19 |website=TVGuide.com |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Hurlburt |first=Roger |date=November 4, 1995 |title=Rating are the target in funny 'Open Season' |work=South Florida Sun Sentinel |pages=3D}}{{Cite news |last=Rodriguez |first=Rene |date=November 3, 1994 |title=Black Day Blue Night |work=The Miami Herald |pages=21G}} Greg Evans of [[Variety (magazine)|''Variety'']] liked the film and of Forbes performance he said that it was "compellingly hard-bitten" and "outdistance the material."{{Cite web |last=Evans |first=Greg |date=1995-11-27 |title=Black Day Blue Night |url=https://variety.com/1995/film/reviews/black-day-blue-night-1200443709/ |access-date=2024-10-19 |website=Variety |language=en-US}} In 1996, Forbes joined the cast of [[NBC]]'s popular police drama ''[[Homicide: Life on the Street]]'', playing chief medical examiner [[Julianna Cox]]. She remained with the show for two years then was let go as part of a major cast overhaul (the series was canceled after one more season). However, she reprised her role in the 2000 TV special ''Homicide: The Movie''. That same year, Forbes became a regular on the [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] series ''[[Wonderland (American TV series)|Wonderland]]'' but it was pulled from the air after only two episodes. Forbes was next seen in a recurring role on the police drama ''[[The District]]''. [[File:Michelle Forbes at True Blood premiere party.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Forbes at the ''[[True Blood]]'' premiere party, June 2009]] She was subsequently given roles in films such as 2001's ''[[Perfume (2001 film)|Perfume]]'' and 2002's ''[[American Girl (2002 film)|American Girl]]'' as well as the 2001 British television film ''[[Messiah (British TV series)|Messiah]]'' (for which she studied [[British sign language]] for a week) and its sequel installments: ''Messiah 2: Vengeance is Mine'' in 2002 and ''Messiah III'' in 2003. During the 2002–2003 TV season, Forbes played the recurring character of presidential aide Lynne Kresge on the second season of the action series ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]''. She followed her role on ''24'' with a guest spot on ''[[Alias (TV series)|Alias]]'' then went on to play Admiral Helena Cain in three episodes of the re-imagining of the classic sci-fi series ''[[Battlestar Galactica]]'' as well as appearing in the television film ''[[Battlestar Galactica: Razor]]''. She followed this up with a recurring role as Agent [[Samantha Brinker]] on the drama ''[[Prison Break]]'' and guest starred on ''[[Boston Legal]]'' and ''[[Lost (2004 TV series)|Lost]]''. Forbes starred as the lead in the adaptation of the comic-book ''[[Global Frequency#Television pilot|Global Frequency]]'', the single produced episode of which [[internet leak|leaked online]] the following year, eight months after the series failed to be picked up by Warner Bros. networks.{{cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/entertainment/music/news/2005/06/67986|title=Rejected TV Pilot Thrives on P2P|website=Wired.com|access-date=July 24, 2008|date=June 27, 2005}} Forbes returned to British television screens with guest roles in both ''[[Holby City]]'' and as a [[Mossad]] agent in ''[[Waking the Dead (TV series)|Waking the Dead]]''. In 2008, Forbes starred in two HBO drama series; ''[[In Treatment]]'', portraying the wife of the central character, and in ''[[True Blood]]'' as a [[Maenad]] named Maryann Forrester.[http://www.tv.com/michelle-forbes/person/5401/summary.html?tag=page_body Biography]{{dead link|date=July 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} TV.com She reprised her semi-regular roles in both series in their respective second seasons in 2009 as well as joining the cast of the Canadian psychological drama series [[Durham County (TV series)|''Durham County'']] for its second season as Dr. Penelope Verity.[http://blogcritics.org/video/article/michelle-forbes-delves-into-the-darkness/ "Michelle Forbes Delves Into The Darkness Of Durham County"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100110012107/http://blogcritics.org/video/article/michelle-forbes-delves-into-the-darkness|date=January 10, 2010}} November 2, 2008, Blogg Critics Forbes played the role of Mitch Larsen in the American television series [[The Killing (American TV series)|''The Killing'']], a 2011 remake of the Danish crime series [[The Killing (Danish TV series)|''Forbrydelsen'']]. Forbes appeared as Retro Girl in the TV series ''[[Powers (American TV series)|Powers]]''.{{cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2014/08/sharlto-copley-lead-christian-walker-powers-michelle-forbes-retro-girl-820846/|title=Sharlto Copley Set As Lead Christian Walker In 'Powers', Michelle Forbes Is Retro Girl|work=Deadline|date= August 18, 2014|access-date=August 18, 2014}} She also landed a prominent supporting role in ''[[The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2]]''. Forbes subsequently played Valerie Edwards in the TV series ''[[Berlin Station (TV series)|Berlin Station]]'' that aired on [[Epix (TV network)|Epix]] from 2016 to 2019. Her character was a no-nonsense administrator who serves as a Berlin Station Internal branch chief. {{short description|American actor}} {{BLP sources|date=December 2014}} {{Infobox person | name = Sherman Howard | image = Mr. Sherman Howard.jpg | alt = | caption = Howard in 2014 | birth_name = | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1949|6|11}} | birth_place = [[Chicago, Illinois]], U.S. | education = [[American Conservatory Theater]] (1971) | occupation = Actor | years_active = 1971–present | spouse = {{marriage|[[Donna Bullock (actress)|Donna Bullock]]|1988}} | children = 1 }} '''Sherman Howard''' (born June 11, 1949) is an American actor. He is best known for his performance as the zombie Bub in [[George A. Romero]]'s ''[[Day of the Dead (1985 film)|Day of the Dead]]'' (1985) and [[Lex Luthor]] on ''[[Superboy (TV series)|Superboy]]'' (1990–1992). He also voiced [[Derek Powers]] / Blight in ''[[Batman Beyond]]'' (1999–2001). ==Theatre== Howard began his career at the [[American Conservatory Theater]] (ACT) in [[San Francisco]] in 1971. While a member of ACT's repertory company, he appeared in the roles of Glendenning in [[David Storey]]'s ''The Contractor'', the archangel [[Gabriel]] in Nagle Jackson's ''The Mystery Cycle'', James in [[Harold Pinter]]'s ''[[The Collection (play)|The Collection]]'', and Gratiano in ''[[The Merchant of Venice]]'', along with roles in both ''[[Antony and Cleopatra]]'' and ''[[Caesar and Cleopatra (play)|Caesar and Cleopatra]]''. He appeared as Archie in [[Tom Stoppard]]'s ''[[Jumpers (play)|Jumpers]]'' in the premiere season of Chicago's Northlight Theatre Company. While a member of the resident company at the [[Actors Theatre of Louisville]] for three seasons during the mid-70s, he played the role of Lucius in [[Jon Jory]]'s ''Andronicus: A Space Musical'', and had roles in ''[[The Runner Stumbles]]'', ''[[The Front Page]]'', ''[[The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui]]'', and the European tour of [[Marsha Norman]]'s ''[[Getting Out]]''. His [[off-Broadway]] credits include [[Shel Silverstein]]'s ''The Crate'' and ''The Lady or the Tiger Show'' as well as [[Sam Shepard]]'s ''[[Geography of a Horse Dreamer]]'' at the [[Ensemble Studio Theatre]], along with ''[[I'm Not Rappaport]]'' at the [[Roundabout Theatre Company]]. He appeared in ''[[Titus Andronicus]]'' and ''Tell Out My Soul'' at [[The Public Theater]], and in [[Lillian Hellman]]'s ''[[Another Part of the Forest]]'' at the Pecadillo Theatre. He most recently appeared in the title role of "Bauer" by Lauren Gunderson at 59 E 59th St in New York City. His regional credits include [[Prospero]] in ''[[The Tempest]]'', [[Henry II of England|King Henry]] in ''[[The Lion in Winter]]'', Spooner in ''[[No Man's Land (play)|No Man's Land]]'', and Lopakhin in ''[[The Cherry Orchard]]'' at the [[Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey]] (STNJ), where he has also appeared in the title roles of both [[Bertolt Brecht]]'s ''[[Life of Galileo]]'' and [[Luigi Pirandello]]'s ''[[Henry IV (Pirandello)|Henry IV]]'' (Enrico IV). He also appeared as Scrooge in the STNJ's production of ''[[A Christmas Carol]]''. He played the role of Benedick in ''[[Much Ado About Nothing]]'', opposite his wife, Donna Bullock, as Beatrice. He played the title roles in both ''[[Hamlet]]'' and ''[[Macbeth]]'' at the [[Kentucky Shakespeare Festival]] and the North Carolina Shakespeare Festival, respectively. He appeared in the title role of ''Sheridan'' at the [[La Jolla Playhouse]]. He appeared in ''[[The Price (play)|The Price]]'' at the [[Pittsburgh Public Theater]] and in ''Nine Armenians'' at the Intiman Theater in [[Seattle]]. His [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] credits include ''[[Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Zoo]]'', ''[[All My Sons]]'', ''[[Inherit the Wind (play)|Inherit the Wind]]'', and [[Gore Vidal]]'s ''[[The Best Man (play)|The Best Man]]''. He recently concluded a run at the [[Old Globe Theatre]] in [[San Diego]] as The Player in Tom Stoppard's ''[[Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead]]'' and appeared in "The Second Mrs. Wilson" at [[George Street Playhouse]] under the direction of Gordon Edelstein. Howard also has a passion for concert hall music. In their 2013/14 season, he performed with the Philadelphia Orchestra in [[Sergei Rachmaninoff]]'s ''[[The Bells (symphony)|The Bells]]'' conducted by [[Vladimir Jurowski]]. He also appeared in the role of Prospero in the New Jersey Symphony Orchestra's presentation of [[Jean Sibelius]]' ''[[The Tempest (Sibelius)|The Tempest Suite]]'' conducted by Jacque Lacombe. He has performed [[Richard Strauss]]'s ''[[Enoch Arden (Strauss)|Enoch Arden]]'' with concert pianist David Kaplan at Bargemusic in Brooklyn and Metropolis Ensemble in Manhattan. ==Personal life== Howard has been married to actress [[Donna Bullock (actress)|Donna Bullock]] since May 1988. {{marriage|Becky Hopkins|1999}} | children = 1 }} '''Gary Rand Graham''' (June 6, 1950 – January 22, 2024) was an American actor. With a career spanning five decades beginning in the 1970s in television and movies, he is perhaps best known for his starring role as Detective Matthew Sikes in the television series ''[[Alien Nation (TV series)|Alien Nation]]'' (1989–1990) and five subsequent ''Alien Nation'' television films (1994–1997), as well as his work in the ''[[Star Trek]]'' franchise, most notably the recurring role of [[Soval]], the [[Vulcan (Star Trek)|Vulcan]] ambassador to Earth in ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''. == Biography and early career == Graham was born in [[Long Beach, California]]. One of his earliest roles was in the 1980 [[CBS]] miniseries ''[[Scruples (miniseries)|Scruples]]'', based on the [[Judith Krantz]] novel starring [[Lindsay Wagner]]. He was cast as a hitman on the television show ''[[Moonlighting (TV series)|Moonlighting]]'' co-starring opposite [[Bruce Willis]]. Graham played more than 38 TV roles and had been in more than 40 movies. As a musician, Graham was in the bands The Gary Graham Garage Band, The Gary Graham Band and The Sons of Kirk. Graham was also a contributor to [[Breitbart News]].{{Cite book |last=Cole |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jkMxCgAAQBAJ&pg=PT187 |title=Republican Party Animal: The "Bad Boy of Holocaust History" Blows the Lid off Hollywood's Secret Right-Wing Underground |date=May 19, 2014 |publisher=Feral House |isbn=978-1-936239-92-4}} Graham died from cardiac arrest in [[Spokane, Washington]] on January 22, 2024, at the age of 73.{{cite web|last=Barnes|first=Mike|title=Gary Graham, Star of 'Alien Nation,' Dies at 73|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/gary-graham-dead-alien-nation-1235804804/|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=January 23, 2024|access-date=January 23, 2024}}{{cite news |last=Watters |first=Bill |date=January 22, 2024 |title=Gary Graham, Star of "Alien Nation", "Enterprise" Has Passed Away |url=https://nerdbot.com/2024/01/22/gary-graham-star-of-alien-nation-enterprise-has-passed-away/ |access-date=January 23, 2024 |publisher=Nerdbot}} ==Later career== === Television === Graham starred in a 2008 television pilot styled after ''[[Sin City]]'' called ''Dead End City''. He also appeared in the December 18, 1984 episode of ''[[Remington Steele]]'', "Let's Steele A Plot" (season 3, episode 11), as Butch Bemis. As well as starring as Detective Matthew Sikes in the television series ''[[Alien Nation (TV series)|Alien Nation]]'' (1989–1990), he resumed this role in the TV movies ''[[Alien Nation: Dark Horizon]]'' (1994), ''[[Alien Nation: Body and Soul]]'' (1995), ''[[Alien Nation: Millennium]]'' (1996), ''[[Alien Nation: The Enemy Within]]'' (1996) and ''[[Alien Nation: The Udara Legacy]]'' (1997). Graham starred on ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'' as the recurring character [[Ambassador Soval]], a [[Vulcan (Star Trek)|Vulcan]] [[Ambassador (diplomacy)|ambassador]] to Earth. He also guest-starred on ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' (1995) once, playing [[Ocampa]]n community leader Tanis in the second-season episode "[[Cold Fire (Star Trek: Voyager)|Cold Fire]]". He played Ragnar in the fan production ''[[Star Trek: Of Gods and Men]]'' and continued that role in ''[[Star Trek: Renegades]]''. In 2015, Graham reprised his role as Ambassador Soval, in the [[fan film]] ''[[Star Trek: Axanar]]''.{{Cite web |last=Howell |first=Elizabeth |date=2015-07-10 |title='Star Trek: Axanar' Fan Film Kicks Fundraising into Warp Drive |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/star-trek-axanar-fan-film-kicks-fundraising-warp-171422536.html |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US}} === Film === Graham's film appearances include ''[[Hardcore (1979 film)|Hardcore]]'', ''[[The Hollywood Knights]]'', ''[[All the Right Moves (film)|All the Right Moves]]'', ''[[The Arrogant]]'', ''The Last Warrior'', ''[[Robot Jox]]'', ''Running Woman'' and ''Siren'' (2006). His most recent films are ''[[InAlienable]]'', ''Action Hero'' and ''[[Dreams Awake]]''. He made his directorial debut in the spring of 2008 with the film ''Interviews,'' which he also wrote. === Web-based work === Graham also made appearances as the "Smoking Jacket Guy" in the introduction and other scenes in the Internet gaming show ''[[The Jace Hall Show]]''.{{cite web|url=http://crackle.com/c/Jace_Hall#id=298717&ml=o%3D12%26fpl%3D297045%26fx%3D|title=Crackle - Watch Movies Online, Free TV Shows, & Original Online Series}} Graham played Dr. David Macavoy in the web series ''Universal Dead''.{{cite web|url=http://www.universaldead.com/ |title=Universal Dead |publisher=Universal Dead |access-date=2012-06-04}} In late June 2010, it was announced that ''Universal Dead'' will be made into a feature film. It never was, as of 2026.{{cite web|url=http://indieintertube.tv/static/universal-dead-full-length-feature|title=Universal Dead full length feature?|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110818124246/http://indieintertube.tv/static/universal-dead-full-length-feature/|archive-date=2011-08-18}} ==Filmography== ===Film=== {| class="wikitable sortable" |- ! '''Susanna Thompson''' (born January 27, 1958)<ref name=msn>{{cite web|url=http://movies.msn.com/celebrities/celebrity-biography/susanna-thompson/|title=Showtimes, reviews, trailers, news and more – MSN Movies|work=msn.com|access-date=2013-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111212022730/http://movies.msn.com/celebrities/celebrity-biography/susanna-thompson/|archive-date=2011-12-12|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.filmreference.com/film/68/Susanna-Thompson.html|title=Susanna Thompson Biography (1958–) |work=Film Reference |access-date=2012-06-29}}</ref> is an American actress. She is known for her roles in films ''[[Little Giants]]'' (1994), ''[[Ghosts of Mississippi]]'' (1996), ''[[Random Hearts]]'' (1999) and ''[[Dragonfly (2002 film)|Dragonfly]]'' (2002). On television, she played Dr. Lenara Kahn in the episode "[[Rejoined]]" in ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' (1995), the [[Borg]] Queen in three episodes of ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' (1999–2000), Karen Sammler on the drama series ''[[Once and Again]]'' (1999–2002), and [[Moira Queen (Arrowverse)|Moira Queen]] on the series ''[[Arrow (TV series)|Arrow]]'' (2012–2020).

== Career ==
Thompson has appeared on stage, winning  a Dramatic Award for her role as Luisa in ''A Shayna Maidel''. She was also nominated for Best Actress by the San Diego Critics Circle for her role in ''Agnes of God''.

She may be best known for her television work, which includes playing Karen Sammler on ''[[Once and Again]]'', Michelle Generoo in [[Space (The X-Files)|an episode of ''The X-Files'']] and a recurring role as the [[Borg#Borg Queen|Borg Queen]] in the ''[[Star Trek: Voyager]]'' two-part episodes "[[Dark Frontier]]" (1999) and "[[Unimatrix Zero]]" (2000).<ref name=tvg /> She also portrayed Denise Hydecker in the 1998 [[television film]] ''[[The Lake (1998 film)|The Lake]]''.

One of Thompson's most controversial television appearances was on an episode of ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' titled "[[Rejoined]]". In the episode, she participated in one of US television's earlier<!-- first was 4 years earlier: "LA Law:He's a crowd"--> same-sex kisses.  The episode first aired on October 30, 1995.

She made a guest appearance on ''[[Law & Order: Special Victims Unit]]'' on October 7, 2003 in the season five episode "Mother", as Dr. Greta Heints, a [[psychiatrist]] who rehabilitates [[sex offenders]] to prepare them to return to society.

Beginning in January 2006, she had a starring role in the short-lived [[NBC]] drama ''[[The Book of Daniel (television)|The Book of Daniel]]''.<ref name=msn /> In November 2006, she made her first appearance as Army [[Lieutenant colonel (United States)|Lieutenant Colonel]] [[Hollis Mann]] on the [[CBS]] series ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'', in the recurring role of [[Special Agent Leroy Jethro Gibbs|Agent Gibbs]]' love interest. That same week, she appeared on ''[[Without a Trace]]''.

In 2009, Thompson starred on the short-lived NBC series ''[[Kings (American TV series)|Kings]]'', based on the biblical story of [[David]], as Queen Rose Benjamin, an analogue of [[Ahinoam]], the wife of [[Saul]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Kings |url=http://www.nbc.com/Kings/about/index.shtml# |author=NBC staff |website=[[NBC]].com |access-date=2019-01-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090318133805/http://www.nbc.com/Kings/about/index.shtml |archive-date=2009-03-18}}</ref>

In 2012, Thompson started a two season run as [[Moira Queen (Arrowverse)|Moira Queen]] in the main cast of the [[The CW Television Network|CW]] series ''[[Arrow (TV series)|Arrow]]'',<ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://insidetv.ew.com/2014/04/23/arrow-postmortem-moira-dead/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140424061041/http://insidetv.ew.com/2014/04/23/arrow-postmortem-moira-dead/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 24, 2014 |title='Arrow' post mortem: Boss opens up about the shocking [spoiler]! |first=Sandra |last=Gonzalez |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=2014-04-23 |access-date=2019-01-29}}</ref> returning as a guest in later seasons. She appeared in the recurring role of Carolyn Preston in the NBC series ''[[Timeless (American TV series)|Timeless]]'' (2016–2018).

== Personal life ==
Thompson earned her [[bachelor's degree]] in drama from [[San Diego State University]].<ref name=tvg>{{cite journal|url=https://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/susanna-thompson/bio/175829|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080530053539/http://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/susanna-thompson/bio/175829|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 30, 2008|title=Susanna Thompson|journal=[[TV Guide]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.buddytv.com/info/susanna-thompson-info.aspx|title=Susanna Thompson|website=BuddyTV.com|access-date=2012-06-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006091204/http://www.buddytv.com/info/susanna-thompson-info.aspx|archive-date=2014-10-06|url-status=dead}}</ref> Her husband, Martin B. Katz, is a professor there.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.sdjewishworld.com/2013/04/20/director-probes-the-lighter-side-of-death/ |title=Director probes the lighter side of death |last=Harrison |first=Donald H. |date=2013-04-20 |access-date=2019-01-29 |website=[[San Diego Jewish World]]}}</ref>

'''John Billingsley''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|ɪ|l|ɪ|ŋ|g|z|l|i}}, born May 20, 1960)<ref name=May20>{{cite web |author=<!--not stated or generic "Staff"--> |title=Intelligence {{!}} John Billingsley |publisher=[[CBS]] |date=2014-01-10 |department=Shows |url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/intelligence/cast/214779/ |access-date=2025-10-14 |quote=His birth date is May 20. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140110030615/http://www.cbs.com/shows/intelligence/cast/214779/ |archive-date=2014-01-10}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Mark |last=Olsen |title=This leading-man wannabe is happy to have a TV role in reserve |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=2003-09-07 |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-sep-07-ca-starbillingsley7-story.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=2025-10-14 |quote=… John Billingsley, 43… |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230526174039/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-sep-07-ca-starbillingsley7-story.html |archive-date=2023-05-26 |url-status=live}}</ref> is an American actor best known for his role as [[Phlox (Star Trek)|Doctor Phlox]] on the television series ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]''.

==Early life and education==
Billingsley was born in [[Media, Pennsylvania]], and subsequently lived in [[Huntsville, Alabama]], and [[Slidell, Louisiana]], before his family settled in [[Weston, Connecticut]].<ref name=Occidental>{{cite web |author=<!--not stated or generic "Staff"--> |title=Guest Artist Bios: John Billingsley |publisher=[[Occidental College]] |date=2012-10-04 |department=Theater |url=http://www.oxy.edu/theater/guest-artists/guest-artist-bios/john-billingsley |access-date=2025-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131113155629/http://www.oxy.edu/theater/guest-artists/guest-artist-bios/john-billingsley |archive-date=2013-11-13 |url-status=dead}}</ref> 

He graduated from [[Bennington College]] in 1982.<ref name=May20/><ref>{{cite web |author=<!--not stated or generic "Staff"-->  |title=John Billingsley {{!}} Biography |website=trademarktalent.com |date=2014-10-19 |url=https://www.trademarktalent.com/johnbillingsley/#bio |access-date=2014-08-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141019012923/http://www.trademarktalent.com/johnbillingsley/ |archive-date=2014-10-19 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
===Early work===
Billingsley's second on-screen role was in 1991 as a difficult customer making a return in a customer service training video produced by Nintendo of America.<ref>{{cite AV media |first=Randy (posted the video) |last=Cornetta |title=Nintendo Training 1991 |date=February 3, 2009 |time=1:46 |format=[[YouTube]]  |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WYjgHLFZMa0 |access-date=January 1, 2017 |quote=A Nintendo training video from 1991 teaching retail workers how to handle customers with defective Nintendo products. |archive-url= https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/WYjgHLFZMa0| archive-date=December 12, 2021 |url-status= live}}</ref> He made an appearance in "It Happened in Juneau", a third-season episode of the TV comedy-drama ''[[Northern Exposure]]'', playing a patient treated by Marilyn. 

Billingsley subsequently appeared in ''[[The X-Files]]'' episode "[[Three of a Kind (The X-Files)|Three of a Kind]]", as a friend of [[the Lone Gunmen]] who turns out to be a government spy. He played [[Bill Gates]] in a sketch on Seattle comedy show ''[[Almost Live!]]''. One of Billingsley's earliest film roles was in the 2001 [[made-for-television]] [[historical drama]] ''[[Just Ask My Children (2001 film)|Just Ask My Children]]'', in which he played corrupt lawyer Andrew Gines.

===2000s===
Billingsley played Dr. John Fallow in a ''[[The West Wing|West Wing]]'' episode that featured the [[Gall–Peters projection]] map ([[Somebody's Going to Emergency, Somebody's Going to Jail|season 2, episode 16]]). He was cast as Professor Miles Ballard in the short-lived television series ''[[The Others (American TV series)|The Others]]''; then as the Denobulan [[Phlox (Star Trek)|Doctor Phlox]] in the fifth live-action ''[[Star Trek]]'' series, ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'', which ran for four seasons. He also played himself in an episode of ''[[Roswell (TV series)|Roswell]]'' that used the ''Enterprise'' set. He also starred in the independent film ''Breathing Hard'' (2000) in the same year. In 2002, he was a guest star in an episode of ''[[Stargate SG-1]]'', playing a scientist who is also a [[Trekkie]], "worshipping at the altar of [[Gene Roddenberry|Roddenberry]]". He played a supporting role in the 2003 thriller ''[[Out of Time (2003 film)|Out of Time]]'' as medical examiner and best friend to the chief of police, played by [[Denzel Washington]].

Billingsley is well known to fans of the series ''[[Cold Case (TV series)|Cold Case]]'' for his guest appearance in the show's second season, playing [[serial killer]] [[List of Cold Case characters#George Marks (John Billingsley)|George Marks]], the only killer on the show to get away with murder. He reprised the role in the season finale, in which Marks was killed. He also appeared as a blunt-force victim in the first season of ''[[Six Feet Under (TV series)|Six Feet Under]]'', in the episode "[[The New Person]]".

Billingsley appeared in the first season of the series ''[[Prison Break]]'' as the mysterious [[Terrence Steadman]], brother of the [[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]], whose death is faked to frame [[Lincoln Burrows]] for murder. Soon after, he was cast as a regular on the series ''[[The Nine (TV series)|The Nine]]''. This left him unable to continue his role as Steadman, and he was replaced in the role by [[Jeff Perry (American actor)|Jeff Perry]]. In 2005, he played the voice of Trask in ''Ultimate Spider-Man''. In November 2006, Billingsley portrayed [[William Bradford (Plymouth governor)|William Bradford]] on two episodes of the podcast ''[[The Radio Adventures of Dr. Floyd]]''. In May 2007 he appeared on ''[[NCIS (TV series)|NCIS]]'' as a blind photographer in the episode, "In The Dark". He appeared in the seventh season of ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]'' as a recurring character. On October 8, 2007, he also made a guest appearance on ''[[Journeyman (TV series)|Journeyman]]'' as Alan Platt. Billingsley played Prof. Harry, a biologist, in the 2007 independent science fiction film ''[[The Man from Earth]]'', as well as the 2017 sequel ''[[The Man from Earth: Holocene]]''. He also made a guest appearance in an October 2007 episode of ''[[CSI: Crime Scene Investigation]]'', and in 2006 on the spinoff series ''[[CSI: NY]]''.

Billingsley appeared as Jacob Nolston in "Crash Into Me", a two-part, fourth-season episode of the TV drama ''[[Grey's Anatomy]]''.

Billingsley and his wife have also appeared as themselves on the [[HGTV]] series ''My House Is Worth What?'', in which a real estate expert toured their home and provided commentary for viewers before providing an appraisal.

In 2008, Billingsley had a supporting role in several episodes of the HBO series ''[[True Blood]]'' as [[coroner]] Mike Spencer. In May of that year, he guest starred as John Harris, the father of the Kiss-Me-Not Killer, in "Never Tell", an episode of ''Women's Murder Club''.

He appeared in the disaster film ''[[2012 (film)|2012]]'', which was released on November 13, 2009, as Professor Frederic West, an American scientist. He subsequently appeared on the ABC series ''[[Scrubs (season 9)|Scrubs]]'' in December 2009.

===2010s===
In August 2010, Billingsley guest starred in an episode of the [[TNT (U.S. TV network)|TNT]] series ''[[Leverage (American TV series)|Leverage]]'' as Coswell, the head of security at the Boston Museum of Art and Antiquities. In November that year he guest starred as amateur psychic Ellis Mars in "Red Moon", an episode of ''[[The Mentalist]]''.

In February 2011 Billingsley played Gidger in the [[Richard Greenberg]]'s play ''[[The Violet Hour]]'' in Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite web |first=Darin |last=Anthony |title=Now Is the Hour for All Good Artists |website=lastagetimes.com |date=2011-02-09 |url=http://www.lastagetimes.com/2011/02/now-is-the-hour-for-all-good-artists/ |access-date=2025-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161005083502/http://thisstage.la/2011/02/now-is-the-hour-for-all-good-artists/ |archive-date=2016-10-05 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In August 2011, Billingsley starred in an episode of the [[USA Network]] drama ''[[Suits (American TV series)|Suits]]'' as the company accountant who is being released for never finishing university.

In October 2012 Billingsley starred in the film ''[[Trade of Innocents]]'' alongside [[Dermot Mulroney]] and [[Mira Sorvino]].<ref>{{cite web |first=Sophia |last=Savage |title=Trade of Innocents' Chosen for Creative Coalition's Spotlight Initiative |website=[[IndieWire]] |date=2012-08-23 |url=https://www.indiewire.com/news/general-news/trade-of-innocents-chosen-for-creative-coalitions-spotlight-initiative-240238/ |access-date=2025-10-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120052428/https://www.indiewire.com/news/general-news/trade-of-innocents-chosen-for-creative-coalitions-spotlight-initiative-240238/ |archive-date=2025-01-20 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On February 12, 2013, a web comedy video was released on [[Yahoo! Screen]] under the title "Forwarders" that featured Billingsley as an Dr. Alan Cooper, a psychologist and expert on compulsive e-mail forwarding.<ref>{{cite AV media |author=<!--not stated or generic "Staff"--> |title=Forwarders |publisher=Principato-Young Entertainment |website=[[Yahoo! Screen]] |date=2013-02-11 |format=video and text |url=http://screen.yahoo.com/sketchy-forwarders-050000283.html |access-date=2025-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130213184340/http://screen.yahoo.com/sketchy-forwarders-050000283.html |archive-date=2013-02-13 |url-status=dead}}</ref> That same year he completed filming of the independent film ''Red Line''.<ref>{{cite web |author=<!--not stated or generic "Staff"--> |title=John Billingsley Remembers "Dear Doctor" |website=[[Star Trek]] |department=Star Trek: Enterprise |date=2013-01-23 |url=https://www.startrek.com/en-ca/news/john-billingsley-remembers-dear-doctor |access-date=2025-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251015043416/https://www.startrek.com/en-ca/news/john-billingsley-remembers-dear-doctor |archive-date=2025-10-15 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On January 7, 2014, CBS television premiered the science fiction drama ''[[Intelligence (American TV series)|Intelligence]]'', on which Billingsley played Dr. Shenandoah Cassidy, the inventor of an implantable microchip that acts as an interface between a human mind and electronic devices.<ref name=May20/>

In November 2014, Billingsley guest-starred in the CBS crime drama series, ''[[Hawaii Five-0 (2010 TV series)|Hawaii Five-0]]'', playing lawyer Eugene Goodman in the Season 5 episode, "Ka Hana Malu".

In May 2015, Billingsley appeared in the second season of the [[AMC (TV channel)|AMC]] period drama, ''[[Turn: Washington's Spies]]'', playing Samuel Townsend, father of American Revolutionary spy, [[Robert Townsend (spy)|Robert Townsend]]. He later returned to the role for the third season.

In July 2017, he appeared as Doctor Ben in the [[Showtime (TV network)|Showtime]] revival of ''[[Twin Peaks (season 3)|Twin Peaks]]''.

===2020s===
Billingsley voiced as Martin / "Clyde" in the 2020 [[science fiction]] [[horror podcast]] ''[[The Left Right Game]]''.

In 2024, Billingsley played [[Joseph Holt]] in the [[Apple TV+]] [[historical drama]] miniseries ''[[Manhunt (2024 TV series)|Manhunt]]''.

==Personal life==
Billingsley is married to fellow actress [[Bonita Friedericy]].<ref name=Occidental/><ref>{{cite AV media |title=John Billingsley and Bonita Friedericy Interview Part 2 |website=[[startrek.com]] |date=2014-11-05 |format=video |url=https://www.startrek.com/en-ca/videos/john-billingsley-and-bonita-friedericy-interview-part-2 |access-date=2025-10-14}}</ref> She first became interested in him after seeing him perform in a stage production of ''[[Great Expectations]]''.<ref>{{cite interview |interviewer-first=Laura |interviewer-last=Winert |subject-first1=Bonita |subject-last1=Friedericy |subject-link1= Bonita Friedericy |subject-first2=John |subject-last2=Billingsley |title=Actors' Dialogue - Bonita Friedericy & John Billingsley |magazine=[[Backstage (magazine)|Backstage]] |date=2013-03-25 |orig-date=July 27, 2004 |url=https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/actors-dialogue-bonita-friedericy-john-billingsley-47117/ |access-date=2025-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210118102506/https://www.backstage.com/magazine/article/actors-dialogue-bonita-friedericy-john-billingsley-47117/ |archive-date=2021-01-18 |url-status=live}}</ref> Friedericy appeared with Billingsley in "[[Regeneration (Star Trek: Enterprise)|Regeneration]]", a 2003 episode of ''[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]'' in which she played Rooney.<ref>{{cite episode|title=Regeneration|series=[[Star Trek: Enterprise]]|network=[[UPN]]|season=2|number=23|airdate=2003-05-07}}</ref> The couple has subsequently appeared in other productions together.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Kevin |last=Herren |title=Kevin Sorbo, John Billingsley and Bonita Friedericy Star in New Audio Drama to Benefit 'A World Fit For Kids' |publisher=MM Media LLC |date=2010-11-18 |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/kevin-sorbo-john-billingsley-and-bonita-friedericy-star-in-new-audio-drama-to-benefit-a-world-fit-for-kids-108931509.html |access-date=2025-10-14 |via=[[PR Newswire]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231216092031/https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/kevin-sorbo-john-billingsley-and-bonita-friedericy-star-in-new-audio-drama-to-benefit-a-world-fit-for-kids-108931509.html |archive-date=2023-12-16 |url-status=live}}</ref>
